title: Heart Attack (MI)
warn: ⛔ TIME IS MUSCLE — Irreversible damage begins within minutes. CALL 112 NOW.
steps: Call 112 immediately — do not drive yourself.
Have patient sit down and rest in a comfortable position (usually semi-reclined).
Loosen any tight clothing around neck and chest.
If conscious, not allergic, and no contraindications: give 325mg aspirin to chew (not swallow whole).
Stay calm and reassure the patient until EMS arrives.
Monitor breathing and pulse continuously.
If patient becomes unresponsive and stops breathing: begin CPR immediately.
Use AED as soon as available.
donot: Do NOT leave the patient alone.
Do NOT give food or water.
Do NOT allow patient to walk around unnecessarily.
Do NOT ignore atypical symptoms (especially in women, elderly, diabetics).
seek: Any suspected heart attack is an absolute emergency. Do not wait for symptoms to worsen.

title: Sudden Cardiac Arrest (SCA)
warn: ⛔ FATAL WITHIN MINUTES — The heart has stopped beating entirely or is quivering uselessly. Act instantly.
steps: Call 112 immediately and put the phone on speaker.
Send someone to get an AED (Automated External Defibrillator) immediately.
Begin chest compressions: Push hard and fast in the center of the chest (100-120 beats per minute, 2 inches deep).
Do not stop compressions unless applying the AED or someone else takes over.
Turn on the AED as soon as it arrives and follow the voice prompts.
Continue CPR and AED use until EMS arrives or the patient wakes up.
donot: Do NOT waste time checking for a pulse for more than 10 seconds.
Do NOT wait for the AED to arrive before starting compressions.
Do NOT stop compressions to give rescue breaths if you are not trained (Hands-Only CPR is highly effective).
seek: Requires continuous advanced life support and immediate hospital transport.

title: Unstable Angina
warn: ⚠️ Chest pain occurring at rest or escalating in severity. High risk of progressing to a full heart attack.
steps: Have the patient stop all physical activity and sit down in a comfortable position.
If the patient has prescribed Nitroglycerin, assist them in taking one dose (usually under the tongue).
Wait 5 minutes. If pain persists, call 112 and assist with a second dose if their doctor’s instructions allow.
Loosen tight clothing and keep the patient calm.
If they do not have Nitroglycerin, give 325mg of aspirin to chew (if no allergies).
donot: Do NOT let the patient drive themselves to the hospital.
Do NOT let them exercise or "walk off" the pain.
Do NOT give Nitroglycerin if the patient has taken erectile dysfunction medication in the last 48 hours (can cause a fatal blood pressure drop).
seek: EMS transport is required. Unstable angina is a warning sign of an impending heart attack.

title: Acute Heart Failure (Pulmonary Edema)
warn: ⛔ FLUID BACKUP IN LUNGS — The patient is effectively drowning in their own body fluids.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Sit the patient straight up with their legs dangling off the side of a bed or chair (this reduces fluid return to the heart and lungs).
Reassure the patient to reduce anxiety, which reduces the heart's oxygen demand.
If they have prescribed oxygen, administer it.
If they stop breathing, begin CPR.
donot: Do NOT lay the patient down flat (this will worsen the fluid buildup in the lungs and cause immediate distress).
Do NOT give them food or water.
Do NOT have them exert any physical effort.
seek: Requires immediate diuretics and positive pressure ventilation at an emergency facility.

title: Hypertensive Crisis
warn: ⚠️ BP > 180/120. Risk of stroke, heart attack, or organ damage is imminent.
steps: Have the patient sit down in a quiet, calm environment.
Check blood pressure again after 5 minutes of resting if a home monitor is available.
If BP remains >180/120 and is accompanied by chest pain, severe headache, back pain, numbness, or vision changes, call 112.
Ask if they have missed any doses of their regular blood pressure medication.
Keep the patient as relaxed as possible.
donot: Do NOT attempt to rapidly lower blood pressure at home with extra unprescribed medication (dropping it too fast can cause a stroke).
Do NOT let the patient walk around or stress themselves.
Do NOT ignore symptoms like chest pain or numbness, even if BP drops slightly.
seek: Requires controlled, gradual blood pressure reduction via IV medications in an ER setting.

title: Cardiogenic Shock
warn: ⛔ SEVERE PUMP FAILURE — The heart suddenly cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This often follows a severe heart attack.
Lay the patient flat on their back.
If there is no difficulty breathing, elevate their legs 12 inches to help blood return to the heart.
Keep the patient warm with a blanket to prevent heat loss.
Check for a pulse and breathing continuously. Be prepared to start CPR.
donot: Do NOT elevate the legs if the patient has chest pain or difficulty breathing (keep them sitting up instead).
Do NOT give anything by mouth.
Do NOT delay calling EMS; survival depends on rapid mechanical or chemical support for the heart.
seek: Absolute emergency. Requires critical care, potentially an intra-aortic balloon pump or inotropes.

title: Aortic Dissection
warn: ⛔ TEAR IN THE AORTA — Highly lethal. Pain is often described as sudden, severe, and "tearing" or "ripping" into the back.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This is a surgical emergency.
Keep the patient perfectly still to keep their blood pressure and heart rate as low as possible.
Have them lie in the most comfortable position they can find.
Do not allow any physical exertion.
Gather their medication list, especially noting any blood thinners or blood pressure medications.
donot: Do NOT give aspirin (this can worsen internal bleeding).
Do NOT allow the patient to walk to the ambulance.
Do NOT mistake the pain for simple back pain if it comes on suddenly with maximal intensity.
seek: Immediate transport to a trauma center or hospital with cardiothoracic surgery capabilities.

title: Cardiac Tamponade
warn: ⛔ HEART COMPRESSION — Fluid fills the sac around the heart, physically preventing it from beating.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Often caused by trauma (steering wheel impact, stab wound) or severe infection/cancer.
Lay the patient flat to maximize blood flow to the brain.
Monitor for Beck's Triad: low blood pressure, bulging neck veins, and muffled/quiet heart sounds.
Provide supplemental oxygen if available and trained.
Prepare for CPR if the patient loses consciousness and pulse.
donot: Do NOT give anything to eat or drink.
Do NOT move the patient excessively, especially if trauma is the suspected cause.
Do NOT wait to see if they improve; the fluid must be drained mechanically.
seek: Requires an emergency pericardiocentesis (needle inserted by a doctor to drain the fluid).

title: Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT)
warn: ⚠️ Heart rate suddenly jumps to 150-220+ bpm at rest. Can cause fainting or heart failure if prolonged.
steps: Have the patient sit or lie down to prevent fainting.
Instruct them to try a Vagal Maneuver: Have them bear down hard (like having a bowel movement) for 10-15 seconds.
Alternatively, have them blow forcefully into a plastic syringe (plunger removed) or a narrow straw.
If the heart rate does not return to normal within a few minutes, or if they experience chest pain or dizziness, call 112.
Monitor their pulse and breathing.
donot: Do NOT attempt carotid massage (rubbing the neck) unless you are a trained medical professional (can cause a stroke).
Do NOT have them exercise to "reset" the heart.
Do NOT ignore symptoms if they have a history of structural heart disease.
seek: If vagal maneuvers fail, ER treatment with medication (Adenosine) or electrical cardioversion is required.

title: Symptomatic Bradycardia
warn: ⚠️ Heart rate drops dangerously low (often <50 bpm), depriving the brain and body of oxygen.
steps: Have the patient lie down immediately to prevent injury from fainting.
Check for symptoms of poor perfusion: confusion, severe dizziness, chest pain, or pale/sweaty skin.
Call 112 if these symptoms are present.
Review their recent medications (beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers often cause this).
Elevate their legs slightly if they feel faint but have no breathing difficulty.
donot: Do NOT allow the patient to stand up quickly.
Do NOT give them caffeine to "speed up" the heart (it is not effective for electrical blocks).
Do NOT delay calling EMS if they lose consciousness.
seek: Requires EMS transport. May require emergency pacing or medications like Atropine.

title: Atrial Fibrillation with RVR
warn: ⚠️ Upper chambers quiver chaotically, driving the lower chambers to beat too fast (Rapid Ventricular Response). High stroke risk.
steps: Have the patient rest in a comfortable seated position.
Encourage slow, deep, calming breaths.
Assess for stroke symptoms (FAST: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time). Afib causes blood clots.
Call 112 if they experience severe shortness of breath, chest pain, or if this is their first time experiencing these symptoms.
If they have prescribed "pill-in-the-pocket" medication for Afib, assist them in taking it.
donot: Do NOT give aspirin unless advised by a doctor (many Afib patients are already on stronger blood thinners).
Do NOT panic, as anxiety will increase the heart rate further.
Do NOT let them engage in strenuous activity.
seek: Needs ER evaluation to slow the heart rate and assess the need for blood thinners to prevent stroke.

title: Ventricular Tachycardia (V-Tach)
warn: ⛔ LETHAL ARRHYTHMIA — The lower chambers beat so fast they cannot fill with blood. Can deteriorate into V-Fib instantly.
steps: Call 112 IMMEDIATELY. This is a pre-arrest or arrest state.
Check responsiveness and pulse. V-Tach can occur with or without a pulse.
If pulseless and unresponsive: Begin CPR immediately and get an AED.
If awake and pulsing but dizzy/chest pain: Keep them lying down, do not let them move, and wait for EMS.
Have an AED nearby and turned on, even if they are awake, as they can lose their pulse at any second.
donot: Do NOT let the patient stand up or walk under any circumstances.
Do NOT delay calling EMS even if the patient says they "feel okay" but their heart is racing uncontrollably.
Do NOT give food or drink.
seek: Requires immediate electrical cardioversion (shock) or antiarrhythmic drugs by paramedics/ER staff.

title: Acute Pericarditis
warn: ⚠️ Inflammation of the heart sac. Pain mimics a heart attack but changes with body position.
steps: Have the patient sit up and lean forward (this relieves the pressure of the heart against the inflamed sac, reducing pain).
Ask about recent viral infections (a common cause).
Call 112 or go to the ER to rule out a heart attack (it is nearly impossible to distinguish the two without an EKG).
Keep the patient calm and at rest.
donot: Do NOT force the patient to lie flat if it causes them severe pain.
Do NOT assume it is just a muscle strain.
Do NOT give pain medication before medical evaluation, as it may mask symptoms.
seek: Must be evaluated by a doctor with an EKG and echocardiogram to rule out MI and check for fluid buildup.

title: Acute Myocarditis
warn: ⚠️ Viral infection directly attacks the heart muscle, weakening its ability to pump.
steps: Have the patient cease all physical exertion immediately (exertion increases the risk of fatal arrhythmias in myocarditis).
Monitor for signs of heart failure (shortness of breath, swelling in legs) or irregular heartbeats.
Call 112 if the patient complains of chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or fainting.
Ensure the patient rests completely in a seated or semi-reclined position.
donot: Do NOT allow the patient to play sports or exercise (can trigger sudden cardiac death).
Do NOT ignore persistent chest pain following a severe flu or viral illness.
Do NOT attempt to treat at home with over-the-counter cold medicines.
seek: Requires hospitalization for monitoring, as the heart muscle is inflamed and prone to sudden failure.

title: Infective Endocarditis
warn: ⚠️ Bacteria attach to the heart valves, destroying them and throwing infectious clots into the bloodstream.
steps: Monitor for a combination of unexplained high fever, chills, new fatigue, and aching joints.
Look for tiny red/purple spots on the skin, whites of the eyes, or inside the mouth (petechiae).
Look for painful red bumps on the pads of fingers/toes (Osler nodes).
Seek emergency medical care, especially if the patient has a history of heart valve disease, IV drug use, or a recent dental procedure.
Keep the patient comfortable and hydrated.
donot: Do NOT ignore a persistent, unexplained fever in someone with known congenital heart defects.
Do NOT assume it is a standard flu if accompanied by unusual skin spots or sudden shortness of breath.
Do NOT delay seeking a blood culture and echocardiogram.
seek: Requires weeks of IV antibiotics and potentially emergency valve replacement surgery.

title: Commotio Cordis
warn: ⛔ INSTANT CARDIAC ARREST — Caused by a sudden, blunt impact to the chest precisely during the heart's electrical cycle.
steps: Recognize it instantly: A person takes a hit to the chest (e.g., baseball, hockey puck, martial arts strike) and collapses unconscious immediately or within seconds.
Call 112 immediately.
Start CPR immediately. There is no structural damage, but the electrical system has short-circuited into V-Fib.
Get an AED and use it as fast as possible. This is highly reversible if shocked within the first 3 minutes.
Continue CPR until the AED arrives and between shocks.
donot: Do NOT assume they just had "the wind knocked out of them" if they remain unresponsive for more than a few seconds.
Do NOT wait to see if they wake up.
Do NOT stop CPR unless the AED is analyzing or the patient wakes up.
seek: Absolute emergency requiring immediate defibrillation.

title: Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy (Broken Heart Syndrome)
warn: ⚠️ Severe emotional or physical stress causes rapid, temporary severe weakening of the heart muscle.
steps: Treat exactly like a classic Heart Attack (MI), as symptoms are identical (chest pain, shortness of breath).
Call 112 immediately.
Have the patient sit and rest.
If no allergies, give 325mg aspirin to chew.
Remove them from the source of emotional or physical stress if possible.
Reassure them constantly.
donot: Do NOT dismiss their pain as an "anxiety attack" or "panic attack," even if they just received terrible news.
Do NOT delay calling EMS (it can cause lethal arrhythmias or cardiogenic shock just like a regular MI).
Do NOT let them walk or exert themselves.
seek: Requires ER evaluation with an EKG and angiogram to differentiate it from a blocked artery.

title: ICD Malfunction (Repeated Shocks)
warn: ⚠️ The patient's Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator (ICD) is delivering inappropriate, repeated shocks.
steps: Have the patient lie down (a shock can cause them to fall and injure themselves).
Call 112 immediately if the device has shocked them more than once, or if they feel unwell after a single shock.
Reassure the patient (the shocks are extremely painful and terrifying).
If the patient becomes unconscious and pulseless, perform CPR (you will not be harmed by touching them if the device shocks).
Keep the patient calm to lower heart rate.
donot: Do NOT place a magnet over the device unless explicitly instructed by a physician or 112 dispatcher (it turns off the shocking function, leaving them unprotected if they actually need it).
Do NOT touch the patient precisely when you feel the muscle twitch from a shock, though it is not dangerous to you.
Do NOT let them drive to the hospital.
seek: Requires immediate interrogation of the device by a cardiologist and potentially reprogramming.

title: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)
warn: ⚠️ A blood clot in a deep vein (usually the leg). If it breaks loose, it travels to the lungs (Pulmonary Embolism) and can be fatal.
steps: Assess for symptoms: one leg is suddenly swollen, red, warm to the touch, and painful (like a severe cramp).
Keep the patient seated or lying down to prevent the clot from dislodging.
Call a doctor immediately or go to the ER.
If they suddenly develop chest pain, shortness of breath, or cough up blood, call 112 immediately (the clot has moved to the lungs).
donot: Do NOT massage or rub the painful area (this can dislodge the clot and send it to the heart/lungs).
Do NOT apply a heating pad.
Do NOT have the patient walk around to "stretch out" the cramp.
seek: Requires urgent ultrasound and blood-thinning medication.

title: Prinzmetal’s (Variant) Angina
warn: ⚠️ A sudden spasm in a coronary artery temporarily blocks blood flow, often occurring at rest or in the middle of the night.
steps: Have the patient sit up and remain calm.
If they have prescribed Nitroglycerin, assist them in taking a dose.
Call 112 if the pain does not subside after 5 minutes or one dose of Nitroglycerin.
Treat the situation seriously, as prolonged spasm can cause a real heart attack or fatal arrhythmia.
Keep the patient warm, as cold exposure can trigger spasms.
donot: Do NOT assume it is indigestion just because it happens at night.
Do NOT let them take triptans (migraine meds) if they have this condition, as it worsens spasms.
Do NOT wait until morning to see if it improves.
seek: Requires ER evaluation to administer calcium channel blockers or nitrates to relieve the spasm.

title: Torsades de Pointes
warn: ⛔ SPECIFIC LETHAL ARRHYTHMIA — A specific type of V-Tach often triggered by medication interactions or low magnesium.
steps: Call 112 immediately. The patient will likely collapse and become unresponsive.
Start CPR immediately if the patient is unconscious and pulseless.
Use an AED as soon as it is available.
If the patient wakes up between episodes, keep them lying completely flat and absolutely still.
Collect all pill bottles (especially antibiotics, anti-nausea, or psychiatric meds), as many drugs prolong the QT interval and cause this.
donot: Do NOT give the patient anything to eat or drink.
Do NOT let them sit up or walk.
Do NOT delay defibrillation if an AED is present.
seek: Requires IV Magnesium Sulfate, defibrillation, and withdrawal of the offending medication in the ICU.

title: Choking — Adult
warn: 🚨 If patient CANNOT speak, cough, or breathe — Act INSTANTLY.
steps: Ask "Are you choking?" — If they can cough forcefully, encourage coughing.
If severe (silent, cannot breathe): stand behind patient, lean them forward slightly.
Give 5 firm back blows with heel of hand between shoulder blades.
Give 5 abdominal thrusts: make fist above navel, pull sharply in and upward.
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until object expelled or patient loses consciousness.
If unconscious: lower to floor, call 112, begin CPR. Each time you open airway to give breaths, look for object.
donot: Do NOT perform blind finger sweeps.
Do NOT give abdominal thrusts to pregnant women — use chest thrusts instead.
seek: If object not cleared, patient loses consciousness, or remains in distress.

title: Choking — Infant
warn: 🚨 Never use abdominal thrusts on infants under 1 year.
steps: Hold infant face-down on your forearm, supporting head.
Give 5 back blows between shoulder blades with heel of hand.
Turn infant face-up, supporting head.
Give 5 chest thrusts with 2 fingers on lower half of sternum.
Repeat until object expelled or infant becomes unconscious.
If unconscious: begin infant CPR (30:2 with 2 fingers), look in mouth before giving breaths.
donot: Do NOT perform abdominal (Heimlich) thrusts on infants.
Do NOT shake infant.
seek: Immediately — call 112 while performing rescue.

title: Pulmonary Embolism (PE)
warn: ⛔ SUDDEN BLOCKAGE IN THE LUNGS — A blood clot has traveled to the pulmonary artery, cutting off oxygen exchange.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Have the patient sit upright in a comfortable position to ease breathing.
Keep the patient as calm and still as possible to reduce oxygen demand.
Ask if they have a history of DVT (blood clots in legs), recent surgery, or long flights.
Monitor for signs of shock or loss of consciousness.
Be prepared to begin CPR if they stop breathing and lose a pulse.
donot: Do NOT allow the patient to walk or exert themselves under any circumstances.
Do NOT dismiss sudden, unexplained shortness of breath, even if the patient is young and healthy.
Do NOT lay the patient flat.
seek: Absolute emergency requiring immediate transport for blood thinners or surgical clot removal.

title: Tension Pneumothorax
warn: ⛔ TRAPPED AIR COMPRESSING THE HEART — Air enters the chest cavity but cannot escape, crushing the lungs and heart.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Note if the patient has suffered recent chest trauma.
Watch for severe, progressive difficulty breathing, distended neck veins, and a shift of the windpipe (trachea) to one side.
Have the patient sit up if conscious, or lie them on their INJURED side if they must lie down (to let the healthy lung expand).
Provide supplemental oxygen if you are trained and equipped.
If they become unresponsive, begin CPR.
donot: Do NOT attempt needle decompression unless you are a specifically trained medical professional (paramedic/doctor).
Do NOT tightly wrap or bind the chest with bandages.
Do NOT assume they are hyperventilating from anxiety.
seek: Requires immediate needle decompression and chest tube placement by advanced medical personnel.

title: Acute COPD Exacerbation
warn: ⚠️ Severe worsening of chronic lung disease, often triggered by infection or pollution.
steps: Help the patient sit up and lean forward slightly (tripod position) to help them breathe.
Assist them in using their prescribed rescue inhalers or nebulizer treatments.
Encourage pursed-lip breathing (breathe in through nose, blow out slowly through pinched lips).
If on home oxygen, ensure it is flowing, but do not aggressively turn up the flow rate without medical advice.
Call 112 if they are confused, severely struggling for air, or their lips/fingers are turning blue.
donot: Do NOT lay the patient down.
Do NOT withhold their prescribed rescue inhaler.
Do NOT crank up their oxygen to max flow (COPD patients rely on low oxygen levels to trigger their breathing drive; too much can stop their breathing).
seek: Needs medical evaluation for systemic steroids, antibiotics, and controlled oxygen therapy.

title: Status Asthmaticus
warn: ⛔ EXTREME ASTHMA ATTACK — Standard medications are failing. The airways are critically tight.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This is a life-threatening escalation of asthma.
Continue administering the rescue inhaler (Albuterol) via spacer every few minutes while waiting for EMS.
Keep the patient sitting upright and try to keep them calm to reduce oxygen consumption.
Listen to their chest: if previous loud wheezing suddenly stops but they are still struggling to breathe ("silent chest"), the airway is almost completely closed.
Prepare for CPR if the patient becomes exhausted and stops breathing.
donot: Do NOT assume "no wheezing" means they are getting better; it often means no air is moving at all.
Do NOT make the patient walk to a car; have the ambulance come to them.
Do NOT give them sedatives or anti-anxiety meds.
seek: Requires immediate IV steroids, continuous nebulization, and potentially intubation.

title: Epiglottitis
warn: ⛔ SUDDEN AIRWAY CLOSURE — The flap covering the windpipe is infected and severely swollen.
steps: Call 112 IMMEDIATELY. This is highly lethal, especially in children.
Keep the patient absolutely calm. Do not make them cry or agitate them (crying can force the swollen epiglottis to snap shut permanently).
Allow them to sit in whatever position is most comfortable (usually leaning forward, chin out, drooling).
Prepare to perform CPR if they stop breathing, though rescue breaths may not pass the obstruction.
donot: Do NOT look inside their mouth or throat (inserting a tongue depressor or finger can trigger sudden, complete airway spasm and closure).
Do NOT try to force them to lie down.
Do NOT try to feed them or give them water (they cannot swallow).
seek: Requires immediate transport via EMS for emergency airway management (intubation or tracheostomy) by an anesthesiologist or surgeon.

title: Severe Croup
warn: ⚠️ Viral infection causing swelling in the windpipe and voice box, mostly in toddlers.
steps: Keep the child as calm as possible (crying worsens the swelling and breathing difficulty).
Listen for a harsh, barking "seal-like" cough and a high-pitched whistling sound when they breathe IN (stridor).
Take the child into a bathroom, turn on the hot shower to create thick steam, and sit with them for 10-15 minutes.
Alternatively, take them out into cool night air, which can shrink the swollen tissues.
Call 112 if the child has stridor while resting quietly, is struggling to breathe, or turns pale/blue.
donot: Do NOT panic, as the child will mimic your anxiety.
Do NOT give cough medicines or sedatives.
Do NOT force the child to lie flat.
seek: If symptoms do not improve with cool air or steam, ER treatment with steroids and nebulized epinephrine is needed.

title: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
warn: ⛔ MASSIVE LUNG INFLAMMATION — The lungs fill with fluid due to systemic injury or severe infection.
steps: Call 112 immediately. ARDS usually develops in patients already ill from pneumonia, sepsis, or severe trauma.
Observe for rapid, labored breathing, extreme fatigue, and blue discoloration of skin/lips.
Keep the patient at strict rest; no physical exertion.
Position them seated upright to maximize whatever lung function remains.
Administer high-flow oxygen if available and trained.
donot: Do NOT attempt to treat at home with inhalers; they will not work for fluid-filled alveoli.
Do NOT lay the patient on their back.
Do NOT offer food or fluids.
seek: Requires ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, and often specialized positioning (proning).

title: Carbon Monoxide (CO) Poisoning
warn: ⛔ SILENT KILLER — Odorless gas that replaces oxygen in the blood, suffocating the body from the inside.
steps: IMMEDIATELY evacuate everyone from the building to fresh air. Do not search for the source.
Call 112 from safely outside the environment.
Assess victims for headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion, or loss of consciousness.
If a victim is unconscious and not breathing, begin CPR in the fresh air environment.
Administer 100% pure oxygen as soon as EMS arrives.
donot: Do NOT ignore a ringing carbon monoxide detector.
Do NOT stay in the house to open windows; get out first.
Do NOT assume someone is okay just because their skin looks pink or "cherry red" (this is a late and dangerous sign of CO poisoning, not a sign of health).
seek: Victims require high-flow oxygen therapy or hyperbaric oxygen therapy at a hospital to clear the CO from their blood.

title: Smoke Inhalation Injury
warn: ⛔ AIRWAY SWELLING — Heat and toxic chemicals from smoke can cause the airway to swell shut hours after the fire.
steps: Move the victim to fresh air immediately while ensuring your own safety.
Call 112.
Check the victim’s face: look for singed nasal hairs, soot in the mouth/nose, or burns around the face (high risk for airway burns).
Listen to their voice; if they are hoarse or have a harsh cough, their airway is swelling.
Keep them sitting upright and loosen tight clothing.
Monitor breathing constantly.
donot: Do NOT assume they are fine just because they escaped the fire; swelling can peak 12-24 hours later.
Do NOT give them water to drink if they are coughing severely or have a hoarse voice (choking hazard).
Do NOT delay calling EMS.
seek: Requires immediate ER evaluation for potential early intubation before the airway swells completely shut.

title: Open Pneumothorax (Sucking Chest Wound)
warn: ⛔ LUNG DEFLATION — A hole in the chest wall allows air to enter the chest cavity from the outside, collapsing the lung.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Locate the wound and expose the chest. Listen for a "sucking" or "hissing" sound as they breathe.
Immediately cover the hole with a gloved hand to stop air from entering.

Apply an occlusive dressing (e.g., a chest seal, plastic wrap, or a plastic bag) and tape it down on THREE sides. Leave the bottom untaped to act as a one-way valve (air escapes out, but doesn't get sucked in).
Check the patient’s back for an exit wound and seal that one completely.
Keep the patient seated or lying on their injured side.
donot: Do NOT remove an impaled object.
Do NOT tape the dressing on all four sides unless it is a commercial vented chest seal (doing so can cause a fatal tension pneumothorax).
Do NOT pack gauze INTO the chest wound.
seek: Requires emergency surgical repair and a chest tube.

title: Flail Chest
warn: ⚠️ MULTIPLE BROKEN RIBS — A segment of the rib cage has detached and moves in the opposite direction of normal breathing.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Usually caused by severe blunt trauma (car crash, high fall).
Observe the chest: if one section sinks IN when they breathe in, and pops OUT when they breathe out, they have a flail chest.
Have the patient rest in the most comfortable position, usually sitting up.
You can have the patient hold a bulky pillow firmly against the injured area to splint the ribs and reduce pain while breathing.
Provide oxygen if available and monitor for signs of a collapsing lung.
donot: Do NOT wrap the chest tightly with tape or bandages (this restricts all breathing and leads to pneumonia/hypoxia).
Do NOT press down hard on the broken segment.
Do NOT lay the patient on their uninjured side.
seek: Requires trauma center evaluation for pain management, respiratory support, and potential surgical fixation of the ribs.

title: High-Altitude Pulmonary Edema (HAPE)
warn: ⛔ FLUID IN LUNGS FROM ALTITUDE — Life-threatening altitude sickness usually occurring above 8,000 feet.
steps: DESCEND IMMEDIATELY. This is the only definitive treatment. Descend at least 1,000 to 3,000 feet as quickly and safely as possible.
Minimize physical exertion for the patient; carry them if possible or have them walk slowly.
Administer supplemental oxygen if available.
If descent is impossible (e.g., storm), use a portable hyperbaric chamber (Gamow bag) if equipped.
Keep the patient warm.
donot: Do NOT wait to see if they get better at the current altitude.
Do NOT let them sleep at the current altitude if they have symptoms (extreme fatigue, breathlessness at rest, coughing up pink frothy fluid).
Do NOT give alcohol or sleeping pills.
seek: Requires descent, oxygen, and potentially medications like Nifedipine. Fatal if left at high altitude.

title: Submersion Injury (Near-Drowning)
warn: ⛔ OXYGEN DEPRIVATION — Even small amounts of water aspirated into the lungs can cause severe respiratory failure.
steps: Safely remove the person from the water.
Check for responsiveness and normal breathing.
If unresponsive and not breathing, begin CPR immediately. For drowning, start with 2 RESCUE BREATHS, then 30 compressions.
If they are breathing and unconscious, place them in the recovery position (on their side) to allow water and vomit to drain.
Call 112 immediately, even if they wake up and seem fine.
Keep the patient warm to prevent hypothermia.
donot: Do NOT attempt the Heimlich maneuver to "pump" water out of the lungs (it wastes time and causes vomiting).
Do NOT assume they are safe if they wake up and cough up the water; "secondary drowning" (pulmonary edema) can occur hours later.
Do NOT enter dangerous water to save them if you are not a trained rescuer; throw them a flotation device.
seek: All submersion victims must be evaluated in an ER, as water washes away lung surfactant, causing delayed respiratory failure.

title: Toxic Chemical Inhalation (e.g., Chlorine, Ammonia)
warn: ⛔ LUNG BURN — Inhaled chemicals react with lung moisture to create acids or bases, burning the respiratory tract.
steps: Evacuate the area immediately. Move upwind and uphill from the chemical source.
Call 112 and request Fire/Hazmat and EMS.
Remove any clothing that may be contaminated with the chemical (if safe to do so) and wash skin.
If the patient’s eyes are burning, flush them with water.
Keep the patient calm and at rest to minimize breathing depth and rate.
Administer oxygen if available and trained.
donot: Do NOT attempt a rescue in a hazardous environment without Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA). You will become a victim.
Do NOT make the patient exert themselves.
Do NOT perform mouth-to-mouth CPR if they have toxic chemicals on their face or in their lungs (use a bag-valve-mask if available, or do hands-only).
seek: Requires specialized decontamination and critical care for chemical burns to the lungs.

title: Hyperventilation Syndrome
warn: ⚠️ Rapid breathing blowing off too much CO2, leading to tingling hands, dizziness, and muscle spasms.
steps: Stay calm and reassure the patient. Panic is driving the rapid breathing.
Move them to a quiet, less stimulating environment.
Coach their breathing: Have them breathe in for 4 seconds, hold for 2, and breathe out for 4 seconds.
If they cannot slow their breathing, have them breathe through pursed lips or through one nostril.
Call 112 if breathing does not return to normal after 15 minutes, if they have chest pain, or if you are unsure it is just anxiety.
donot: Do NOT have them breathe into a paper bag (this is outdated advice and can be dangerous if they are actually having a heart attack or asthma attack).
Do NOT tell them to "just calm down" (this usually increases panic).
Do NOT ignore chest pain, as hyperventilation can accompany a heart attack.
seek: If symptoms persist or are accompanied by chest pain or fainting, seek ER evaluation to rule out PE or cardiac issues.

title: Spontaneous Pneumothorax
warn: ⚠️ A small blister (bleb) on the lung bursts without warning, causing the lung to partially collapse.
steps: Recognize the sudden onset of sharp, stabbing chest pain on one side, accompanied by shortness of breath.
Have the patient sit in a comfortable upright position.
Keep the patient calm to slow their breathing rate.
Call 112 or transport to the nearest emergency department.
Monitor vital signs.
donot: Do NOT let the patient exert themselves.
Do NOT mistake it for a muscle spasm if the shortness of breath persists.
Do NOT give them anything to eat or drink in case they need surgery.
seek: Requires chest X-ray. Small collapses may heal on their own with oxygen; larger ones require a chest tube.

title: Severe Pertussis (Whooping Cough)
warn: ⚠️ Violent, uncontrollable coughing fits that can completely exhaust the patient and prevent them from taking a breath.
steps: During a coughing fit, stay with the person and ensure they are seated safely so they do not fall.
If it is an infant, hold them upright or slightly forward to help clear mucus.
Wait for the coughing fit to end; there is little you can do to stop it mid-spasm.
Call 112 immediately if the patient turns blue, pauses in their breathing for a long time (apnea), or vomits repeatedly from coughing.
Keep the environment free of irritants like smoke or strong odors.
donot: Do NOT try to put your fingers in their mouth to clear mucus.
Do NOT give over-the-counter cough suppressants (they do not work for pertussis and can be dangerous for babies).
Do NOT expose infants to anyone with a lingering cough.
seek: Infants often require hospitalization for oxygen and suctioning. Antibiotics are needed to stop contagion.

title: Laryngospasm
warn: ⛔ TEMPORARY AIRWAY CLOSURE — The vocal cords suddenly spasm and shut completely, usually triggered by irritation or reflux.
steps: Stay completely calm. This is terrifying but usually breaks on its own within 30-60 seconds.
Instruct the patient to try to take slow, gentle sniffs of air through their nose, rather than gasping hard through their mouth.
Have them sit upright.
If the spasm does not break and the patient loses consciousness, the muscles will usually relax. Begin CPR immediately with rescue breaths.
Call 112 if the spasm lasts longer than a minute, if they pass out, or if their lips turn blue.
donot: Do NOT panic; telling them to gasp for air will make the cords lock tighter.
Do NOT try the Heimlich maneuver unless you are certain they choked on a foreign object (laryngospasm has no object to dislodge).
Do NOT give them water to "wash it down" while they are spasming.
seek: If it resolves quickly, follow up with a doctor. If it persists or causes unconsciousness, EMS is required.

title: Massive Aspiration Pneumonitis
warn: ⛔ STOMACH ACID IN LUNGS — Vomiting while unconscious or heavily intoxicated leads to inhalation of stomach acid, destroying lung tissue.
steps: PREVENTION: Always place unconscious, breathing patients in the recovery position (on their side).
If aspiration has just occurred, immediately turn the patient on their side to drain remaining vomit from the mouth.
Use a cloth or fingers to rapidly sweep visible vomit out of the cheeks/mouth.
Call 112 immediately.
If the patient stops breathing, clear the airway as best as possible and begin CPR.
Provide oxygen if available.
donot: Do NOT leave an unconscious, intoxicated person sleeping on their back.
Do NOT pour water into their mouth to "clean it out."
Do NOT wait to see if they develop a fever; acid burns the lungs instantly.
seek: Requires immediate emergency transport. They will likely need intubation and intensive care.

title: Pleurisy (Pleuritis)
warn: ⚠️ Inflammation of the lung lining causes severe, sharp, stabbing pain exactly when taking a deep breath.
steps: Have the patient rest in a comfortable position. They may find relief by lying exactly ON the painful side (this splints the chest wall and limits movement).
Instruct them to take shallow breaths if deep breaths are agonizing, but encourage them to periodically try to breathe deeper to prevent pneumonia.
Call a doctor for evaluation.
Go to the ER or call 112 if the pain is accompanied by high fever, coughing up blood, or extreme shortness of breath.
donot: Do NOT assume it is a heart attack if the pain ONLY happens during a breath or cough (heart attack pain is usually constant). However, if in doubt, treat as cardiac.
Do NOT tightly wrap the chest.
Do NOT ignore it if the patient has a history of cancer, DVT, or recent surgery.
seek: Needs medical evaluation (often an X-ray) to rule out pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, or tuberculosis.

title: Severe Hemorrhage
warn: ⛔ Exsanguination (lethal blood loss) can occur in 3-5 minutes from major arterial injury.
steps: Apply immediate, firm direct pressure with clean cloth or gauze.
Maintain constant pressure — do NOT lift cloth to check (add layers if soaking).
Elevate injured extremity above heart level if possible.
For limb bleeding not controlled by direct pressure: apply tourniquet 2-3 inches above wound.
Write time tourniquet applied on patient.
Pack deep wounds with gauze and apply pressure.
Call 112.
Treat for shock: lay patient flat, elevate legs, keep warm.
donot: Do NOT remove a tourniquet once applied.
Do NOT apply tourniquet over a joint.
seek: All severe bleeding requires immediate medical attention.

title: Traumatic Brain Injury
warn: ⚠️ Deteriorating neuro signs = rapid intracranial pressure increase. Call 112.
steps: Keep patient still; stabilize cervical spine if high mechanism.
Call 112 for moderate/severe TBI.
Assess AVPU scale: Alert, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive.
Control scalp bleeding with gentle pressure.
Keep head slightly elevated (30°) if no spinal injury concern.
Do NOT give medications.
Monitor pupils every 5 minutes.
Signs of worsening: unequal pupils, vomiting, worsening headache, seizures.
donot: Do NOT move patient if spinal injury possible.
Do NOT apply direct pressure to depressed skull fracture.
seek: Any loss of consciousness, amnesia, repeated vomiting, or worsening symptoms.

title: Spinal Injury
warn: ⚠️ Incorrect movement can cause permanent paralysis. Minimize motion.
steps: If spinal injury is possible (MOI, neck/back pain, neuro symptoms): do NOT move patient.
Stabilize head and neck in neutral position with hands.
Call 112 immediately.
If patient must be moved (fire, drowning): use logroll with sufficient personnel to maintain spinal alignment.
Monitor breathing — if compromised, airway management takes priority.
donot: Do NOT flex or rotate head/neck.
Do NOT give patient anything by mouth.
seek: Immediate — all suspected spinal injuries are emergencies.

title: Traumatic Amputation
warn: ⛔ MASSIVE BLOOD LOSS — Stop the bleeding first. Preserving the amputated part is the secondary priority.
steps: Ensure scene safety. Call 112 immediately.
Apply direct, heavy pressure to the stump.
If bleeding continues from an arm or leg, apply a tourniquet 2-3 inches above the wound. Tighten until bleeding completely stops.
Note the exact time the tourniquet was applied.
Recover the amputated part if possible. Rinse it gently with clean water (do not scrub).
Wrap the part in a slightly moist, sterile gauze or clean cloth.
Place the wrapped part in a watertight plastic bag, then place that bag into another container with ice and water.
donot: Do NOT place the amputated part directly on ice or in water (freezing destroys the tissue).
Do NOT remove the tourniquet once it is applied.
Do NOT delay transport to search for a missing part if the patient is bleeding to death.
seek: Requires level 1 trauma center and microvascular surgery for replantation.

title: Open (Compound) Fracture
warn: ⛔ HIGH INFECTION & BLEEDING RISK — The bone has pierced the skin, exposing the deep tissue to the outside environment.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Control bleeding by applying gentle pressure AROUND the bone, not directly on it.
Cover the entire wound and exposed bone with a sterile, moist dressing if available, or the cleanest cloth you have.
Immobilize the joint above and below the fracture site.
Keep the patient warm to prevent shock.
donot: Do NOT attempt to push the bone back into the skin.
Do NOT try to clean or wash the wound (this can push debris deeper into the bone marrow).
Do NOT attempt to straighten an angulated open fracture.
seek: Requires emergency orthopedic surgery to clean the bone (debridement) and set the fracture.

title: Severe Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)
warn: ⛔ RISING BRAIN PRESSURE — Internal bleeding in the skull crushes brain tissue. Symptoms can rapidly worsen minutes or hours after impact.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Assume a spinal injury and stabilize the neck manually.
Monitor the patient’s level of consciousness constantly.
Look for warning signs: unequal pupil size, clear fluid leaking from nose/ears, projectile vomiting, or posturing (stiffening of arms/legs).
If the patient must vomit, roll their entire body (log-roll) as a single unit to the side to keep the airway clear without twisting the neck.
Keep the patient’s head elevated about 30 degrees if possible, without bending the neck.
donot: Do NOT apply direct pressure to a bleeding head wound if you suspect a skull fracture (you could push bone into the brain).
Do NOT move the patient unless they are in immediate danger.
Do NOT give the patient anything to eat, drink, or any pain medication.
seek: Requires immediate CT scan and potential emergency neurosurgery to relieve intracranial pressure.

title: Abdominal Evisceration
warn: ⛔ EXPOSED INTERNAL ORGANS — High risk of massive infection, tissue death, and severe shock.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Have the patient lie flat on their back with their knees bent (this relaxes the abdominal muscles).
Cover the exposed organs with a sterile dressing moistened with clean, warm water or saline.
Cover the moist dressing with an occlusive dressing (plastic wrap, plastic bag, or aluminum foil) to trap the moisture and heat.
Treat the patient for shock by keeping them warm with blankets.
donot: Do NOT try to push the organs back into the abdominal cavity.
Do NOT apply direct pressure to the exposed organs.
Do NOT use dry dressings or toilet paper/tissues that will stick to or shred on the organs.
seek: Immediate trauma surgery is required to clean the organs, return them to the body, and repair the abdominal wall.

title: Blunt Force Internal Bleeding
warn: ⛔ INVISIBLE HEMORRHAGE — The patient can bleed to death entirely inside their own body cavity (abdomen or chest).
steps: Call 112 immediately if the patient has suffered high-energy trauma (e.g., steering wheel impact, high fall).
Monitor for signs of shock: pale/cool/clammy skin, rapid shallow breathing, rapid weak pulse, confusion.
Look for rigid, distended, or severely painful abdomen, or large dark bruising (which may take time to appear).
Lay the patient flat and elevate their legs slightly (if no suspected spinal or leg injuries).
Keep the patient warm to slow the onset of shock.
donot: Do NOT give the patient anything by mouth (no water, no food), as they will likely need emergency surgery.
Do NOT assume they are fine just because there is no external blood.
Do NOT let them stand up or walk around.
seek: Requires emergency trauma evaluation, FAST ultrasound, and surgical intervention.

title: Pelvic Fracture
warn: ⛔ MASSIVE PELVIC HEMORRHAGE — The pelvis houses major blood vessels. A fracture can tear these, hiding liters of blood.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This is a common injury in motorcycle crashes, pedestrian impacts, and falls from height.
Keep the patient absolutely still. Do NOT roll them unless they are choking on vomit.

If trained and a commercial pelvic binder is unavailable, you can use a folded bedsheet tightly wrapped and tied around the hips (greater trochanters, NOT the waist) to compress the pelvis and slow bleeding.
Treat for severe shock (keep warm).
Monitor airway and breathing.
donot: Do NOT "rock" or press down on the pelvis to test if it is broken (this can tear more blood vessels and dislodge clots).
Do NOT move the patient’s legs.
Do NOT elevate the legs.
seek: A true trauma emergency requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation, blood transfusions, and surgical fixation.

title: Femur (Thigh Bone) Fracture
warn: ⚠️ HIGH BLEEDING RISK — A broken femur can sever the femoral artery or hide up to 1.5 liters of blood in the thigh tissue.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Keep the patient still and lying flat.
Look for classic signs: the injured leg may appear significantly shorter than the other, and the foot is often rotated outward.
Support the leg in the position found using rolled blankets or clothing alongside it.
If bleeding externally, apply direct pressure (or a tourniquet if it is massive arterial bleeding).
Monitor for shock.
donot: Do NOT attempt to pull traction or straighten the leg unless you are a specifically trained medical provider with a traction splint.
Do NOT allow the patient to attempt to stand or bear weight.
Do NOT elevate the leg.
seek: Requires EMS transport, pain management, and orthopedic surgery (often a titanium rod insertion).

title: Major Thermal Burn (2nd/3rd Degree)
warn: ⛔ SEVERE TISSUE DAMAGE & SHOCK RISK — High risk of hypothermia, fluid loss, and airway swelling if near the face.
steps: Stop the burning process safely (stop/drop/roll, smother flames, move away from heat source).
Call 112 immediately for burns covering >10% of the body, involving the face/hands/genitals, or encircling a limb.
Cool the burn immediately with cool (not cold) running water for 10-20 minutes. Stop if the patient starts shivering.
Remove jewelry, belts, and tight clothing near the burn before swelling begins.
Cover the burn loosely with a clean, dry, sterile dressing or a lint-free cloth (like a clean sheet).
donot: Do NOT use ice or ice water (causes further tissue damage and hypothermia).
Do NOT pop blisters.
Do NOT apply butter, ointments, toothpaste, or grease to a severe burn (they trap heat and complicate hospital treatment).
seek: Requires a specialized Burn Center for fluid resuscitation, skin grafting, and infection control.

title: Electrical Shock / Lightning Strike
warn: ⛔ INTERNAL DESTRUCTION & ARRHYTHMIA — Electricity cooks from the inside out and instantly disrupts the heart rhythm.
steps: Ensure the power source is OFF before approaching. Do not touch the patient if they are still in contact with the current.
Call 112 immediately.
If the patient is unresponsive and pulseless, begin CPR immediately (Use an AED if available).
Look for an entry wound and an exit wound (often on the hands and feet) and dress them with sterile gauze.
Assume a spinal injury, especially if the shock threw the patient or they fell.
donot: Do NOT touch the patient with bare hands if they are touching a live wire.
Do NOT use a conductive object (like a metal pole or wet wood) to push the wire away.
Do NOT assume they are fine if they are awake; fatal arrhythmias can occur hours later.
seek: All electrical shocks require ER evaluation with an EKG to monitor for delayed cardiac arrhythmias and check for internal muscle breakdown.

title: Chemical Burn
warn: ⚠️ CONTINUOUS BURNING — The chemical will continue destroying tissue until it is completely washed away or neutralized.
steps: Ensure your own safety (wear gloves/eye protection).
Brush off any DRY chemicals using a gloved hand or cloth BEFORE applying water (some dry chemicals ignite with water).
Flush the affected area continuously with massive amounts of cool, low-pressure running water for at least 20-30 minutes.
Remove all contaminated clothing and jewelry while flushing.
If the chemical is in the eye, flush from the nose outward to avoid washing the chemical into the good eye.
donot: Do NOT try to neutralize an acid with a base (or vice versa) on the skin; the reaction generates severe thermal heat and causes a worse burn.
Do NOT stop washing after just a few minutes, even if the pain stops.
Do NOT rub the eyes.
seek: Identify the chemical if possible and bring the container/name to the ER. Requires specialized decontamination.

title: Neck Laceration
warn: ⛔ EXSANGUINATION & AIR EMBOLISM — Veins in the neck can suck in air, causing a fatal air bubble in the heart.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Apply direct, firm pressure to the bleeding vessel immediately using a gloved hand and sterile dressing.
Apply an occlusive dressing (plastic wrap or petroleum gauze) over the wound to prevent air from being sucked into the vein.
Keep the patient sitting upright if possible to reduce blood pressure in the head and neck, but lay them flat if they are in shock.
Keep the patient calm.
donot: Do NOT apply a tourniquet around the neck.
Do NOT wrap a bandage entirely around the neck (you will strangle the patient).
Do NOT remove the pressure until medical help takes over.
seek: Absolute emergency requiring emergency vascular surgery to repair the carotid artery or jugular vein.

title: Impaled Object
warn: ⚠️ THE OBJECT IS A PLUG — Pulling it out releases the pressure and can trigger massive, uncontrollable bleeding.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Leave the object exactly where it is.
Expose the wound area by cutting clothing away (do not lift clothing over the object).
Control bleeding by applying direct pressure AROUND the object, not on it.
Stabilize the object by packing bulky dressings (like rolled gauze or clean towels) tightly around its base, and tape them securely to prevent any movement.
donot: Do NOT remove the object under ANY circumstances, unless it is impaled through the cheek and completely blocking the airway.
Do NOT cut or shorten the object unless its size makes transport impossible (and only if you can do so without vibrating it).
Do NOT move the patient unnecessarily.
seek: Requires surgical removal in an operating room where surgeons have direct access to the clamped blood vessels.

title: Penetrating Eye Trauma / Globe Rupture
warn: ⚠️ SYMPATHETIC MOVEMENT — Eyes move together. If the good eye looks around, the injured eye moves and takes further damage.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Have the patient lie flat on their back and tell them to keep their eyes closed and still.
Do not apply ANY pressure to the injured eye.
Place a rigid shield over the injured eye (like a paper cup or protective glasses) to prevent anything from touching it. Tape it to the facial bones.
Cover the GOOD eye with a patch or bandage to prevent the patient from looking around.
donot: Do NOT try to remove an object sticking out of the eye.
Do NOT apply direct pressure or a tight bandage to the injured eye (this will squeeze the internal eye fluids out).
Do NOT let the patient rub their eye.
seek: Requires emergency ophthalmologic surgery to save the eye and preserve vision.

title: Crush Syndrome
warn: ⛔ TOXIC RELEASE — Releasing a crushing weight after >30 minutes sends deadly toxins (myoglobin, potassium) to the heart, causing sudden cardiac arrest.
steps: Call 112 immediately and request specialized rescue teams.
If the object has been crushing the patient for MORE than 30 minutes, wait for EMS before removing the weight if possible. They need IV fluids and medication BEFORE the weight is lifted.
If you must remove the weight (e.g., fire, asphyxiation), be prepared for the patient to suddenly deteriorate or go into cardiac arrest.
Apply a tourniquet above the crush injury BEFORE lifting the weight if it is a limb, to trap the toxins until EMS arrives.
Keep the patient warm and calm.
donot: Do NOT blindly remove heavy weight from a trapped patient if they have been pinned for hours without EMS present.
Do NOT assume they are fine just because they are awake and talking while pinned (the "smiling death").
Do NOT let them drink large amounts of water.
seek: Requires aggressive IV fluid therapy, sodium bicarbonate, and often emergency dialysis to save the kidneys and heart.

title: Traumatic Asphyxia
warn: ⛔ REVERSE BLOOD FLOW — Extreme compression of the chest forces blood backward out of the heart into the veins of the neck and brain.
steps: Remove the crushing weight from the chest immediately (unlike limb crush syndrome, chest compression restricts breathing and must be removed instantly).
Call 112 immediately.
Look for classic signs: the patient’s head, neck, and shoulders will be deeply bruised, swollen, and purple/red, with bulging bloodshot eyes.
Support airway and breathing; provide rescue breaths or CPR if unresponsive and pulseless.
Keep the patient seated upright if conscious to relieve blood pressure in the head.
donot: Do NOT delay removing a weight that is resting on the torso or chest.
Do NOT let the patient lie flat if they are conscious and breathing (elevate the head/shoulders).
Do NOT assume normal breathing means they are out of danger (internal damage is severe).
seek: Requires immediate advanced trauma life support and treatment for internal bleeding and lung contusions.

title: Blast Injury
warn: ⛔ MULTI-SYSTEM TRAUMA — Explosions cause invisible pressure damage to lungs and ears (primary), shrapnel wounds (secondary), and impact injuries (tertiary).
steps: Ensure scene safety (beware of secondary explosive devices or structural collapse).
Call 112. Triage multiple patients if necessary.
Address catastrophic bleeding first with tourniquets and pressure dressings.
Monitor breathing closely. Blast waves rupture lung tissue (blast lung), causing sudden severe shortness of breath and coughing up blood.
Keep the patient on their side (recovery position) if they are bleeding from the mouth/nose, to keep the airway clear.
donot: Do NOT ignore a patient who looks uninjured but was close to the blast; pressure wave injuries to the lungs and intestines can be fatal hours later.
Do NOT let patients with hearing loss or ringing ears walk around unassisted (their balance center may be damaged).
Do NOT delay treating massive hemorrhage.
seek: Requires comprehensive trauma center evaluation for hidden internal injuries, eardrum ruptures, and shrapnel.

title: Severe Facial Trauma (Le Fort Fracture)
warn: ⛔ AIRWAY COMPROMISE — Broken facial bones and massive bleeding into the mouth/throat will cause the patient to drown in their own blood.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Airway management is the absolute priority.
If the patient is conscious and has no suspected spinal injury, have them lean completely forward (sitting) so blood and broken teeth drain OUT of the mouth, not down the throat.
If the patient is unconscious, place them in the recovery position (on their side) immediately to allow drainage.
Use a finger sweep ONLY to remove visible, loose obstructions (like broken teeth) from the mouth.
Manually support the jaw if it is severely fractured.
donot: Do NOT lay a patient with severe facial bleeding flat on their back (they will aspirate blood).
Do NOT insert a nasal airway device (NPA) if there is mid-face trauma or clear fluid leaking from the nose (it can enter the brain).
Do NOT apply a tight bandage around the jaw and head if they are vomiting or bleeding inside the mouth.
seek: Requires surgical airway (cricothyrotomy) by EMS if completely blocked, and complex maxillofacial surgery.

title: Degloving Injury
warn: ⚠️ MASSIVE TISSUE DAMAGE — The skin and underlying tissue are violently peeled away from the muscle and bone, often by machinery or rings.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Control bleeding with direct pressure. If it is a limb and bleeding is severe, use a tourniquet.
If the skin flap is still attached, lay it gently back over the wound to protect the exposed tissue.
Cover the entire area with a thick, moist, sterile dressing.
If the skin was completely detached, recover it, wrap it in moist gauze, place in a plastic bag, and put on ice (like an amputation).
Immobilize the affected limb.
donot: Do NOT attempt to wash away grease or debris embedded in the muscle.
Do NOT cut off the hanging skin flaps.
Do NOT wear rings when operating heavy machinery or jumping over fences (prevention).
seek: Requires complex plastic and reconstructive surgery, skin grafting, and high-dose antibiotics.

title: Acute Compartment Syndrome
warn: ⚠️ LIMB DEATH — Swelling inside a closed muscle compartment cuts off blood flow, suffocating the muscle and nerves.
steps: Recognize the signs (The 5 Ps): Pain (out of proportion to the injury), Pallor (pale skin), Paresthesia (pins and needles), Pulselessness, and Paralysis.
Call 112 or go to the ER immediately. This often develops hours after a fracture, crush injury, or tight cast application.
Remove all constricting clothing, jewelry, or bandages from the limb.
Keep the limb exactly at heart level (not elevated, not hanging down).
Do not apply ice.
donot: Do NOT elevate the limb above the heart (this reduces the already compromised arterial blood flow).
Do NOT apply ice (causes vasoconstriction, worsening the blood flow).
Do NOT ignore a patient complaining of agonizing pain inside a cast.
seek: Requires an emergency fasciotomy (surgeons slice open the muscle compartment to relieve the pressure) within 6 hours to save the limb.

title: Basilar Skull Fracture
warn: ⛔ BRAIN EXPOSURE — A break at the base of the skull tears the lining of the brain, leaking spinal fluid and risking meningitis.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Assume a severe cervical spine injury and immobilize the head/neck manually.
Look for late signs: bruising behind the ears (Battle’s sign) or bruising around both eyes (Raccoon eyes).
Look for clear, watery fluid or blood draining from the ears or nose (cerebrospinal fluid).
To test if bloody fluid contains CSF, let a drop fall on a gauze pad. If a yellowish ring forms around the blood, it is a "Halo sign" indicating CSF.
Keep the patient still and calm.
donot: Do NOT try to stop the flow of blood or fluid from the nose or ears (do not pack them with gauze); this increases pressure inside the skull.
Do NOT allow the patient to blow their nose or sneeze forcefully.
Do NOT move the patient’s head.
seek: Requires trauma center admission, prophylactic antibiotics, and constant neurological monitoring.

title: Superficial Burn (1st Degree)
warn: ⚠️ Damage is limited to the top layer of skin (epidermis). Healing usually takes 3-6 days.
steps: Remove the patient from the heat source immediately.
Cool the burn by running cool (not cold) water over it for 10-15 minutes, or apply a cool, wet compress.
Remove any tight items, such as rings or bracelets, from the burned area before it swells.
Apply a soothing, water-based lotion or aloe vera gel once the skin is cooled.
Protect the burn from friction and direct sunlight while it heals.
donot: Do NOT apply ice or ice water directly to the skin (this causes frostbite and further tissue damage).
Do NOT apply butter, grease, oil, or toothpaste to the burn (they trap heat).
Do NOT use adhesive bandages directly on the burned skin.
seek: Seek medical advice if the burn covers a large portion of the body or does not improve after a few days.

title: Partial-Thickness Burn (2nd Degree)
warn: ⚠️ Damage extends through the epidermis to the underlying dermis. Blisters will form.
steps: Cool the burn immediately with cool running water for at least 20 minutes.
Remove constricting clothing or jewelry near the burn site.
Wash the area gently with mild soap and water (do not scrub).
Cover the burn loosely with a sterile, non-stick gauze dressing to protect it from air and infection.
Elevate the burned limb above the heart if possible to reduce swelling.
donot: Do NOT pop, puncture, or drain blisters (the blister is a sterile, natural barrier protecting the healing skin).
Do NOT apply cotton balls or fluffy cotton tissue directly to the burn (fibers will stick to the wound).
Do NOT peel off dead skin.
seek: Seek medical care if the burn is larger than 3 inches in diameter, or if it is on the face, hands, feet, groin, or over a major joint.

title: Full-Thickness Burn (3rd Degree)
warn: ⛔ SEVERE TISSUE DESTRUCTION — Destroys all layers of skin and nerve endings, meaning the burn itself may not hurt, though surrounding areas will.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This is a life-threatening medical emergency.
Ensure the scene is safe and the burning process has completely stopped.
Check for airway, breathing, and circulation. Be prepared to start CPR.
Cover the burn loosely with a sterile, dry, non-stick dressing or a clean, lint-free sheet.
Keep the patient warm with blankets (placed over unburned areas) to prevent severe hypothermia from skin loss.
Elevate the burned area above heart level if it does not cause pain or further injury.
donot: Do NOT submerge a large 3rd-degree burn in cold water (can cause fatal hypothermia and shock).
Do NOT try to remove clothing that is melted or stuck to the burn.
Do NOT apply any ointments, creams, or wet dressings.
seek: Requires immediate transport to a specialized Burn Center for fluid resuscitation and surgical grafting.

title: Severe Scald Burn
warn: ⚠️ Scalds spread rapidly over the skin and get trapped inside clothing, cooking the tissue.
steps: Remove the heat source and immediately strip off all wet/hot clothing or diapers holding the hot liquid against the skin.
Run cool (not cold) tap water over the scalded area for 20 continuous minutes.
Keep the rest of the patient warm while cooling the specific burn to prevent hypothermia, especially in children.
Cover the cooled burn loosely with cling wrap (plastic wrap) applied lengthwise (do not wrap tightly around the limb).
Assess the total body surface area affected.
donot: Do NOT delay removing soaked hot clothing.
Do NOT cool the burn for just 2 or 3 minutes (the tissue underneath will continue burning).
Do NOT apply plastic wrap to the face.
seek: Go to the ER immediately if the scald covers more than 10% of the body, affects a child/elderly person, or forms immediate severe blisters.

title: Chemical Burn to the Eyes
warn: ⛔ IMMEDIATE VISION THREAT — Alkali chemicals (like lye, drain cleaner, bleach) are especially dangerous as they liquefy eye tissue.
steps: Do not wait. Immediately flush the affected eye(s) with copious amounts of cool or lukewarm tap water.
Hold the eyelids open physically while flushing.
Flush from the inner corner of the eye (near the nose) OUTWARD, so the chemical does not wash into the unaffected eye.
Remove contact lenses if they do not wash out immediately on their own.
Continue flushing continuously for at least 20-30 minutes, or until EMS arrives.
Call 112 or have someone else call while you are flushing.
donot: Do NOT let the patient rub their eyes.
Do NOT attempt to neutralize the chemical (e.g., do not put an acid in the eye to neutralize a base).
Do NOT bandage the eyes while waiting for EMS (keep flushing).
seek: Requires immediate emergency ophthalmologic care to assess and preserve vision.

title: Dry Chemical Burn
warn: ⚠️ Adding water to certain dry chemicals (like dry lime) creates a boiling exothermic reaction, worsening the burn.
steps: Put on heavy protective gloves to protect your own hands.
BRUSH the dry powder entirely off the skin and clothing using a dry cloth or soft brush.
Carefully remove contaminated clothing and jewelry.
ONLY AFTER all dry powder is completely brushed away, flush the area with massive amounts of cool running water for 20 minutes.
Cover the area with a dry, sterile dressing after flushing.
donot: Do NOT use water to wash off the powder initially (brush it first).
Do NOT brush the powder into the patient’s eyes or airway, or onto yourself.
Do NOT handle the contaminated clothing with bare hands.
seek: Seek ER evaluation, bringing the chemical container or Safety Data Sheet (SDS) if safe to do so.

title: Hydrofluoric Acid (HF) Burn
warn: ⛔ LETHAL CHEMICAL EXPOSURE — HF penetrates deep into tissue, destroying bone and pulling calcium from the blood, which can trigger sudden cardiac arrest.
steps: Call 112 immediately and specifically state it is a Hydrofluoric Acid exposure.
Ensure rescuer safety (wear heavy nitrile/neoprene gloves).
Remove contaminated clothing immediately.
Flush the area with massive amounts of water for 5 minutes (shorter flush time than other acids because treatment is urgent).
IMMEDIATELY apply Calcium Gluconate gel (2.5%) continuously, massaging it deeply into the skin until pain subsides.
If Calcium Gluconate is unavailable, keep flushing with water until EMS takes over.
donot: Do NOT underestimate the burn; HF burns often look mild initially (no redness/blisters) but cause excruciating, deep pain.
Do NOT touch the patient with bare hands.
Do NOT wait for pain to start before treating; symptoms can be delayed up to 24 hours for lower concentrations.
seek: Absolute emergency requiring cardiac monitoring, IV calcium, and specific antidotes in a hospital.

title: Hot Tar or Asphalt Burn
warn: ⚠️ Tar acts as an extreme heat reservoir, cooking the flesh beneath it while remaining stuck to the skin.
steps: Stop the burning process immediately by cooling the tar with large amounts of cold water for at least 20 minutes.
Continue cooling until the tar is completely hardened and cooled all the way through.
Cover the hardened tar and surrounding skin with a sterile, loose dressing.
Keep the patient warm once the local burn is cooled, as extensive cooling can cause hypothermia.
donot: Do NOT try to peel, scrape, or pull the tar off the skin (this will rip off the underlying flesh).
Do NOT use harsh solvents (gasoline, paint thinner) to dissolve the tar on the scene.
Do NOT apply ice directly.
seek: Requires ER evaluation where medical professionals will use specific medical-grade mineral oil or petroleum jelly to slowly dissolve and remove the tar over hours/days.

title: Flash Burn (Arc Eye / Welder’s Eye)
warn: ⚠️ Ultraviolet light burns the cornea of the eye. Symptoms (extreme pain, feeling of sand in the eye) often delay by 3-12 hours.
steps: Have the patient rest with their eyes closed in a dark or dimly lit room.
Remove contact lenses if the patient wears them.
Apply cold, moist compresses gently over the closed eyelids to reduce pain and swelling.
Give over-the-counter oral pain relievers (like ibuprofen or acetaminophen) if the patient has no contraindications.
Prevent the patient from rubbing their eyes.
donot: Do NOT allow the patient to drive.
Do NOT use unprescribed anesthetic eye drops (they delay healing and mask damage).
Do NOT try to pry the eyelids open if they are spasming shut.
seek: Requires evaluation by an eye doctor or ER to check for permanent damage and receive proper medicated eye drops.

title: Thermal Airway Burn
warn: ⛔ IMMINENT AIRWAY CLOSURE — Inhaling superheated air or steam instantly burns the throat and vocal cords, causing them to swell shut rapidly.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This is a critical airway emergency.
Move the patient to fresh air.
Keep the patient seated upright to make breathing as easy as possible.
Look for warning signs: singed facial hair, soot in saliva, severe hoarseness, or stridor (high-pitched whistling when inhaling).
Loosen any tight clothing around the neck and chest.
Keep the patient entirely calm and at rest. Prepare for CPR if they lose the airway completely.
donot: Do NOT give the patient food or water (swallowing will be impaired, leading to choking).
Do NOT attempt to look deep into their throat (can trigger a laryngospasm and instant closure).
Do NOT assume they are fine if they are breathing normally right after the fire; swelling peaks hours later.
seek: Requires immediate pre-hospital advanced life support for rapid sequence intubation before the airway is totally lost.

title: Stroke (FAST)
warn: ⛔ TIME IS BRAIN — 1.9 million neurons die per minute untreated. Call 112 NOW.
steps: Use FAST: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 112.
Note exact time symptoms began (critical for thrombolysis eligibility <4.5 hours).
Call 112 immediately.
Keep patient calm and lying down.
Do NOT give food, water, or medication.
Measure blood glucose if able.
Loosen tight clothing.
If vomiting or unconscious: recovery position on affected side.
Continuous monitoring of neuro status.
donot: Do NOT give aspirin — stroke may be hemorrhagic.
Do NOT give food or water (aspiration risk).
seek: Any suspected stroke = immediate 112. Do NOT drive to hospital — paramedics begin treatment en route.

title: Seizure — Generalized
warn: ⚠️ Seizure >5 minutes = Status Epilepticus. Call 112.
steps: Time the seizure from onset.
Protect from injury: clear surroundings, cushion head.
Do NOT restrain the person.
Turn on side (recovery position) when jerking stops.
Do NOT put anything in mouth.
Stay with patient until fully conscious.
Call 112 if: first seizure, >5 minutes, not recovering, injured, pregnant, or diabetic.
donot: Do NOT hold patient down.
Do NOT put objects in mouth.
Do NOT give water until fully conscious.
seek: First seizure, prolonged, or not recovering to baseline.

title: Syncope / Fainting
warn: ⚠️ Distinguish from cardiac arrest — check pulse! Cardiac syncope is dangerous.
steps: Lower patient to ground (prevent fall injury).
Check pulse immediately.
Elevate legs 12-18 inches above heart level.
Loosen tight clothing.
Cool environment if overheated.
Usually recovers within 1-2 minutes.
Keep supine for 10-15 minutes after recovery.
donot: Do NOT sit patient up quickly after recovery.
Do NOT give anything by mouth until fully conscious.
seek: Syncope after exertion, cardiac history, ECG abnormality, or repetitive episodes.

title: Status Epilepticus
warn: ⛔ BRAIN DAMAGE RISK — A seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes, or multiple seizures without waking up in between.
steps: Call 112 IMMEDIATELY. This is a life-threatening medical emergency.
Clear the area of hard or sharp objects to prevent physical injury.
Place something soft and flat under the patient’s head.
Roll the patient onto their side (recovery position) to keep the airway clear of saliva and vomit.
Note the exact time the seizure started and report it to EMS.
Monitor breathing closely; prepare to perform CPR if they stop breathing once the convulsions stop.
donot: Do NOT attempt to hold the person down or stop their movements.
Do NOT put anything in their mouth (no spoons, no wallets, no fingers).
Do NOT give them water or pills until they are fully awake.
seek: Requires immediate IV anticonvulsants (like Lorazepam/Diazepam) administered by paramedics or ER staff.

title: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH)
warn: ⛔ RUPTURED ANEURYSM — Often described by the patient as "the worst headache of my life," occurring instantly.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Keep the patient as still and calm as possible to prevent further spikes in blood pressure.
Keep the patient in a quiet, dark room if possible (they may be extremely sensitive to light).
If they vomit, roll them onto their side to prevent choking.
Gather their medical history, especially history of high blood pressure or blood thinners.
donot: Do NOT give the patient aspirin, ibuprofen, or any blood-thinning pain relievers.
Do NOT let the patient fall asleep or brush it off as a migraine if it reached maximum intensity in seconds.
Do NOT allow any physical exertion.
seek: Requires immediate CT scan and emergency neurosurgery to clip or coil the bleeding blood vessel.

title: Epidural Hematoma
warn: ⛔ THE "TALK AND DIE" SYNDROME — An arterial bleed outside the brain. The patient may get knocked out, wake up and seem fine, then suddenly deteriorate and die.
steps: Call 112 immediately following any severe head trauma (like a baseball bat to the temple or a motorcycle crash).
Monitor the patient constantly, even if they claim they feel fine after waking up.
Watch for sudden neurological collapse: pupil on the side of the impact becoming huge (blown pupil), severe headache, vomiting, or sudden unconsciousness.
Keep the patient’s head elevated about 30 degrees to reduce intracranial pressure.
Maintain cervical spine stabilization.
donot: Do NOT leave the patient alone after a head injury where they lost consciousness.
Do NOT let the patient sleep unmonitored.
Do NOT give them any pain medication, as it masks neurological deterioration.
seek: Requires immediate neurosurgical evacuation (drilling into the skull) to relieve the crushing pressure on the brain.

title: Subdural Hematoma
warn: ⚠️ A slow, venous bleed under the skull. Symptoms may take days or weeks to appear after a seemingly minor head bump.
steps: Assess the patient’s history: Are they elderly? Are they an alcoholic? Are they on blood thinners? (These groups are at massive risk).
Watch for gradual personality changes, confusion, slurred speech, one-sided weakness, or a lingering headache.
Call 112 or go to the ER immediately if these symptoms present, even if the fall happened two weeks ago.
Keep the patient safe from further falls.
donot: Do NOT dismiss confusion in an elderly person as "just dementia" if they recently had a fall or bumped their head.
Do NOT delay medical evaluation if they are on drugs like Warfarin or Eliquis.
seek: Requires a CT scan to identify the blood pool. May require surgical drainage if it is large or causing severe symptoms.

title: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
warn: ⚠️ A "mini-stroke" where blood flow is temporarily blocked but restores itself. It is a massive red flag for an impending major stroke.
steps: Conduct the FAST test (Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty).
Note the EXACT time the symptoms started, even if they are already fading away.
Call 112 immediately. DO NOT wait to see if the symptoms completely disappear.
Keep the patient resting comfortably.
Prepare a list of the patient’s current medications.
donot: Do NOT ignore the symptoms just because the patient returns to normal in 10 minutes.
Do NOT let the patient drive themselves to the doctor or hospital.
Do NOT give them anything to eat or drink.
seek: Must be evaluated in an ER immediately to find the source of the clot and begin preventative treatment before a massive stroke hits.

title: Bacterial Meningitis
warn: ⛔ RAPIDLY FATAL INFECTION — Brain and spinal cord linings become severely inflamed. Can kill within 24 hours.
steps: Call 112 immediately if a sudden high fever is paired with a stiff neck (inability to touch chin to chest) and severe headache.
Look for a purple, bruise-like rash. Do the "Glass Test": Press a clear drinking glass firmly against the rash. If the rash does NOT fade under pressure, it is a medical emergency.
Keep the patient away from bright lights (photophobia is common).
Protect yourself (wear a mask and wash hands), as some forms are highly contagious via respiratory droplets.
donot: Do NOT delay seeking medical help; antibiotics must be started within hours to prevent brain damage or death.
Do NOT give ibuprofen/acetaminophen and wait to see if the fever breaks if the neck is stiff or a rash is present.
seek: Requires an emergency lumbar puncture (spinal tap) and immediate, aggressive IV antibiotics.

title: Viral Encephalitis
warn: ⚠️ Direct viral infection of the brain tissue itself (often from herpes simplex, ticks, or mosquitoes).
steps: Observe for flu-like symptoms that rapidly escalate to confusion, hallucinations, personality changes, or seizures.
Call 112 immediately.
If the patient has a seizure, protect them from injury and turn them on their side.
Keep the patient cool if they have a dangerously high fever.
Keep the environment calm and quiet.
donot: Do NOT assume severe confusion or hallucinations are a psychiatric breakdown if accompanied by a fever.
Do NOT restrain the patient if they are confused and agitated, unless necessary for immediate safety.
seek: Requires ER evaluation, MRI, and antiviral medications (like Acyclovir) to stop the virus from destroying brain tissue.

title: Cauda Equina Syndrome
warn: ⛔ PERMANENT PARALYSIS RISK — The nerve roots at the base of the spinal cord are severely compressed.
steps: Assess for red-flag symptoms: sudden loss of bowel or bladder control (wetting/soiling themselves unexpectedly), or inability to urinate.
Ask if they have "saddle anesthesia" (numbness in the areas that would touch a saddle: groin, buttocks, inner thighs).
If these accompany severe lower back pain or leg weakness, go to the ER immediately.
Keep the patient lying flat to reduce pressure on the spine.
donot: Do NOT wait to see your primary care doctor next week.
Do NOT ignore sudden incontinence associated with back pain.
Do NOT take painkillers and go to sleep.
seek: Requires an emergency MRI and often immediate decompressive spinal surgery to prevent permanent paralysis and loss of bodily functions.

title: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)
warn: ⛔ SUFFOCATION RISK — The immune system attacks the nerves, causing paralysis that starts in the feet and moves up to the lungs.
steps: Recognize the pattern: tingling and weakness starting in the feet/legs and spreading upward over hours or days.
Ask about a recent viral or bacterial infection (often a stomach bug or respiratory infection 1-3 weeks prior).
Call 112 immediately if the weakness reaches the chest, causing difficulty breathing, speaking, or swallowing.
Monitor breathing continuously. Prepare to perform CPR if respiratory arrest occurs.
donot: Do NOT assume tingling in both legs is just "falling asleep" if it is accompanied by progressive weakness.
Do NOT let the patient eat or drink if they are having any trouble swallowing or speaking.
seek: Requires ICU monitoring, potential mechanical ventilation, and treatments like IVIG or plasma exchange.

title: Myasthenic Crisis
warn: ⛔ RESPIRATORY COLLAPSE — A severe complication of Myasthenia Gravis where the muscles controlling breathing and swallowing completely fail.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Keep the patient sitting upright to facilitate breathing and prevent choking on their own saliva.
Do not allow the patient to exert any physical energy (weakness worsens rapidly with use).
