Check if they have missed their medications (like Pyridostigmine) or have a concurrent infection (a common trigger).
Prepare to use a bag-valve-mask or perform mouth-to-mouth if they stop breathing.
donot: Do NOT give them food, water, or oral medications during a crisis (they will aspirate/choke).
Do NOT leave them alone for even a minute.
Do NOT dismiss their complaints of "feeling too weak to breathe."
seek: Requires immediate advanced airway management (intubation) and specialized medication in an ICU.

title: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)
warn: ⛔ FATAL MEDICATION REACTION — A rare, life-threatening reaction to antipsychotic drugs (like Haloperidol) causing "lead-pipe" muscle rigidity and extreme fever.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Look for the classic triad: altered mental status, severe muscle rigidity (arms/legs won't bend), and a rapidly rising fever (>104°F/40°C).
Start cooling the patient aggressively: apply ice packs to the neck, armpits, and groin, and fan them.
Gather all pill bottles to show EMS exactly what psychiatric medications they are taking.
Monitor airway and breathing.
donot: Do NOT give the patient their psychiatric medication.
Do NOT give them over-the-counter fever reducers (they will not work for NMS and may harm the liver).
Do NOT delay EMS transport; muscle breakdown will destroy their kidneys.
seek: Requires ICU admission for muscle relaxants (Dantrolene), aggressive cooling, and IV fluids.

title: Serotonin Syndrome
warn: ⚠️ TOXIC SEROTONIN LEVELS — Caused by mixing certain medications (e.g., SSRIs with cough medicine, or MDMA/Ecstasy).
steps: Assess for symptoms: extreme agitation, confusion, heavy sweating, dilated pupils, shivering, and severe muscle twitching/jerking (clonus).
Call 112 or go to the ER immediately.
Keep the patient calm and in a safe environment (they may be highly agitated or combative).
Cool the patient if they are sweating profusely and feel hot.
Collect all medications and recreational drugs the patient may have taken.
donot: Do NOT physically restrain the patient unless absolutely necessary for safety (struggling increases muscle breakdown and heat).
Do NOT assume they are just having a panic attack.
Do NOT let them "sleep it off."
seek: Requires ER evaluation to stop the offending drugs, provide IV fluids, and administer serotonin blockers if severe.

title: Autonomic Dysreflexia
warn: ⛔ DEADLY BLOOD PRESSURE SPIKE — Occurs in people with spinal cord injuries (T6 and above). A lower-body irritation causes massive, unchecked upper-body hypertension.
steps: SIT THE PATIENT UP IMMEDIATELY. Do not let them lie down (sitting up uses gravity to lower blood pressure in the head).
Loosen any tight clothing, belts, or shoes.
FIND AND REMOVE THE TRIGGER: The most common cause is a full bladder. Check their urinary catheter for kinks or blockages. Empty the leg bag immediately.
If there is no catheter, or if fixing it doesn't help, check for bowel impaction, skin pressure sores, or ingrown toenails.
Call 112 if symptoms (pounding headache, flushed face above the injury, goosebumps below) do not resolve immediately after removing the trigger.
donot: Do NOT lay the patient down.
Do NOT ignore a pounding headache in a paraplegic/quadriplegic patient.
Do NOT wait for EMS before checking the catheter line.
seek: If the trigger cannot be found or BP does not drop, emergency IV blood pressure medications are required to prevent a stroke.

title: Increased Intracranial Pressure (ICP) / Herniation
warn: ⛔ BRAIN CRUSHING — Swelling pushes the brain stem down through the base of the skull, causing death.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This is the end-stage of brain tumors, severe strokes, or major trauma.
Look for Cushing's Triad: 1. Dangerously high blood pressure, 2. Abnormally slow heart rate (bradycardia), 3. Irregular, gasping breathing.
Check the pupils: One pupil remaining huge and unreactive to light (blown pupil) indicates herniation is actively occurring.
Elevate the head of the bed/patient 30 degrees to help blood drain from the head.
Keep the neck perfectly straight (no bending or twisting) to allow jugular veins to drain.
donot: Do NOT lay the patient flat.
Do NOT let the patient cough or bear down, if conscious (this spikes brain pressure).
Do NOT flex their neck forward.
seek: Absolute emergency requiring intubation, hyperventilation by EMS, and emergency neurosurgery or osmotic drugs (Mannitol).

title: Temporal Arteritis (Giant Cell Arteritis)
warn: ⚠️ INFLAMED HEAD ARTERIES — High risk of sudden, irreversible blindness if the artery to the optic nerve clots.
steps: Look for classic signs in patients over 50: severe throbbing headache at the temples, scalp tenderness (pain when brushing hair), and jaw pain when chewing.
Ask if they have experienced any sudden blurriness, double vision, or temporary loss of vision in one eye.
Go to the Emergency Room immediately if these symptoms present.
Keep the patient resting and calm.
donot: Do NOT treat this as a standard tension headache or TMJ issue if accompanied by vision changes or if the temple is tender to the touch.
Do NOT wait to see an eye doctor next week; ER evaluation is needed today.
Do NOT apply heat or ice to the temple.
seek: Requires immediate high-dose IV steroids (Prednisone) to save the patient’s vision, followed by a temporal artery biopsy.

title: Wernicke’s Encephalopathy
warn: ⚠️ ACUTE VITAMIN B1 STARVATION — Destroys brain tissue. Most common in severe alcoholics, malnourished, or severe eating disorder patients.
steps: Look for the classic triad: 1. Sudden confusion/memory problems, 2. Ataxia (staggering, inability to walk straight), 3. Eye abnormalities (nystagmus/jerking eyes or inability to move eyes normally).
Call 112 or transport to the ER.
Prevent the patient from walking unassisted, as their balance center is severely impaired and they will fall.
Gather information about their diet and alcohol intake.
donot: Do NOT give the patient food or sugary drinks/glucose before they receive medical help. (Giving glucose WITHOUT thiamine first can trigger irreversible brain damage/Korsakoff syndrome).
Do NOT assume they are just "drunk" if they exhibit these specific eye and walking abnormalities.
seek: Requires immediate IV Thiamine (Vitamin B1) BEFORE any glucose is administered.

title: Acute Spinal Cord Compression
warn: ⛔ IMPENDING PARALYSIS — A tumor, abscess, or massive herniated disc is pressing on the spinal cord.
steps: Assess for sudden onset of severe back pain accompanied by a "band-like" tightness around the chest or abdomen.
Check for a sensory level: Is there a specific line on their torso below which they cannot feel sharp touches or temperature?
Check for rapidly worsening weakness in both legs.
Keep the patient perfectly flat and still.
Call 112 immediately.
donot: Do NOT let the patient walk or bear weight.
Do NOT bend their back or neck.
Do NOT ignore new, severe back pain in a patient with a history of cancer.
seek: Emergency MRI is required. Needs high-dose steroids (Dexamethasone) and emergency radiation or surgery to save spinal function.

title: Malignant Hyperthermia
warn: ⛔ LETHAL SURGICAL COMPLICATION — A genetic reaction to general anesthesia gases, causing muscles to enter a hyper-metabolic state, cooking the body from the inside.
steps: This almost exclusively happens during or immediately after surgery/anesthesia.
If in a post-op setting, alert medical staff immediately if the patient becomes completely rigid (especially the jaw) and feels extremely hot.
If you are an EMS provider responding to an outpatient surgical center: prepare for aggressive cooling and rapid transport.
Apply ice packs to the neck, armpits, and groin.
Provide 100% oxygen.
donot: Do NOT delay notification of staff; death can occur within minutes due to cardiac arrest from potassium release.
Do NOT cover the patient with blankets.
Do NOT assume muscle rigidity after surgery is just shivering from being cold.
seek: Requires the immediate administration of the specific antidote, Dantrolene, and intensive care cooling protocols.

title: Focal Impaired Awareness Seizure (Complex Partial)
warn: ⚠️ The patient is awake but completely unaware of their surroundings. They may perform repetitive, bizarre actions.
steps: Guide the person gently away from hazards (stairs, traffic, sharp objects).
Speak calmly and reassuringly, even if they do not seem to understand you.
Observe for automatisms: lip smacking, picking at clothes, chewing motions, or wandering aimlessly.
Stay with them until the seizure ends and they regain full awareness (usually 1-3 minutes).
Time the seizure. Call 112 if it lasts longer than 5 minutes or if they are injured.
donot: Do NOT grab or physically restrain the person, as they may react aggressively out of fear/confusion.
Do NOT shout at them or expect them to follow commands.
Do NOT assume they are intoxicated or having a psychiatric episode.
seek: If it is their first seizure of this type, or if it lasts >5 minutes, seek emergency medical care.

title: Bell’s Palsy (Rule Out Stroke)
warn: ⚠️ Sudden paralysis of one side of the face. While not life-threatening itself, it MUST be evaluated in an ER to prove it is not a stroke.
steps: Ask the patient to smile, close their eyes tightly, and raise their eyebrows.
CRITICAL DIFFERENCE: In Bell's Palsy, the ENTIRE side of the face is paralyzed (they cannot wrinkle their forehead or close that eye). In a stroke, the forehead usually still wrinkles.
Check for arm weakness or speech slurring (if these are present, it is likely a stroke).
Protect the affected eye: if they cannot blink, tape the eye closed or use eye drops to prevent corneal abrasions.
Go to the Emergency Room to get an official diagnosis.
donot: Do NOT diagnose this yourself at home. Let a doctor rule out a stroke.
Do NOT let the affected eye dry out.
Do NOT ignore other neurological symptoms (weakness, numbness) assuming it is just Bell's Palsy.
seek: Requires medical evaluation. If confirmed as Bell's Palsy, treatment includes oral steroids and antiviral medications.

title: Anaphylaxis — Full Systemic
warn: ⛔ Biphasic reaction possible up to 12 hours later. ALWAYS go to hospital after EpiPen.
steps: Recognize: hives, flushing, throat tightening, wheezing, hypotension, collapse.
Administer EpiPen 0.3mg IM outer thigh immediately (through clothing if needed).
Call 112.
Lay patient flat with legs elevated (UNLESS dyspnea — then upright).
Repeat EpiPen in 5-15 minutes if no improvement.
Administer antihistamines (diphenhydramine) and steroids (prednisolone) as secondary measures only.
Monitor airway continuously.
All patients must go to hospital — biphasic reaction risk.
donot: Do NOT delay EpiPen for antihistamines.
Do NOT send patient home after EpiPen — must observe minimum 4-6 hours.
seek: All anaphylaxis — no exceptions.

title: Food-Induced Anaphylaxis
warn: ⛔ RAPID ONSET — Food allergies are the leading cause of anaphylaxis outside of a hospital. Symptoms can peak in 5 to 30 minutes.
steps: Administer Epinephrine auto-injector IMMEDIATELY into the outer thigh. Do not wait.
Call 112 and state the patient is having a severe allergic reaction to food.
Remove the remaining food away from the patient.
Have the patient lie flat on their back. If they are vomiting or having trouble breathing, sit them up slightly or roll them on their side.
If symptoms do not improve after 5-15 minutes, administer a second dose of Epinephrine if available.
Wipe the patient's mouth and face with a wet cloth to remove any remaining allergen.
donot: Do NOT assume they will be fine because they "only had a tiny bite." Micro-traces can trigger fatal reactions.
Do NOT try to induce vomiting (this risks aspiration and worsens airway swelling).
Do NOT give antihistamines (like Benadryl) INSTEAD of Epinephrine; they do not treat airway closure or shock.
seek: Transport via EMS is required, as biphasic (secondary) reactions can occur hours after the food is ingested.

title: Insect Sting Anaphylaxis
warn: ⛔ VENOM ABSORPTION — Severe reactions to venom drop blood pressure rapidly, causing shock within minutes.
steps: Administer Epinephrine IMMEDIATELY if the person has a known severe allergy or is showing systemic signs (hives, wheezing, dizziness).
Call 112.
Remove the stinger immediately if it is still in the skin. Scrape it away with a fingernail or the edge of a credit card.
Lay the patient flat and elevate their legs to treat shock (unless they are struggling to breathe, then let them sit up).
Loosen tight clothing and keep them warm.
donot: Do NOT use tweezers to pull the stinger if you can avoid it (squeezing the venom sac pushes more venom into the patient).
Do NOT wait for a rash to appear; respiratory symptoms can occur without skin symptoms.
Do NOT let the patient walk or stand up (can cause sudden cardiac arrest due to low blood pressure).
seek: Requires immediate EMS transport and potentially IV fluids to support blood pressure.

title: Medication Anaphylaxis
warn: ⛔ DIRECT BLOODSTREAM THREAT — Medications (especially IV/injections) can cause the fastest and most severe allergic shock.
steps: If the medication is currently being administered (e.g., an IV drip), STOP THE INFUSION IMMEDIATELY.
Administer Epinephrine auto-injector if available.
Call 112 immediately.
Gather the pill bottle or IV bag so EMS knows exactly what triggered the reaction.
Monitor the airway and be prepared to start CPR if the patient stops breathing.
donot: Do NOT let the patient take any more of the suspected medication.
Do NOT give them water or other pills to "flush it out."
Do NOT ignore "minor" symptoms like lip tingling right after taking a new antibiotic.
seek: Even if Epinephrine resolves the symptoms, EMS evaluation is mandatory.

title: Acute Angioedema
warn: ⚠️ MASSIVE DEEP TISSUE SWELLING — Swelling of the tongue and throat can completely block the airway without any hives or itching.
steps: Assess the airway: Ask the patient to speak and swallow. If their voice is hoarse or they are drooling, the airway is closing.
Call 112 immediately if the swelling involves the lips, tongue, neck, or throat.
Keep the patient sitting upright (laying down makes gravity pull the swollen tongue back over the airway).
Ask if they take blood pressure medication (specifically ACE inhibitors like Lisinopril), as this is a common, sometimes delayed cause.
donot: Do NOT try to look deep into their throat with a finger or spoon (can trigger complete airway spasm).
Do NOT assume allergy pills (antihistamines) will work; if it is ACE-inhibitor induced, antihistamines and epinephrine often fail.
seek: Requires ER management. May require emergency intubation or a surgical airway if the swelling does not stop.

title: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS)
warn: ⛔ SKIN SLOUGHING — A severe, delayed immune reaction to medication where the epidermis separates from the dermis, acting like a massive 3rd-degree burn.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This usually starts 1-3 weeks after starting a new medication (often antibiotics, anti-seizure meds, or gout meds).
Look for flu-like symptoms followed by a painful red/purple rash that spreads and blisters, especially affecting the mouth, eyes, and genitals.
Stop all suspected new medications immediately.
Treat the patient like a severe burn victim: cover blistering areas loosely with clean, dry, sterile dressings.
Keep the patient warm, as severe skin loss causes hypothermia.
donot: Do NOT pop the blisters or peel away dead skin.
Do NOT apply any creams, ointments, or wet dressings to the skin.
Do NOT delay transport; this progresses rapidly and is life-threatening.
seek: Requires ICU or specialized Burn Unit care for pain management, fluid replacement, and infection control.

title: Acute Systemic Urticaria (Severe Hives)
warn: ⚠️ Widespread, intensely itchy welts. While usually not life-threatening alone, it is often the first warning sign of impending anaphylaxis.
steps: Assess for Anaphylaxis: Check for difficulty breathing, throat tightness, dizziness, or vomiting. If ANY of these are present, treat as Anaphylaxis (Epinephrine & call 112).
If it is ONLY skin hives and the patient is breathing normally: Help them take an over-the-counter antihistamine (like Cetirizine or Diphenhydramine).
Apply cool compresses to the hives to soothe the intense itching.
Keep the patient in a cool environment (heat worsens hives).
donot: Do NOT let the patient take a hot shower or bath to soothe the skin (heat vasodilates and makes the rash much worse).
Do NOT leave the patient alone; hives can progress to airway swelling within minutes.
Do NOT scratch the hives, as it releases more histamine.
seek: Seek ER care if hives spread rapidly across the whole body, involve the face/neck, or if antihistamines do not provide relief.

title: Exercise-Induced Anaphylaxis (EIA)
warn: ⚠️ Physical exertion combined with a specific trigger (often a food eaten hours prior) causes sudden allergic shock.
steps: STOP ALL EXERCISE IMMEDIATELY at the first sign of hives, flushing, or sudden exhaustion.
Have the patient lie flat on their back and elevate their legs (exercise dilates blood vessels, causing blood pressure to crash rapidly during this reaction).
Administer Epinephrine immediately.
Call 112.
Cool the patient down.
donot: Do NOT let the patient "walk it off" or push through the workout.
Do NOT let them stand up abruptly after collapsing.
Do NOT assume it is just asthma if they also have widespread hives or severe stomach cramping.
seek: Requires emergency transport. Survivors must see an allergist to identify the specific food-exercise combination trigger.

title: Alpha-Gal Syndrome Reaction
warn: ⚠️ A highly unusual, delayed anaphylaxis caused by a tick bite. Reactions occur 3-8 hours AFTER eating mammalian meat (beef, pork, lamb).
steps: Recognize the delay: The patient may wake up in the middle of the night in anaphylactic shock from a dinner eaten hours ago.
Administer Epinephrine immediately if signs of systemic reaction are present (hives, airway swelling, severe vomiting/diarrhea).
Call 112.
Position the patient safely (lying down, or on their side if vomiting).
donot: Do NOT rule out a food allergy just because they finished eating hours ago without an immediate reaction.
Do NOT give them dairy products to settle their stomach (dairy also contains the alpha-gal carbohydrate and will worsen the reaction).
seek: Requires standard anaphylaxis treatment in an ER and strict avoidance of mammalian products.

title: Contrast Dye Reaction
warn: ⛔ INTRAVENOUS REACTION — Anaphylactoid reaction triggered by radiology contrast dye. Occurs rapidly because it is injected directly into the veins.
steps: If you are a patient/bystander: Yell for the radiology technician to stop the scan and the IV injection IMMEDIATELY.
Medical staff will administer Epinephrine, IV fluids, and oxygen.
Keep the patient laying flat on the imaging table unless they are vomiting.
Monitor for signs of cardiovascular collapse (loss of pulse).
donot: Do NOT ignore a "metallic taste" in the mouth or sudden hot flush if it rapidly escalates to shortness of breath or hives during a scan.
Do NOT leave the patient alone in the scanning room.
seek: This occurs in a medical setting, so immediate intervention by the attending radiologist and rapid response team is required.

title: Latex Allergy Anaphylaxis
warn: ⚠️ Contact with or inhalation of latex proteins (often carried on the powder of gloves/balloons) triggers systemic shock.
steps: REMOVE THE LATEX SOURCE IMMEDIATELY (take off gloves, remove blood pressure cuffs, get away from balloons).
Administer Epinephrine if systemic symptoms (wheezing, facial swelling, low blood pressure) occur.
Call 112 and EXPLICITLY TELL DISPATCH it is a latex allergy, so paramedics know to bring latex-free equipment.
Wash the contact area with mild soap and water to remove remaining latex proteins.
donot: Do NOT allow first responders to touch the patient with standard latex medical gloves.
Do NOT stay in a room with powdered latex gloves, as the allergen remains suspended in the air.
seek: Requires ER evaluation and strict adherence to latex-free environments.

title: Idiopathic Anaphylaxis
warn: ⛔ UNKNOWN CAUSE — Severe anaphylaxis occurring without any identifiable trigger. Treat exactly the same as known anaphylaxis.
steps: Administer Epinephrine IMMEDIATELY. Do not waste time trying to figure out what caused it.
Call 112.
Lay the patient flat with legs elevated to combat shock.
Monitor airway and breathing continuously.
If symptoms worsen, give a second dose of Epinephrine after 5-15 minutes.
donot: Do NOT delay treatment because you cannot find a cause.
Do NOT let the patient downplay the symptoms because "I haven't eaten anything new." Internal triggers can cause this.
seek: Requires immediate EMS transport and extensive follow-up with a specialist to attempt to find the hidden trigger.

title: Cold Urticaria / Cold Anaphylaxis
warn: ⚠️ ALLERGY TO COLD — Exposure to cold air or cold water causes massive histamine release. Jumping into a cold pool can cause instant, fatal shock.
steps: Remove the patient from the cold environment IMMEDIATELY (pull them out of the water, get them indoors).
Remove cold, wet clothing and wrap them in warm, dry blankets.
Administer Epinephrine if they are having trouble breathing, are dizzy, or have widespread hives.
Call 112.
Provide warm (not boiling) drinks if they are fully conscious and can swallow.
donot: Do NOT apply ice packs to this patient for other injuries.
Do NOT let them swim in cold water alone.
Do NOT place them in a hot bath rapidly (can cause blood pressure to crash further).
seek: Emergency medical care is needed if systemic symptoms occur. Requires carrying an EpiPen at all times.

title: Kounis Syndrome (Allergic Angina)
warn: ⛔ ALLERGY-INDUCED HEART ATTACK — The inflammatory mediators released during an allergic reaction cause the coronary arteries to spasm or clot.
steps: Recognize the dual symptoms: The patient is having an allergic reaction (hives, swelling) BUT ALSO crushing chest pain and shortness of breath.
Call 112 immediately and state you suspect a heart attack triggered by an allergy.
Administer Epinephrine for the allergy (though medical control must carefully manage this, as Epi can stress the heart, it is still the first-line for anaphylaxis).
Keep the patient seated comfortably and entirely calm.
Prepare an AED if the patient becomes unresponsive.
donot: Do NOT ignore chest pain during an allergic reaction as just "anxiety."
Do NOT give them anything to eat or drink.
Do NOT allow any physical exertion.
seek: A complex emergency requiring both an allergist and a cardiologist in the ER to manage simultaneous anaphylaxis and cardiac ischemia.

title: Severe Allergic Contact Dermatitis
warn: ⚠️ Delayed, extreme allergic reaction of the skin. Becomes an emergency if it severely involves the face, eyes, or genitals.
steps: Remove any clothing that may have come in contact with the plant resin or chemical.
Wash the skin thoroughly with specialized soap (like Tecnu) or copious amounts of degreasing dish soap and cool water to remove the invisible oil (urushiol).
Apply cool compresses or calamine lotion to weeping blisters.
If the eyes are swelling shut or the rash covers a massive area of the body, go to Urgent Care or the ER.
donot: Do NOT burn poison ivy/oak brush (inhaling the smoke causes severe respiratory anaphylaxis).
Do NOT use hot water to wash the oils off (heat opens pores and lets the oil deeper into the skin).
Do NOT pop the blisters (though the fluid inside does not spread the rash, it risks infection).
seek: Requires systemic oral steroids (like Prednisone) from a doctor if the reaction is severe, widespread, or on the face.

title: Red Man Syndrome (Vancomycin Flushing)
warn: ⚠️ Not a true allergy, but a severe histamine release caused by infusing the antibiotic Vancomycin too quickly.
steps: STOP THE IV INFUSION IMMEDIATELY. This is the most critical step.
Notify medical staff immediately.
Observe for intense red flushing of the face, neck, and upper torso, accompanied by itching and sometimes a drop in blood pressure.
Administer antihistamines (like Diphenhydramine) as ordered by a physician.
Monitor blood pressure and breathing.
donot: Do NOT continue the infusion hoping it will go away.
Do NOT panic; unlike true anaphylaxis, stopping the drug and giving antihistamines usually resolves this quickly without needing Epinephrine.
seek: Medical staff will usually restart the medication at a much slower rate once symptoms resolve.

title: Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage
warn: ⛔ Massive GI bleed can lead to hypovolemic shock rapidly.
steps: Recognize: vomiting blood (red or coffee-ground), black tarry stools (melena).
Call 112.
Lay patient flat, elevate legs.
Keep NPO (nothing by mouth).
Establish IV access if trained.
Monitor vital signs every 5 minutes.
Prepare for endoscopy at hospital.
donot: Do NOT give aspirin or NSAIDs.
seek: Immediate emergency.

title: Acute Appendicitis
warn: ⚠️ Perforation risk increases with delay. Do NOT give food/water.
steps: Recognize: periumbilical pain migrating to right lower quadrant (McBurneys point), nausea, fever.
Call 112 or transport urgently to hospital.
Keep NPO.
Do NOT give laxatives or heat to abdomen.
Surgery is definitive treatment.
donot: Do NOT give painkillers that may mask symptoms before diagnosis.
Do NOT apply heat to abdomen.
seek: Suspected appendicitis = urgent surgical evaluation.

title: Bleeding Esophageal Varices
warn: ⛔ MASSIVE UPPER GI BLEED — Enlarged veins in the esophagus rupture, causing rapid, life-threatening blood loss.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This is an absolute medical emergency with a high mortality rate.
Have the patient lean forward or lay them on their side (recovery position) if they are vomiting blood, to prevent drowning in their own blood.
Treat for hypovolemic shock: keep them warm with blankets.
Prepare to begin CPR if the patient loses consciousness and their heart stops from blood loss.
Keep the patient perfectly calm to keep their blood pressure as low as possible.
donot: Do NOT lay the patient flat on their back while they are actively vomiting.
Do NOT give the patient anything to drink or eat.
Do NOT wait to see if the vomiting stops on its own.
seek: Requires immediate emergency transport for airway protection, blood transfusions, and endoscopic banding.

title: Perforated Peptic Ulcer
warn: ⛔ STOMACH ACID IN ABDOMEN — An ulcer burns completely through the stomach wall, spilling acid and food into the abdominal cavity.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Recognize the sudden, extreme, "knife-like" pain in the upper abdomen that quickly spreads to the entire belly.
Notice if the patient's abdomen becomes completely rigid (hard as a board) to the touch.
Have the patient rest in a position of comfort, usually lying down with their knees drawn up to their chest.
Keep the patient strictly NPO (nothing by mouth).
donot: Do NOT give antacids or milk thinking it will soothe the stomach (the hole is already there).
Do NOT give pain medication (masks symptoms for the surgeons).
Do NOT apply a heating pad.
seek: Requires emergency surgery to wash out the abdominal cavity and patch the hole.

title: Acute Pancreatitis
warn: ⚠️ AUTODIGESTION — The pancreas becomes inflamed and its own digestive enzymes begin destroying it.
steps: Assess for severe, constant pain in the upper middle abdomen that often radiates directly straight through to the back.
Ask the patient to lean forward while sitting; if this relieves the pain slightly, pancreatitis is highly likely.
Monitor for severe nausea and vomiting.
Go to the Emergency Room or call 112 if the pain is unbearable or accompanied by a high fever.
Keep the patient completely NPO (nothing by mouth) to stop the pancreas from producing more enzymes.
donot: Do NOT let the patient eat or drink anything, not even a sip of water.
Do NOT assume it is a simple stomach ache if the pain is radiating to the back.
Do NOT give alcohol.
seek: Requires hospitalization, aggressive IV fluids, and powerful pain management while the organ rests.

title: Small Bowel Obstruction
warn: ⚠️ INTESTINAL BLOCKAGE — Food, fluid, and gas cannot pass through the intestines, leading to severe swelling and potential rupture.
steps: Look for severe, wave-like cramping pain accompanied by loud, high-pitched bowel sounds (early stage) or no sounds (late stage).
Observe for vomiting. In severe or lower blockages, the vomit may smell and look like feces.
Check if the patient is unable to pass gas or have a bowel movement.
Go to the ER immediately.
Keep the patient NPO.
donot: Do NOT give laxatives or enemas (forcing a blocked bowel to contract can cause it to explode).
Do NOT give the patient food or water to "push it through."
Do NOT give pain medication before medical evaluation.
seek: Requires hospital admission, a nasogastric (NG) tube to pump out stomach contents, and potentially surgery.

title: Mesenteric Ischemia
warn: ⛔ BOWEL DEATH — A blood clot blocks the artery feeding the intestines, causing the bowel tissue to rapidly die.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This is highly lethal.
Look for the classic sign: "Pain out of proportion to the physical exam." (The patient is in blinding agony, but their belly is soft and pressing on it doesn't make it much worse).
Check the patient’s history: high risk for elderly patients, smokers, or those with atrial fibrillation (Afib).
Keep the patient calm, lying down, and warm to prevent shock.
donot: Do NOT dismiss the patient’s pain just because their belly feels soft and normal.
Do NOT delay calling EMS; the bowel becomes irreversibly dead within a few hours.
Do NOT give food or drink.
seek: Absolute emergency requiring emergency vascular surgery to remove the clot and potentially remove dead intestines.

title: Strangulated Hernia
warn: ⛔ BLOOD SUPPLY CUT OFF — A piece of intestine pushes through the abdominal wall and gets trapped tightly, choking off its blood supply.
steps: Assess the hernia (a bulge in the groin or abdomen). If it is suddenly hard, severely painful, red/purple, and cannot be pushed back in, it is strangulated.
Call 112 or go to the ER immediately.
Have the patient lie on their back with their knees bent to relax the abdominal muscles.
Keep the patient NPO (nothing by mouth).
donot: Do NOT try to forcefully push the hernia back in (you can rupture the trapped, dying bowel).
Do NOT apply a warm compress (increases swelling).
Do NOT ignore a hernia that suddenly changes color or becomes excruciatingly painful.
seek: Requires emergency surgery to release the trapped intestine before it turns gangrenous.

title: Esophageal Food Impaction
warn: ⚠️ CHOKING VS. IMPACTION — Food is stuck in the food pipe (esophagus), not the windpipe. The patient can breathe, but cannot swallow their own saliva.
steps: Confirm the airway is clear (Can they speak? Can they breathe?). If yes, do NOT do the Heimlich maneuver.
Give the patient a cup to spit their saliva into (they will drool continuously because it cannot go down).
Have the patient sit upright.
Go to the Emergency Room if the food does not pass within a few minutes.
Reassure the patient, as panicking makes the esophageal spasms worse.
donot: Do NOT do back blows or the Heimlich maneuver if they are breathing normally (you could force the food up into their windpipe).
Do NOT force them to drink large gulps of water to "wash it down" (it will just pool on top of the food and they will inhale it into their lungs).
Do NOT try to reach down their throat with your fingers.
seek: If it doesn't pass, an ER doctor will use an endoscope to push the food into the stomach or pull it out.

title: Boerhaave Syndrome (Esophageal Rupture)
warn: ⛔ TORN ESOPHAGUS — Often caused by violent vomiting, the food pipe tears, spilling food and acid directly into the chest cavity.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This has one of the highest mortality rates of any GI emergency.
Recognize the classic presentation: severe vomiting (like food poisoning or heavy drinking), followed by a sudden "snap" or tearing feeling, and immediate severe lower chest pain.
Listen to their voice; it may sound strangely muffled or nasal.
Feel the skin around their neck and collarbones; if it feels like bubble wrap (subcutaneous emphysema), air is leaking from the torn esophagus into the tissues.
Keep the patient sitting upright and entirely NPO.
donot: Do NOT mistake the pain for a heart attack if it immediately followed violent vomiting, though both require EMS.
Do NOT let the patient drink water to soothe their throat.
Do NOT lay the patient flat.
seek: Requires emergency cardiothoracic surgery to open the chest, clean the infection, and repair the tear.

title: Button Battery Ingestion
warn: ⛔ ELECTRICAL BURN — If a button battery gets stuck in the esophagus, its electrical current creates lye, burning a hole through the tissue in just 2 hours.
steps: Go to the ER immediately or call 112. Treat this as a life-or-death emergency for children.
If the child is over 1 year old AND you have honey immediately available, give 2 teaspoons of honey every 10 minutes while driving to the ER (it coats the battery and slows the burn).
Keep the child upright.
Bring the device the battery came from, or a matching battery, to the ER so they know exactly what size/chemistry they are dealing with.
donot: Do NOT induce vomiting (this brings the corrosive battery acid back up the throat).
Do NOT let the child eat or drink anything else.
Do NOT wait to see if it passes in their stool if there is ANY chance it is stuck in the esophagus.
seek: Requires an immediate X-ray and emergency endoscopic removal.

title: Multiple Magnet Ingestion
warn: ⛔ INTESTINAL TEAR — If two or more magnets are swallowed, they will attract each other through different loops of the intestines, pinning the tissue together until it dies and tears open.
steps: Go to the ER immediately if you suspect a child swallowed more than one magnet, or a magnet and a piece of metal.
Keep the child completely NPO (no food or drink) in preparation for surgery.
Monitor for severe abdominal pain, vomiting, or fever (signs that the bowel is already tearing).
Bring similar magnets to the ER to show the doctors the strength and size.
donot: Do NOT wait for them to pass in the stool.
Do NOT give laxatives to speed up passage.
Do NOT assume it is safe just because the child feels fine right now.
seek: Requires immediate X-ray tracking and likely surgical or endoscopic removal before they pinch the bowel.

title: Acute Cholecystitis
warn: ⚠️ INFLAMED GALLBLADDER — A gallstone completely blocks the exit of the gallbladder, causing it to swell and become infected.
steps: Assess for severe, sharp pain in the Upper Right Quadrant (RUQ) of the abdomen, just under the ribcage.
Note if the pain radiates to the right shoulder or right shoulder blade.
Ask if the pain started shortly after eating a large, fatty, or greasy meal.
Go to the ER if the pain lasts longer than 2 hours, or is accompanied by fever, chills, or yellowing of the eyes (jaundice).
Keep the patient NPO.
donot: Do NOT give the patient more food to "settle" their stomach.
Do NOT ignore a fever, as it indicates the gallbladder is actively infected and could rupture.
Do NOT give strong pain meds without a doctor’s assessment.
seek: Requires ultrasound and often surgical removal of the gallbladder (cholecystectomy).

title: Ascending Cholangitis
warn: ⛔ LETHAL BILIARY INFECTION — Bacteria travel up a blocked bile duct directly into the liver. Highly fatal if untreated.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This is a severe, rapidly progressing emergency.
Look for Charcot’s Triad: 1. Fever/Chills, 2. Jaundice (yellow skin/eyes), 3. Severe Right Upper Quadrant pain.
Look for Reynolds’ Pentad (indicating severe shock): The triad above PLUS confusion and dangerously low blood pressure.
Have the patient lie down and treat for shock (keep warm).
Gather their medical history (history of gallstones or liver procedures is key).
donot: Do NOT treat the fever at home with Tylenol and wait to see if it improves.
Do NOT give any food or liquids.
Do NOT let the patient stand or walk if they are dizzy (blood pressure is dropping).
seek: Requires immediate IV antibiotics and an emergency ERCP procedure to unblock the bile duct.

title: Severe Lower GI Bleed
warn: ⚠️ MASSIVE COLON BLEEDING — Rapid loss of bright red or dark maroon blood from the rectum, often from diverticulosis or vascular malformations.
steps: Assess the amount of blood. A few drops on toilet paper is a hemorrhoid; a toilet bowl full of blood or passing large clots is an emergency.
Call 112 or go to the ER if the patient is passing large amounts of blood, feels dizzy, lightheaded, or faints.
Have the patient lie down and elevate their legs to keep blood flowing to the brain.
Keep a record of how many times they pass blood to inform the ER staff.
Keep the patient warm.
donot: Do NOT let the patient walk to the car if they feel dizzy (they will pass out and hit their head).
Do NOT assume it is "just hemorrhoids" if there is a large volume of blood.
Do NOT give aspirin or ibuprofen.
seek: Requires hospital admission, blood typing, and a colonoscopy to clip or cauterize the bleeding vessel.

title: Toxic Megacolon
warn: ⛔ COLON RUPTURE RISK — A complication of inflammatory bowel disease where the colon rapidly widens, paralyzes, and prepares to burst.
steps: Go to the ER immediately. This occurs in patients with known ulcerative colitis or severe C. diff infections.
Look for severe abdominal bloating, extreme pain, high fever, and a rapid heart rate.
Keep the patient perfectly still and lying down. Any sudden movements or pressure could cause the fragile colon to explode.
Keep the patient absolutely NPO.
Monitor for signs of shock.
donot: Do NOT give anti-diarrhea medications (like Imodium) to a patient with severe infectious diarrhea or IBD, as this can trap the toxins and TRIGGER toxic megacolon.
Do NOT press deeply on their abdomen.
Do NOT give pain medication before arrival at the hospital.
seek: Requires ICU monitoring, high-dose IV steroids/antibiotics, and potentially emergency removal of the colon.

title: Gastric Volvulus
warn: ⛔ TWISTED STOMACH — The stomach flips and twists on itself, cutting off both its entry/exit and its blood supply.
steps: Go to the ER immediately. This is an extremely painful surgical emergency.
Look for Borchardt's Triad: 1. Severe sudden upper abdominal/chest pain, 2. Violent retching but inability to actually vomit anything up, 3. Inability for a doctor to pass an NG tube.
Have the patient sit in whatever position provides the least pain.
Keep the patient strictly NPO.
donot: Do NOT give the patient water to help them vomit (it will just stretch the esophagus and cause tearing).
Do NOT assume it is a heart attack just because the pain is in the lower chest (though EMS should treat it as such until proven otherwise).
Do NOT delay transport.
seek: Requires emergency surgery to untwist the stomach and stitch it to the abdominal wall so it cannot happen again.

title: Acute Liver Failure (Acetaminophen Toxicity)
warn: ⛔ LIVER DESTRUCTION — Overdosing on Acetaminophen (Tylenol/Paracetamol) destroys the liver silently over 48 hours.
steps: If an overdose is suspected, call 112 or National Poison Information Centre — call 1800-116-117 IMMEDIATELY. Do not wait for symptoms.
Early symptoms (first 24 hours) are extremely mild: just nausea, sweating, or no symptoms at all. DO NOT be fooled.
Bring all pill bottles to the ER to calculate the exact dosage ingested.
If you have activated charcoal AND are instructed by National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117), administer it.
Keep the patient calm and at rest.
donot: Do NOT wait for the patient to look sick or turn yellow (jaundice). By the time liver symptoms appear, the damage is often irreversible.
Do NOT let them sleep it off.
Do NOT induce vomiting unless explicitly told to by National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117).
seek: Requires an ER visit to administer the antidote (N-acetylcysteine or NAC) within the first 8-24 hours to save the liver.

title: Severe Diverticulitis
warn: ⚠️ RUPTURED POUCHES — Small pouches in the colon wall become infected. If they burst, they spill feces into the abdomen.
steps: Assess for severe, localized pain in the Lower Left Quadrant (LLQ) of the abdomen.
Check for fever, chills, nausea, and changes in bowel habits (either constipation or diarrhea).
Go to the ER if the pain is severe, if they have a high fever, or if they cannot keep fluids down.
Have the patient rest quietly.
Keep the patient NPO in case they need a CT scan or surgery.
donot: Do NOT use a heating pad on the abdomen.
Do NOT give laxatives or enemas to treat the constipation (can cause the infected pouch to burst).
Do NOT give pain meds.
seek: Requires a CT scan to confirm it hasn't ruptured, followed by a liquid diet and strong antibiotics.

title: Hepatic Encephalopathy
warn: ⚠️ BRAIN POISONING — A failing liver cannot filter ammonia from the blood, which builds up and poisons the brain.
steps: Look for signs of severe confusion, sleepiness, or drastic personality changes in a patient with known liver disease (cirrhosis).

Check for "asterixis" (flapping tremor): Have the patient hold their arms straight out and bend their hands back like they are signaling "Stop." If their hands jerk or flap uncontrollably, ammonia levels are critically high.
Call 112 or transport to the ER immediately.
Keep the patient safe from falls, as they are likely highly disoriented.
donot: Do NOT assume they are intoxicated (though it mimics severe drunkenness).
Do NOT let them drive or wander.
Do NOT give sedatives to calm them down (the failing liver cannot process the sedatives, leading to a coma).
seek: Requires ER administration of Lactulose (a laxative that binds to ammonia and forces it out in the stool).

title: Intussusception
warn: ⚠️ PEDIATRIC BOWEL TRAP — One section of the intestine slides inside the adjacent part (like a telescope), cutting off blood supply.
steps: Recognize the classic signs in infants/toddlers: sudden, loud crying with knees pulled to the chest, occurring in episodes every 15-20 minutes.
Between episodes, the child may appear perfectly normal or extremely exhausted/lethargic.
Check the diaper: look for the classic "red currant jelly stool" (stool mixed with blood and mucus).
Go to the pediatric ER immediately.
Keep the child NPO (nothing by mouth).
donot: Do NOT assume it is just colic or gas if the pain is severe, episodic, and accompanied by lethargy.
Do NOT ignore blood in a baby’s stool.
Do NOT feed the baby.
seek: Requires an emergency ultrasound. Often treated non-surgically with an air or contrast enema that pushes the intestine back into place.

title: Ischemic Colitis
warn: ⚠️ LOW COLON BLOOD FLOW — Temporary reduction of blood flow to the large intestine, causing painful ulcers and bleeding.
steps: Assess for sudden, mild-to-moderate abdominal cramping on the left side, followed shortly by an urgent need to defecate.
Note the passage of bright red or maroon blood mixed with stool within 24 hours of the pain starting.
This often occurs in elderly patients with heart disease or those who recently ran a marathon (runner's colitis due to dehydration).
Go to the ER or urgent care for evaluation.
Keep the patient hydrated if they are not vomiting.
donot: Do NOT give anti-diarrhea medications.
Do NOT assume it is a GI infection (like food poisoning) if there is significant visible blood.
Do NOT ignore it in elderly patients, as it can progress to colon gangrene.
seek: Most cases resolve with IV fluids and bowel rest, but a CT scan is needed to rule out dead bowel tissue.

title: Acute Compartment Syndrome
warn: ⛔ LIMB DEATH IMMINENT — Pressure inside a muscle compartment cuts off blood flow, destroying muscle and nerve tissue within hours.
steps: Recognize the classic sign: Pain that is severely out of proportion to the visible injury, especially when stretching the muscle.
Check the 5 Ps: Pain, Pallor (pale skin), Paresthesia (numbness/tingling), Pulselessness (late sign), Paralysis (late sign).
Remove ANY restrictive clothing, bandages, splints, or jewelry immediately.
If the patient is wearing a cast and experiencing this, call 112 or get to an ER to have the cast split (bivalved) immediately.
Keep the affected limb exactly at heart level.
donot: Do NOT elevate the limb above the heart (this decreases arterial blood flow and worsens the starvation of the tissue).
Do NOT apply ice (cold causes blood vessels to constrict, worsening blood starvation).
Do NOT give pain meds and tell them to "sleep it off."
seek: Requires an emergency fasciotomy (surgical slicing of the fascia) to release the pressure before the limb requires amputation.

title: Septic Arthritis
warn: ⚠️ JOINT DESTRUCTION — Bacteria actively eating away the cartilage inside a joint cavity. Can destroy the joint permanently in days.
steps: Observe for a single joint (often the knee or hip) that becomes suddenly red, hot, swollen, and excruciatingly painful to move.
Check for systemic signs of infection, like fever or chills.
Keep the joint completely immobilized in a comfortable position.
Keep the patient strictly resting (NPO - nothing by mouth) in case emergency surgery is needed.
Call a doctor or go to the ER immediately.
donot: Do NOT attempt to massage or manipulate the joint.
Do NOT assume it is just a gout flare or arthritis acting up if there is a fever or if it is a new occurrence.
Do NOT apply a heating pad.
seek: Requires immediate joint aspiration (drawing fluid with a needle) to identify the bacteria, followed by IV antibiotics and surgical washout.

title: Knee Dislocation (Tibiofemoral)
warn: ⛔ VASCULAR EMERGENCY — A true dislocation of the knee joint (not just the kneecap) frequently tears the popliteal artery, risking loss of the leg.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This requires massive trauma, like a car crash or severe sports impact.
Look for severe deformity of the knee. (Note: It may have popped back into place on its own, but the artery may still be torn).
Check the pulse in the foot. If you cannot feel a pulse, the leg is dying.
Immobilize the leg exactly in the position you found it.
Keep the patient warm and treat for shock.
donot: Do NOT attempt to pop the knee back into place (you can sever the artery or nerves completely).
Do NOT let the patient walk or bear any weight.
Do NOT ignore a knee that "gave out" and popped back during a high-speed accident; the artery must be checked.
seek: Requires immediate ER evaluation with vascular imaging (CT Angiogram) to ensure blood flow to the lower leg is intact.

title: Hip Dislocation
warn: ⚠️ BONE DEATH RISK — The hip bone is out of the socket, stretching the blood vessels. The femoral head can die (avascular necrosis) if not reduced within 6 hours.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Often caused by knees hitting the dashboard in a car crash.
Look for the classic posture: The affected leg is usually shortened, bent at the knee, and turned completely INWARD (pointing toward the other leg).
Keep the patient lying completely flat and perfectly still.
Support the leg with rolled blankets or clothing in the exact position it is in.
Treat for shock and keep the patient calm.
donot: Do NOT try to straighten the leg.
Do NOT try to pull traction or pop the hip back into the socket.
Do NOT move the patient unless there is immediate danger (e.g., car fire).
seek: Requires emergency reduction (putting it back in place) under heavy sedation or general anesthesia in a hospital.

title: Open (Compound) Fracture
warn: ⛔ BONE INFECTION RISK — The broken bone has pierced the skin, exposing the sterile bone marrow to the outside environment.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Control massive bleeding by applying pressure AROUND the bone, not directly on it.
Cover the exposed bone and wound with the cleanest material available (preferably a sterile, saline-moistened dressing).
Immobilize the joints above and below the fracture to prevent the bone from moving and slicing more tissue.
Keep the patient warm to prevent shock.
donot: Do NOT attempt to push the bone back inside the skin.
Do NOT wash the wound or bone with water or antiseptics (this washes dirt deeper into the bone marrow).
Do NOT try to straighten a severely angled limb.
seek: Requires immediate IV antibiotics, a tetanus shot, and emergency orthopedic surgery to clean the bone (debridement) and fix the fracture.

title: High-Pressure Injection Injury
warn: ⛔ DECEPTIVE AMPUTATION RISK — Paint, grease, or solvents are injected into the hand at high pressure. It looks like a tiny pinprick but destroys the entire hand internally.
steps: Call 112 or go to the nearest trauma center immediately. Time is highly critical.
Keep the affected hand elevated to heart level.
Keep the hand completely immobilized in a functional position.
Identify exactly what substance was injected (paint, hydraulic fluid, grease, water) and bring the container/details to the ER.
Keep the patient NPO (nothing by mouth) as they will need immediate surgery.
donot: Do NOT ignore it just because it looks like a tiny cut or bee sting. The chemical is spreading through the tendon sheaths.
Do NOT squeeze or press the wound to try and push the fluid out (this forces it deeper).
Do NOT apply a tourniquet.
seek: Absolute surgical emergency. Requires wide surgical opening of the hand and arm to clean out the toxic substance and save the limb.

title: Rhabdomyolysis
warn: ⛔ KIDNEY FAILURE RISK — Massive muscle death releases myoglobin into the blood, which clogs and destroys the kidneys.
steps: Recognize the triad: Severe muscle aching/weakness, extreme muscle swelling, and dark tea-colored or cola-colored urine.
Identify the cause: extreme unaccustomed exercise (e.g., 1000 squats), prolonged immobilization (lying on the floor for 12 hours after a fall), or a crush injury.
Have the patient stop all physical activity immediately.
If the patient is fully conscious and not vomiting, have them drink large amounts of water to flush the kidneys.
Go to the ER immediately.
donot: Do NOT ignore dark urine after a heavy workout or a fall.
Do NOT give ibuprofen or naproxen for the muscle pain (these medications further stress the kidneys).
Do NOT let them continue exercising.
seek: Requires aggressive, massive IV fluid flushing in a hospital for several days to save kidney function.

title: Necrotizing Fasciitis (Flesh-Eating Bacteria)
warn: ⛔ LETHAL INFECTION — Bacteria spread along the muscle fascia, destroying tissue at a rate of an inch per hour. Mortality is very high.
steps: Call 112 or go to the ER immediately.
Look for disproportionate pain (a minor scrape that hurts agonizingly), rapid swelling, and redness that spreads visibly while you watch.
Check for skin that turns purple, black, or forms fluid-filled blisters (bullae).
Feel the skin: a crackling sensation underneath (crepitus) indicates gas-producing bacteria.
Draw a line around the red area with a pen and write the time to show doctors how fast it is spreading.
donot: Do NOT wait to see if oral antibiotics work.
Do NOT assume it is a simple spider bite or rash if the pain is excruciating and the patient has a high fever.
Do NOT apply warm compresses (this can speed bacterial growth).
seek: Requires immediate, aggressive surgical removal of the dead tissue (amputation is sometimes necessary) and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.

title: Acute Osteomyelitis
warn: ⚠️ INFECTION INSIDE THE BONE — Difficult to treat because blood flow to the bone marrow is limited. Can cause bone death.
steps: Observe for localized, deep, throbbing bone pain accompanied by fever and chills.
Check if the area over the bone is warm, red, and swollen.
Identify risk factors: recent bone surgery, metal hardware in the body, uncontrolled diabetes, or a recent severe staph infection.
Immobilize the affected limb to reduce pain.
Seek medical evaluation immediately.
donot: Do NOT wait for the pain to go away on its own.
Do NOT apply heat to the area.
Do NOT bear weight on the affected limb, as the infected bone is weak and prone to snapping (pathologic fracture).
seek: Requires bone biopsy, MRI, and often 4-6 weeks of intensive IV antibiotics. Surgical scraping of the infected bone may be needed.

title: Shoulder Dislocation
warn: ⚠️ NERVE COMPRESSION RISK — The head of the humerus pops out of the socket, risking damage to the axillary nerve.
steps: Look for a visible deformity: the shoulder will look "squared off" rather than rounded, with a visible bulge in the front or armpit.
Immobilize the arm exactly in the position the patient is holding it (usually slightly away from the body and supported by the other hand).
Use a sling and swathe (a bandage wrapping the arm to the torso) to prevent movement.
Check for numbness over the outside of the shoulder muscle (deltoid) which indicates axillary nerve damage.
Transport to the ER or urgent care.
donot: Do NOT attempt to pop it back into place yourself like in the movies (you can fracture the bone, tear the labrum, or crush nerves).
Do NOT force the arm straight to put on a splint.
Do NOT let the patient eat or drink in case they need sedation to put it back.
seek: Requires X-rays to ensure there are no fractures before a doctor performs a medical reduction to pop it back into place.

title: Open Book Pelvic Fracture
warn: ⛔ MASSIVE HEMORRHAGE — The front of the pelvis splits open, tearing the massive blood vessels residing in the pelvic bowl.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Mechanism is usually a severe crush, motorcycle crash, or fall from a height >15 feet.
Keep the patient lying completely flat on their back. Do NOT move them.
If trained, apply a commercial pelvic binder. If not, use a folded bedsheet: wrap it around the hips (at the greater trochanters/hip bones, NOT the waist) and pull tight to close the "open book".
Treat for severe hemorrhagic shock (keep them warm with blankets).
Be prepared for the patient to lose consciousness due to blood loss.
donot: Do NOT "rock" or press down on the hips to see if they are broken (this tears clots and increases bleeding).
Do NOT roll the patient onto their side (log-roll) unless they are choking on vomit.
Do NOT elevate the legs.
seek: Requires massive blood transfusions and immediate trauma surgery (often interventional radiology to plug the bleeding arteries).

title: Femoral Shaft Fracture
warn: ⛔ SHOCK RISK — The largest bone in the body is broken. The thigh can hide up to 1.5 liters of internal bleeding.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Keep the patient lying flat and entirely still.
Control any external bleeding with direct pressure or a tourniquet if it is massive and spurting.
Support the leg with rolled towels or blankets along the sides to prevent it from rolling or moving.
Keep the patient warm to prevent shock.
Monitor airway and breathing.
donot: Do NOT pull traction on the leg unless you are an EMS provider with a specific traction splint.
Do NOT elevate the broken leg.
Do NOT allow the patient to attempt to stand or bear any weight whatsoever.
seek: Requires EMS transport, heavy pain management, and orthopedic surgery (intramedullary nailing).

title: Pediatric Supracondylar Humerus Fracture
warn: ⚠️ ARTERY AND NERVE ENTRAPMENT — A common break just above the elbow in kids. The sharp bone fragments easily sever the brachial artery.
steps: Keep the child completely calm and still. This usually happens when falling on an outstretched arm (e.g., falling off monkey bars).
Immobilize the arm exactly in the position found. Do not straighten it.
Check the hand immediately: Is it pale, cold, or blue? Can you feel a pulse at the wrist?
Ask the child to wiggle their fingers and check if they feel numbness (nerve check).
Go to the ER immediately, especially if the hand is cold or numb.
donot: Do NOT bend or straighten the elbow to put it in a sling.
Do NOT wrap a bandage tightly around the elbow.
Do NOT delay medical care if the hand is pale or pulseless (Volkmann’s contracture can permanently claw the hand).
seek: Requires urgent orthopedic evaluation. If pulseless, requires immediate surgery to pin the bone and restore blood flow.

title: Achilles Tendon Rupture
warn: ⚠️ LOSS OF MOBILITY — The tendon connecting the calf to the heel snaps entirely, often feeling like being kicked in the back of the leg.
steps: Have the patient stop moving immediately.
Ask what they felt: A loud "pop" or "snap," feeling like someone kicked them, and sudden inability to point their toes downward.
Have the patient lie on their stomach and bend their knee to 90 degrees. Squeeze the calf muscle. If the foot DOES NOT point (plantarflex) when you squeeze, the tendon is ruptured (Thompson Test).
Apply ice to the back of the ankle.
Keep weight completely off the foot.
donot: Do NOT let the patient try to walk it off.
Do NOT massage the calf or tendon.
Do NOT stretch the calf muscle.
seek: Requires orthopedic evaluation for a walking boot/cast (conservative) or surgical repair to reattach the tendon.

title: Ankle Fracture-Dislocation
warn: ⚠️ SKIN AND NERVE THREAT — The ankle is broken and completely out of joint. If the bone pushes hard against the skin, the skin will die from lack of blood flow.
steps: Call 112 or go to the ER immediately. The foot may be pointing in a completely unnatural direction.
Check the skin where the bone is pressing against it from the inside (tenting). If the skin is stark white and stretched tight, it is a critical emergency.
Check for a pulse in the foot and check capillary refill in the toes.
Immobilize the leg with a pillow splint (wrap a bulky pillow around the ankle and tape it gently).
Elevate the leg slightly if it does not cause increased pain.
donot: Do NOT try to pull the foot back into alignment unless you are a trained medic and the foot is pulseless/blue.
Do NOT let the patient bear any weight.
Do NOT apply a tight wrap or ACE bandage.
seek: Requires emergency reduction in the ER to relieve pressure on the skin/nerves, followed by surgery (ORIF) with plates and screws.

title: Osteoporotic Spinal Compression Fracture
warn: ⚠️ VERTEBRAL COLLAPSE — The bone is so brittle that a simple sneeze, cough, or minor bump causes the vertebrae to crush downward.
steps: Suspect this in an elderly patient complaining of sudden, severe mid-to-low back pain after a very minor event.
Have the patient lie flat on their back, which usually relieves the pain by taking weight off the spine.
Check for any signs of nerve compression: numbness in the legs, weakness, or loss of bowel/bladder control.
Call a doctor or go to the ER if pain is severe or nerve symptoms are present.
Help them roll gently onto their side to get up, rather than sitting straight up.
donot: Do NOT force the patient to sit or stand if it causes agonizing pain.
Do NOT perform spinal manipulations or massages.
Do NOT ignore new back pain in the elderly, assuming it is just a muscle ache.
seek: Requires an X-ray to confirm. Severe cases may require a procedure called kyphoplasty, where cement is injected into the crushed bone.

title: Clavicle (Collarbone) Fracture
warn: ⚠️ PUNCTURE RISK — Sharp fragments of the broken collarbone can threaten the lung underneath or the subclavian blood vessels.
steps: Look for the classic signs: The patient supports the arm of the injured side with their other hand, and the shoulder drops forward and down.
Check the skin over the collarbone for a visible bump or "tenting" where the sharp bone is pushing up.
Immobilize the arm in a sling to take the weight of the arm off the broken collarbone.
Apply an ice pack to the swelling.
Transport to an ER or urgent care.
donot: Do NOT attempt to push the bone bump back down.
Do NOT let the patient raise their arm above their shoulder.
Do NOT use a figure-eight brace tightly (it is largely outdated and can compress nerves).
seek: Requires X-rays. Most heal in a sling, but if the bone is severely displaced or tenting the skin, surgery (plating) is needed.

title: Extensor/Flexor Tendon Laceration
warn: ⚠️ LOSS OF FUNCTION — A deep cut to the hand severs the cables (tendons) that pull the fingers straight or curl them into a fist.
steps: Control the bleeding with direct pressure and elevate the hand.
Assess function: Ask the patient to bend and straighten the finger beyond the cut. If the tip of the finger stays floppy or they cannot make a fist/open the hand, a tendon is cut.
Do not probe the wound or try to find the ends of the tendon.
Clean the wound gently if dirty, and cover with a sterile dressing.
Immobilize the hand in a bulky dressing or splint.
donot: Do NOT ignore a deep cut just because the bleeding stopped (if the tendon is cut, the finger will be permanently disabled).
Do NOT pull on anything visible in the wound.
Do NOT use superglue to close a deep hand wound.
seek: Requires prompt evaluation by a hand surgeon. Tendons retract like rubber bands when cut and must be surgically fished out and sewn together.

title: Acute Gout Flare
warn: ⚠️ CRYSTAL ARTHRITIS — Uric acid crystallizes inside the joint. It mimics an infection and causes such extreme pain that even a bedsheet touching it is agonizing.
steps: Recognize the typical presentation: Sudden onset (usually overnight) of extreme pain, redness, and swelling, most commonly in the base of the big toe.
Have the patient rest and elevate the foot.
Protect the joint from any physical contact (use a rigid box over the foot if sleeping to keep blankets off).
If the patient has prescribed gout medications (like Colchicine or Indomethacin), have them take it immediately.
Apply ice wrapped in a towel for 20 minutes to reduce inflammation.
donot: Do NOT take aspirin, as it can worsen the uric acid levels.
Do NOT drink alcohol or eat red meat/shellfish during a flare.
Do NOT apply heat to the joint.
seek: If it is the first attack, a doctor must evaluate it to rule out a severe joint infection (Septic Arthritis). Prescriptions are needed to break the flare.

title: Extremity Crush Injury (Prolonged)
warn: ⛔ TOXIC RELEASE — If a limb is crushed for over 30 minutes, releasing the pressure sends deadly potassium and acid to the heart.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Note exactly how long the limb has been pinned.
If the limb has been crushed for MORE than 30 minutes, wait for EMS to arrive before removing the weight if the scene is safe. They must start IV fluids first.
If you MUST remove the weight to save their life from immediate danger (fire, collapse), apply two tourniquets tight side-by-side ABOVE the crush injury BEFORE lifting the weight.
This traps the deadly toxins in the dead limb until a hospital can manage it.
Keep the patient warm and calm.
donot: Do NOT suddenly release a heavy load from a limb after an hour without applying a tourniquet or having EMS present (it causes "smiling death" - they seem fine, then their heart stops).
Do NOT remove the tourniquets once applied.
Do NOT give the patient anything to eat or drink.
seek: Requires advanced life support, massive fluid resuscitation, sodium bicarbonate to protect the heart, and potential emergency amputation or fasciotomy.

title: Infant CPR
warn: ⛔ Use 2-finger technique. Compression depth 1.5 inches. Rate 100-120/min.
steps: Check responsiveness: flick bottom of foot.
Call 112 (or instruct someone to call).
Check breathing (no more than 10 seconds).
If no breathing: 30 compressions with 2 fingers on lower half of sternum.
Compression depth: 1.5 inches (4cm). Rate 100-120/min.
2 rescue breaths: cover mouth AND nose with your mouth, gentle puff until chest rises.
Continue 30:2 ratio until EMS arrives.
donot: Do NOT compress on xiphoid process.
Do NOT give full adult breaths — small gentle puffs only.
seek: Immediate — all pediatric cardiac arrest.

title: Infant Choking (Under 1 Year)
warn: ⛔ NO HEIMLICH MANEUVER — Infants require back slaps and chest thrusts. Abdominal thrusts will crush their internal organs.
steps: Assess: If the baby cannot cry, cough, or breathe, act immediately.
Call 112 or shout for someone to do it.
Sit down. Support the baby face-down along your forearm, resting on your thigh. Support their head/jaw with your hand.
Deliver 5 firm back slaps between the shoulder blades using the heel of your other hand.
If the object doesn't dislodge, flip the baby face-up on your other forearm.
Place 2 fingers in the center of the baby's chest (just below the nipple line) and give 5 quick chest thrusts (about 1.5 inches deep).
Repeat 5 back slaps and 5 chest thrusts until the object pops out or the baby becomes unconscious. Begin infant CPR if unconscious.
donot: Do NOT perform a blind finger sweep (you will push the object deeper into the tiny airway).
Do NOT pick the baby up by the feet.
Do NOT perform abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) on an infant under 1 year old.
seek: Always seek medical evaluation after a choking event, even if the object is expelled, to check for airway damage.

title: Fever in a Neonate (<28 Days Old)
warn: ⛔ IMMUNE SYSTEM DEFICIT — Any rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a baby under 28 days old is a medical emergency.
steps: Take the baby’s temperature rectally (it is the only accurate method for newborns).
If the temperature is 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, go to the pediatric emergency room immediately.
Observe for other signs of neonatal sepsis: extreme lethargy, poor feeding, grunting while breathing, or a bulging soft spot (fontanelle) on the head.
Keep the baby lightly clothed to prevent further overheating, but do not induce shivering.
donot: Do NOT give Tylenol (Acetaminophen) or Motrin (Ibuprofen) to a newborn to bring the fever down (it masks the severity of the infection and delays lifesaving care).
Do NOT assume it is just a cold or that they are wrapped in too many blankets.
Do NOT wait until morning to call the pediatrician.
seek: Requires immediate ER evaluation for blood cultures, a spinal tap (lumbar puncture), and IV antibiotics to prevent fatal sepsis or meningitis.

title: Swallowed Button Battery
warn: ⛔ INTERNAL TISSUE BURN — A button battery stuck in the esophagus completes an electrical circuit, burning a hole through the throat in under 2 hours.
steps: Go to the Emergency Room immediately if you even SUSPECT a child swallowed a button battery.
If the child is over 1 year old and you have pure honey, give 2 teaspoons of honey every 10 minutes while on the way to the ER. (Honey coats the battery and slows the tissue burn).
Keep the child upright.
Bring the device the battery came from or the battery packaging to the ER to identify the size/chemistry.
donot: Do NOT induce vomiting (the battery will burn the esophagus again on the way up).
Do NOT give honey to a child under 1 year old (risk of infant botulism).
Do NOT let the child eat or drink anything else.
seek: Requires immediate emergency X-ray and surgical/endoscopic removal to save the child’s esophagus and vocal cords.

title: Intussusception
warn: ⚠️ TELESCOPING BOWEL — The intestine folds inside itself like a telescope, cutting off its own blood supply. Most common between 6 to 36 months.
steps: Watch for a classic pattern: The child suddenly screams and pulls their knees to their chest in agonizing pain, then appears completely fine and playful 15 minutes later, only to repeat the cycle.
Check the diaper: A late, critical sign is stool mixed with blood and mucus (often described as looking like "currant jelly").
The child may vomit frequently and become progressively weaker.
Go to the ER immediately if this pain cycle occurs.
donot: Do NOT ignore the severe pain just because the child seems perfectly fine between spasms.
Do NOT give pain medication or laxatives at home.
Do NOT give the child anything to eat or drink.
seek: Requires an emergency ultrasound. Often treated with an air or contrast enema to pop the intestine back out; requires surgery if the enema fails.

title: Nursemaid’s Elbow (Radial Head Subluxation)
warn: ⚠️ PARTIAL DISLOCATION — Caused by a sudden pull on a child’s straight arm (e.g., swinging them by the hands or pulling them up a curb).
steps: Recognize the sign: The child will suddenly cry and refuse to use one arm, holding it slightly bent and pressed against their stomach. They will strongly resist you touching or moving it.
There is usually no visible swelling or bruising.
Keep the arm in the position the child finds most comfortable.
Support the arm and take the child to urgent care or the ER.
Distract the child with toys or videos to keep them calm.
donot: Do NOT try to pop the elbow back into place yourself (you could cause a fracture if the injury is actually a broken bone).
Do NOT force the child to straighten the arm.
Do NOT swing children by their hands or wrists.
seek: A doctor or triage nurse can perform a simple, quick physical maneuver to snap the ligament back into place, providing instant relief.

title: BRUE (Brief Resolved Unexplained Event)
warn: ⚠️ TERRIFYING BUT RESOLVED — The infant suddenly turns pale or blue, stops breathing, and goes totally limp or stiff, but then returns to completely normal within a minute.
steps: Stay calm. If the child is fully back to normal, the immediate crisis has passed.
Call 112 or immediately drive to the Pediatric ER (this is a massive red flag for underlying cardiac, respiratory, or neurological issues).
Note exactly how long the event lasted, what color the baby turned, and if they were stiff or limp.
Take a video of the child’s breathing or behavior afterward if anything seems off, to show the doctor.
Keep the child stimulated and awake.
donot: Do NOT shake the baby if they stop breathing (rub their back or flick the soles of their feet instead).
Do NOT ignore the event just because the baby seems perfectly fine now.
Do NOT put the baby down for a nap immediately afterward without medical clearance.
seek: Requires a thorough pediatric evaluation (EKG, observation) to rule out seizures, heart arrhythmias, or severe reflux.

title: Abusive Head Trauma (Shaken Baby Syndrome)
warn: ⛔ FATAL BRAIN DAMAGE — Violent shaking destroys a baby’s fragile brain tissue and shears blood vessels, causing massive internal bleeding.
steps: Call 112 immediately if a baby suddenly becomes completely unresponsive, has a seizure, or has extreme difficulty breathing without a clear cause.
If the baby stops breathing, begin infant CPR.
Look for subtle signs if the baby is conscious: extreme irritability, inability to track movement with their eyes, pale/blue skin, or vomiting without a fever.
Provide doctors with absolute honesty about what happened; knowing the child was shaken dictates the immediate CT scans needed to save their life.
donot: Do NOT ever shake a baby out of frustration (put the baby in a safe crib and walk out of the room if you are overwhelmed).
Do NOT delay calling EMS out of fear of getting in trouble.
Do NOT pick the baby up roughly or move their head/neck more than necessary.
seek: Absolute emergency requiring pediatric ICU care. Medical staff are required by law to report suspected abuse.

title: Severe RSV / Bronchiolitis
warn: ⚠️ AIRWAY SWELLING — A common virus in adults causes thick mucus and severe inflammation in the tiny airways of infants, acting like an asthma attack.
steps: Remove the baby’s shirt and watch their chest: If the skin is sucking in deeply between the ribs or at the base of the neck with every breath (retractions), they are in respiratory distress.
Listen for a grunting sound every time they breathe out, or look for their nostrils flaring open wide.
Keep the infant upright to make breathing easier.
Use a nasal aspirator (like a NoseFrida) and saline drops to suck out as much mucus from the nose as possible (infants are obligate nose-breathers).
Go to the ER or call 112 if they cannot feed due to breathing difficulty or if their lips turn blue.
donot: Do NOT give over-the-counter cough or cold medicines to infants.
Do NOT lay the baby flat on their back if they are struggling to breathe.
Do NOT expose the child to cigarette smoke, which severely worsens the condition.
seek: May require hospitalization for deep suctioning, IV fluids, and high-flow oxygen support.

title: Swallowed Multiple Magnets
warn: ⛔ BOWEL DESTRUCTION — If two or more high-powered magnets are swallowed, they will attract each other through the walls of different intestines, ripping holes in the bowel.
steps: Go to the Emergency Room IMMEDIATELY if you suspect a child swallowed more than one magnet, or a magnet and a piece of metal.
Keep the child strictly NPO (nothing by mouth) as they will likely need emergency surgery.
Bring a sample of the magnet (if you have the toy) to show the doctors the size and strength.
Monitor for signs of bowel perforation: severe abdominal pain, a hard/rigid stomach, and vomiting.
donot: Do NOT induce vomiting.
Do NOT assume "it will just pass" like a coin (a single magnet might pass, but multiple magnets are a surgical emergency).
Do NOT give the child anything to eat or drink to "push it down."
seek: Requires immediate X-rays. If the magnets are in different loops of the bowel, emergency surgery is required to remove them before they erode the tissue.

title: Pyloric Stenosis
warn: ⚠️ SEVERE DEHYDRATION RISK — The valve leaving the stomach thickens and shuts completely, forcefully blocking milk from entering the intestines. Usually occurs at 3-6 weeks of age.
steps: Recognize the classic sign: Forceful, projectile vomiting of milk (shooting several feet across the room) immediately after feeding.
Note that the baby is usually extremely hungry immediately after vomiting.
Check for signs of severe dehydration: no wet diapers for 6 hours, no tears when crying, and a sunken soft spot on the head.
Go to the ER or pediatric urgent care.
donot: Do NOT mistake this for normal baby spit-up (spit-up dribbles out; pyloric stenosis is violent and forceful).
Do NOT keep trying to force-feed the baby large amounts if they are continuously vomiting.
Do NOT give water to a newborn.
seek: Requires an ultrasound to diagnose. It is completely cured with a minor, routine surgery (pyloromyotomy) to open the valve.

title: Tet Spell (Hypercyanotic Spell)
warn: ⛔ SUDDEN OXYGEN DROP — In children with specific congenital heart defects, sudden crying or agitation causes blood to bypass the lungs, turning the child rapidly blue.
steps: IMMEDIATELY place the child in a knee-to-chest position (tuck their knees firmly up against their chest). This forces blood back into the lungs.
For an older toddler, instruct them to squat down.
Calm the child down as quickly as possible (crying worsens the oxygen drop). Hold them, rock them, and speak soothingly.
Call 112 if the spell does not resolve within a minute of the knee-to-chest position, or if the child becomes limp/unresponsive.
Provide supplemental oxygen if you have it prescribed at home.
donot: Do NOT let the child continue crying or throwing a tantrum.
Do NOT lay the child flat on their back with their legs straight.
Do NOT panic; your anxiety will agitate the child further.
seek: Requires emergency medical intervention with medications (like morphine to calm them and beta-blockers) if the knee-to-chest position fails.

title: Pediatric Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
warn: ⛔ FATAL ACID BUILDUP — Often the very first sign a child has undiagnosed Type 1 Diabetes. The blood turns acidic because there is no insulin.
steps: Look for the classic lead-up: Weeks of excessive thirst, constant urination (even bedwetting in potty-trained kids), and weight loss despite eating.
Recognize the DKA crisis: Deep, rapid, heavy breathing (Kussmaul respirations), vomiting, extreme lethargy, and breath that smells like fruity nail polish remover.
Call 112 or go to the ER immediately if the child is vomiting and confused.
If the child is a known diabetic, check their blood sugar and ketones immediately.
donot: Do NOT assume the rapid breathing is an asthma attack or a respiratory infection if they don't have a cough/wheeze.
Do NOT give sugary fluids to a child in DKA.
Do NOT give large doses of insulin at home if they are vomiting and lethargic (they need specialized IV fluids in the ICU to prevent brain swelling).
seek: Requires Pediatric ICU admission for carefully calculated IV insulin drips and fluid replacement to prevent cerebral edema.

title: Toxic Ingestion (e.g., Iron Pills, Blood Pressure Meds)
warn: ⛔ ONE PILL CAN KILL — Certain adult medications (like heart meds, opioids, or adult iron supplements) are fatal to a toddler in a single dose.
steps: If you find a child with an open pill bottle or suspect they swallowed medication, call National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) (or 112 in emergencies) IMMEDIATELY.
Find the exact pill bottle to tell the operator the name and dosage of the medication.
Sweep the child’s mouth with your finger to remove any unswallowed pills.
Estimate how many pills are missing.
If the child is unconscious, seizing, or having trouble breathing, call 112 immediately and prepare for CPR.
donot: Do NOT induce vomiting (give syrup of ipecac) unless explicitly instructed by National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) (it is largely outdated and dangerous).
Do NOT give milk or water to "dilute" it unless told to do so.
Do NOT wait for symptoms to appear (iron poisoning, for example, has a delayed phase where the child seems fine before liver failure sets in).
seek: Requires immediate ER observation, potential stomach pumping (lavage), activated charcoal, or specific antidotes.

title: Midgut Volvulus (Malrotation)
warn: ⛔ INTESTINAL DEATH — The intestines twist around themselves, cutting off their main blood supply. The bowel can die within hours.
steps: Recognize the ultimate red flag: Bilious (dark green or bright yellow-green) vomiting in an infant or child.
The child will have a swollen, hard, and extremely tender belly.
They may be screaming in agony and pulling their legs up.
Go to the Emergency Room IMMEDIATELY. Do not wait for a pediatrician appointment.
Keep the child strictly NPO (no food, no milk, no water).
donot: Do NOT ignore green vomit in a baby. It is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise.
Do NOT feed the baby to see if they can keep the next meal down.
Do NOT give pain medicine, which could mask the worsening condition.
seek: Absolute surgical emergency. Requires immediate upper GI contrast study and emergency surgery to untwist the bowel.

title: Testicular Torsion
warn: ⚠️ ORGAN LOSS RISK — The testicle twists on its own spermatic cord, cutting off its blood supply. Most common in boys ages 12-18.
steps: Acknowledge the complaint: Sudden, severe, one-sided pain in the scrotum or lower abdomen, often waking the boy up from sleep.
Look for extreme swelling, redness, or one testicle sitting much higher than the other.
Go to the Emergency Room immediately. You have a 4 to 6-hour window to save the testicle.
Keep the patient NPO (no food or drink) as they will likely need surgery.
donot: Do NOT delay going to the ER out of embarrassment (assure the teen that doctors see this every day).
Do NOT assume it is a sports strain or pulled groin muscle if the testicle itself is swollen and agonizingly painful.
Do NOT apply heat.
seek: Requires immediate ultrasound and emergency urologic surgery to untwist the cord and pin both testicles down to prevent recurrence.

title: Kawasaki Disease
warn: ⚠️ HEART ANEURYSM RISK — Unexplained inflammation of the blood vessels, particularly the coronary arteries surrounding the heart. Primarily affects kids under 5.
