steps: Watch for the main diagnostic criteria: A high fever lasting 5 or more days that does NOT respond to Tylenol/Motrin.

Look for the physical signs: Bloodshot eyes (without crusty discharge), bright red chapped lips, a "strawberry" tongue (red and bumpy), swollen lymph nodes in the neck, and a rash on the torso/genitals.
Check the hands and feet: they will often be red and swollen, and the skin may peel later on.
Go to the pediatric ER or doctor immediately if these symptoms align.
donot: Do NOT ignore a fever lasting more than 5 days in a child.
Do NOT assume it is just a stubborn viral rash.
Do NOT give aspirin to a child unless explicitly instructed by a doctor (this is the ONE exception where doctors WILL use aspirin in kids to treat Kawasaki, but it must be heavily monitored).
seek: Requires hospitalization for IV Immunoglobulin (IVIG) and high-dose aspirin to prevent permanent coronary artery aneurysms.

title: Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C)
warn: ⛔ IMMUNE SYSTEM OVERDRIVE — A rare but severe complication occurring 2-6 weeks after a viral infection (like COVID-19), causing severe organ inflammation.
steps: Look for an ongoing fever accompanied by severe abdominal pain, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Watch for a red rash, bloodshot eyes, and extreme exhaustion or confusion.
Go to the ER immediately if the child exhibits signs of shock: pale/blue skin, racing heart, rapid breathing, or severe lethargy.
Inform the doctors if the child had a known viral infection or exposure in the past month, even if they were asymptomatic then.
donot: Do NOT write off severe abdominal pain and fever as a simple "stomach bug" if the child becomes lethargic or develops a rash.
Do NOT wait to see if they improve at home if they are showing signs of shock or extreme weakness.
seek: Requires Pediatric ICU admission for cardiac monitoring, steroids, IVIG, and blood pressure support.

title: Breath-Holding Spell (Cyanotic)
warn: ⚠️ TERRIFYING BUT HARMLESS — During extreme crying or a tantrum, a toddler (usually 1-3 years old) exhales, stops breathing, turns blue, and passes out.
steps: Stay completely calm. This is an involuntary reflex, not intentional bad behavior, and it does not cause brain damage.
Lay the child flat on their back or side. Once they pass out, their body’s autonomic nervous system will reset and force them to take a breath within 30-60 seconds.
Protect their head from hitting the floor if they collapse.
Ensure the airway is clear.
Once they wake up, comfort them, but do not give in to the tantrum that caused it (which reinforces the behavior).
donot: Do NOT start CPR or chest compressions unless they do not start breathing on their own after a minute.
Do NOT throw water on their face or shake them.
Do NOT put anything in their mouth.
seek: Discuss with a pediatrician at the next visit to rule out iron-deficiency anemia or arrhythmias, but emergency care is rarely needed unless they don’t wake up.

title: Severe Pediatric Dehydration
warn: ⚠️ RAPID DETERIORATION — Children lose body fluids much faster than adults and can go into hypovolemic shock rapidly from simple gastroenteritis.
steps: Assess for severe signs: The child has absolutely no tears when crying, a dry/sticky mouth, sunken eyes, and has not peed in 8+ hours (dry diapers).
Assess mental status: Are they unusually sleepy, difficult to wake up, or limp? (This is a late, critical sign).
If conscious and able to swallow, give tiny, frequent sips of an oral rehydration solution (Pedialyte) via a syringe (e.g., 1 teaspoon every 5 minutes).
If they cannot keep fluids down, or are extremely lethargic, go to the ER immediately.
donot: Do NOT give plain water, apple juice, or sports drinks to a severely dehydrated infant or toddler (it lacks the correct sodium balance and worsens diarrhea).
Do NOT force large gulps of fluid (they will just vomit it back up).
Do NOT give anti-diarrhea medications (like Imodium) to young children.
seek: Requires hospital evaluation for IV fluids or a nasogastric tube to rehydrate safely.

title: Reye’s Syndrome
warn: ⚠️ DEADLY MEDICATION ERROR — Caused by giving aspirin to a child recovering from a viral infection (like the flu or chickenpox). Causes massive brain swelling and liver failure.
steps: Recognize the sudden onset: A child recovering from a virus suddenly starts vomiting uncontrollably and acting unusually aggressive, confused, or deeply lethargic.
Check all medications the child was given recently (look for bismuth subsalicylate/Pepto-Bismol, or anything containing acetylsalicylic acid).
Call 112 or go to the ER immediately.
Keep the child’s head elevated to help reduce brain swelling.
donot: Do NOT ever give Aspirin to anyone under 18 unless specifically directed by a doctor.
Do NOT dismiss continuous vomiting after a viral illness as just a "relapse."
Do NOT delay emergency care; brain damage occurs rapidly.
seek: Requires immediate Pediatric ICU admission to manage intracranial pressure, prevent bleeding, and support liver function.

title: Heat Stroke
warn: ⛔ Core temp >104°F (40°C). Brain damage begins rapidly. COOL AGGRESSIVELY.
steps: Move to cool environment immediately.
Call 112.
Remove excess clothing.
Aggressive cooling: ice packs to neck, axillae, groin, and wrists.
Immerse in cold water if available and patient conscious.
Fan patient while misting with cool water.
Do NOT give oral fluids if altered consciousness.
Target core temp <102°F before hospital transport.
donot: Do NOT give aspirin or paracetamol (ineffective, may worsen).
Do NOT use ice bath if patient has exertional heat stroke and IV access not available (vasoconstriction).
seek: All heat stroke = immediate emergency.

title: Hypothermia
warn: ⚠️ Ventricular fibrillation risk at core temp <86°F (30°C). Handle gently.
steps: Move to warm environment. Prevent further heat loss.
Remove wet clothing; cover with blankets.
Handle patient gently — avoid jostling (VFib risk in cold heart).
Warm center of body first (core warming): warm blankets, warm drinks if conscious.
Warm IV fluids if available.
Do NOT rub extremities.
CPR if arrested — may require prolonged resuscitation until warmed.
donot: Do NOT rub extremities.
Do NOT give alcohol.
Do NOT apply direct heat.
seek: Moderate/severe hypothermia always requires hospital. "Not dead until warm and dead."

title: Heat Exhaustion
warn: ⚠️ PRECURSOR TO HEAT STROKE — The body is losing water and salt rapidly, but the core temperature is still manageable.
steps: Move the patient to a cool, shaded, or air-conditioned environment immediately.
Have them lie down and elevate their legs to improve blood flow to the brain.
Remove extra clothing and heavy gear.
Provide cool water or a sports drink. Have them take small, frequent sips rather than chugging it.
Cool the skin by spraying water or applying cool, wet cloths to the head and neck.
Call 112 if they vomit, become confused, or if symptoms do not improve after 30 minutes.
donot: Do NOT give salt tablets (they can cause stomach cramps and worsen dehydration).
Do NOT give alcohol or caffeinated drinks.
Do NOT let them return to the hot environment or physical activity that day.
seek: If mental confusion starts or sweating suddenly stops, it has progressed to Heat Stroke (a critical emergency).

title: Severe Frostbite
warn: ⚠️ TISSUE DEATH — Ice crystals form inside the skin and muscle cells, destroying them. High risk of amputation.
steps: Move the patient to a warm environment as soon as possible.
Remove any wet clothing and constricting items (like tight rings or watches) before swelling begins.
Protect the frozen area from further cold or physical trauma.
If medical help is delayed AND there is ZERO chance the tissue will refreeze, gently submerge the area in warm (NOT hot, ~104°F/40°C) water for 20-30 minutes until the skin turns red/purple and soft.
Loosely bandage the area with dry, sterile dressings. Place gauze between affected fingers or toes.
donot: Do NOT rub or massage the frozen tissue (this grinds the ice crystals into the cells, destroying them).
Do NOT use dry heat like a hair dryer, radiator, or campfire (frozen skin cannot feel heat and will severely burn).
Do NOT thaw the tissue if there is any chance it could freeze again (refreezing thawed tissue guarantees amputation).
seek: Requires hospital management for pain control (thawing is excruciating) and specialized wound care to save the limb.

title: Venomous Snakebite (Pit Vipers/Elapids)
warn: ⛔ SYSTEMIC TOXICITY — Venom can cause rapid tissue necrosis, uncontrolled bleeding, or respiratory paralysis depending on the snake.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Time to antivenom is the most critical factor.
Keep the patient completely calm and still to slow the spread of venom through the lymphatic system.
Remove all rings, watches, and tight clothing near the bite immediately, as massive swelling will occur.
Keep the bitten limb immobilized and positioned roughly at or slightly below heart level.
Note the time of the bite and the appearance of the snake (if seen safely). Do NOT try to catch it.
donot: Do NOT apply a tourniquet (this concentrates the venom and guarantees loss of the limb).
Do NOT cut the wound or attempt to suck the venom out (this is a Hollywood myth and causes severe infections).
Do NOT apply ice to the bite (it worsens tissue necrosis).
seek: Requires immediate transport to an ER equipped with specific antivenom.

title: Toxic Spider Bite (Widow/Recluse)
warn: ⚠️ SEVERE VENOM REACTION — Black Widow venom causes agonizing, rigid muscle spasms. Brown Recluse venom destroys localized tissue.
steps: Wash the bite area gently with soap and water.
For a suspected Black Widow bite: Apply an ice pack to reduce pain and swelling. Keep the patient calm.
For a suspected Brown Recluse bite: Elevate the limb and avoid applying heat.
Watch for systemic symptoms: severe abdominal cramping, difficulty breathing, sweating, or a dark blister forming at the site.
Go to the Emergency Room or urgent care.
donot: Do NOT attempt to cut out the venom or bite area.
Do NOT assume severe abdominal cramps are appendicitis if the patient felt a sharp pinprick shortly before (classic Black Widow symptom).
Do NOT ignore a bite that develops a red, white, and blue "bullseye" pattern.
seek: Widow bites may require muscle relaxants, pain meds, or specific antivenom. Recluse bites require wound monitoring to prevent severe necrotic ulcers.

title: Severe Jellyfish Sting (Box Jelly/Irukandji)
warn: ⛔ CARDIAC ARREST RISK — Tropical Box Jellyfish venom is among the deadliest on earth and can stop the heart within minutes.
steps: Get the patient out of the water immediately.
Call 112 for any sting in tropical waters causing severe pain, or if the patient has difficulty breathing.
DOUSE the area liberally with VINEGAR for at least 30 seconds. This deactivates the un-fired stinging cells (nematocysts).
Pluck any visible tentacles off with tweezers or a gloved hand AFTER vinegar application.
If vinegar is not available, rinse with seawater.
Monitor airway and breathing constantly; be prepared to start CPR.
donot: Do NOT rinse with fresh water or bottled water (this causes all remaining cells to fire their venom immediately).
Do NOT pee on it (urine is not acidic enough and can trigger the stinging cells).
Do NOT rub the area with a towel or sand.
seek: Tropical stings require immediate emergency medical care and potentially Box Jellyfish antivenom. Note: Non-tropical/minor stings are treated with hot water immersion, not vinegar.

title: High-Altitude Cerebral Edema (HACE)
warn: ⛔ LETHAL BRAIN SWELLING — The brain swells due to lack of oxygen at high altitudes, pushing against the skull.
steps: DESCEND IMMEDIATELY. Do not wait for morning. This is the only definitive cure.
Recognize the hallmark sign: Ataxia. Ask the person to walk a straight line heel-to-toe. If they stagger like they are heavily intoxicated, they have HACE.
Other signs include severe confusion, hallucinations, and extreme lethargy.
Administer supplemental oxygen if available.
If descent is impossible due to weather/terrain, place the patient in a portable hyperbaric chamber (Gamow bag) if equipped.
donot: Do NOT let the patient sleep or rest at the current altitude.
Do NOT let them descend alone (they are confused and will get lost or fall).
Do NOT confuse HACE with simple fatigue.
seek: A dire emergency. Requires immediate descent, oxygen, and steroids (Dexamethasone) administered by a medical professional.

title: Decompression Sickness (The Bends)
warn: ⛔ NITROGEN BUBBLES IN TISSUE — Ascending too fast from a dive causes dissolved nitrogen to form physical bubbles in the blood, joints, and brain.
steps: Call 112 and explicitly state the patient is a scuba diver with suspected decompression sickness.
Administer 100% pure oxygen immediately if available (this helps wash nitrogen out of the blood).
Lay the patient completely flat. If they are vomiting, place them in the recovery position (on their side).
Keep the patient warm and hydrated with non-alcoholic fluids if they are fully conscious.
Gather their dive computer or log to give to the medical team.
donot: Do NOT put the diver back in the water to try and "recompress" them (this is highly dangerous and fatal).
Do NOT let the patient fly or drive to high altitude (this makes the bubbles expand further).
Do NOT use pain medications that mask symptoms.
seek: Requires specialized treatment in a Hyperbaric Oxygen Chamber to crush the bubbles and safely off-gas the nitrogen.

title: Toxic Plant / Mushroom Ingestion
warn: ⛔ DELAYED ORGAN FAILURE — Some highly toxic mushrooms (like the Death Cap) cause initial vomiting, followed by a false recovery, and then total liver failure days later.
steps: Call National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) or 112 immediately upon suspected ingestion of an unknown wild plant, berry, or mushroom.
Collect a sample of the exact plant or mushroom eaten. Include leaves, stems, roots, and the soil it was growing in if possible. Place it in a paper bag (not plastic).
Take photos of where it was growing.
If the patient becomes unconscious, seizes, or stops breathing, begin CPR and call 112.
Keep the patient calm and at rest.
donot: Do NOT induce vomiting unless specifically instructed by National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117).
Do NOT rely on plant identification apps to determine if the patient needs the hospital; go to the ER.
Do NOT assume they are safe just because the initial vomiting stops.
seek: Requires ER evaluation, toxicological analysis, and specific antidotes (like NAC for liver protection) before organ damage becomes irreversible.

title: Stingray Puncture Wound
warn: ⚠️ HEAT-LABILE VENOM — The stingray barb causes a jagged physical puncture wound and injects venom that causes excruciating, agonizing pain.
steps: Get the patient safely out of the water.
Control severe bleeding with direct pressure if the barb sliced a vein/artery.
Immerse the affected limb in HOT water (as hot as the patient can tolerate without burning the skin, around 110-114°F / 43-45°C).
The heat rapidly breaks down (denatures) the venom protein, providing massive and almost instant pain relief.
Keep soaking for 30-90 minutes or until the pain subsides.
donot: Do NOT remove the barb if it is impaled in the chest, abdomen, or neck (it must be removed surgically).
Do NOT apply ice (cold water makes the pain significantly worse).
Do NOT pour scalding boiling water on the limb and cause a thermal burn in the panic.
seek: Requires a trip to the ER/Urgent Care for X-rays (barbs often break off inside the flesh), tetanus shot, and antibiotics.

title: Snow Immersion Asphyxiation (Avalanche/Tree Well)
warn: ⛔ SUFFOCATION HAZARD — The primary killer in an avalanche or tree-well burial is lack of oxygen, not the cold. You have roughly 15 minutes to save them.
steps: If you witness the burial, mark the last seen point and begin a beacon search immediately.
Once located, DIG STRATEGICALLY: Dig in from the downhill side to create a platform, not straight down from the top.
Uncover the HEAD and AIRWAY first. Clear snow from the mouth and nose immediately.
If the victim is unconscious and not breathing once the chest is uncovered, begin CPR immediately, even while their legs are still buried.
Once fully extracted, handle them very gently to avoid triggering a lethal heart arrhythmia (due to severe hypothermia).
donot: Do NOT leave the scene to get help unless absolutely necessary (they will suffocate before you return).
Do NOT focus on digging out their skis or legs before their face.
Do NOT abruptly warm a severely hypothermic victim with hot water or vigorous rubbing.
seek: Requires immediate emergency transport via ski patrol/helicopter for core rewarming and advanced airway management.

title: Opioid Overdose
warn: ⛔ Fentanyl may require multiple naloxone doses. Respiratory depression is fatal.
steps: Recognize: unresponsive, slow/absent breathing, blue lips, pinpoint pupils.
Call 112.
Administer naloxone (Narcan) 0.4-2mg IM/IN (intranasal) immediately.
Begin rescue breathing if not breathing.
Repeat naloxone every 2-3 minutes if no response (fentanyl may need 3+ doses).
Recovery position when breathing restored.
Do NOT leave alone — naloxone wears off in 45-90 minutes.
All patients require hospital observation.
donot: Do NOT leave patient after naloxone — respiratory depression can recur.
seek: All opioid overdoses require emergency evaluation.

title: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning
warn: ⛔ INVISIBLE KILLER — CO is odorless and colorless. The whole building may be affected. Rescuers can become victims instantly.
steps: Do NOT enter the building or confined space without breathing protection — you will also be incapacitated.
Call 112 immediately from outside the building.
Remove the patient to fresh air immediately if it is safe to do so.
Lay the patient down and loosen tight clothing.
If the patient is unconscious and not breathing, begin CPR.
Administer 100% high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask as soon as available — this is the primary antidote.
Identify and shut off the source (faulty heater, generator, car engine) if it can be done safely from outside.
All exposed persons, even those who feel fine, must be evaluated at hospital for hyperbaric oxygen therapy.
donot: Do NOT re-enter the building for any reason without self-contained breathing apparatus.
Do NOT assume the patient is drunk — CO poisoning mimics intoxication perfectly.
Do NOT give low-flow oxygen; 100% O2 is required to displace CO from haemoglobin.
seek: All CO exposure requires ER evaluation. Severe cases, pregnant women, and children require hyperbaric oxygen therapy.

title: Organophosphate / Pesticide Poisoning
warn: ⛔ NERVE AGENT CLASS — Causes massive over-stimulation of every gland and muscle. Rescuers must wear gloves and avoid contact with the patient's skin or vomit.
steps: Call 112. Wear gloves before touching the patient — organophosphates absorb through skin.
Remove the patient from the contaminated area. Remove and bag all clothing.
Flush exposed skin and eyes with large amounts of water for at least 15 minutes.
Recognize the SLUDGE toxidrome: Salivation, Lacrimation (tearing), Urination, Defecation, GI distress, Emesis.
If trained: Atropine 2–4mg IV/IM is the antidote — repeat every 5–10 minutes until secretions dry.
If trained: Pralidoxime (2-PAM) should be given alongside atropine to reactivate acetylcholinesterase.
If the patient stops breathing, begin CPR with a bag-valve mask (avoid mouth-to-mouth due to contamination risk).
Bring the pesticide container or its label to the ER.
donot: Do NOT touch the patient's skin or clothing without gloves.
Do NOT induce vomiting (risk of aspiration and further exposure).
Do NOT use mouth-to-mouth rescue breathing — use a bag-valve mask with a filter.
seek: Absolute emergency. Requires continuous IV atropine, pralidoxime, and ICU-level airway management.

title: Alcohol Poisoning (Ethanol Overdose)
warn: ⚠️ ASPIRATION RISK — The leading cause of death from alcohol poisoning is choking on vomit while unconscious. Never leave the patient alone.
steps: Call 112 if the person is unconscious, cannot be woken, breathing slowly or irregularly, has seizures, or their skin is pale, cold, or blue.
If unconscious but breathing, place in the recovery position (on their side) immediately to prevent choking on vomit.
Never leave them alone, even for a moment.
Monitor breathing rate and responsiveness continuously.
Keep them warm — alcohol causes dangerous heat loss (hypothermia).
Do not give coffee, food, or water — the stomach cannot process them and vomiting may follow.
If they stop breathing, begin CPR.
donot: Do NOT let them "sleep it off" without monitoring — blood alcohol continues to rise even after drinking stops.
Do NOT give coffee, cold showers, or food (these do not sober a person up and can cause additional harm).
Do NOT lay them on their back (aspiration of vomit is fatal).
Do NOT leave them alone at any point.
seek: Unconsciousness, seizures, breathing rate under 8 breaths/minute, or blue lips require immediate emergency care.

title: Tricyclic Antidepressant (TCA) Overdose
warn: ⛔ RAPID DETERIORATION — A patient who is walking and talking can collapse into cardiac arrest within minutes. Do not leave unmonitored.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Note the name of the medication and number of tablets missing.
Keep the patient awake and talking — monitor for sudden deterioration in consciousness.
Lay the patient on their left side (reduces drug absorption from stomach).
Watch for the deadly triad: seizures, widened QRS on ECG, and severe low blood pressure.
If trained: IV Sodium Bicarbonate is the specific antidote for cardiac toxicity.
If the patient seizes, protect their airway and begin CPR immediately if they lose their pulse.
Bring the pill bottle to the ER.
donot: Do NOT give any food, milk, or activated charcoal at home unless directed by National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117).
Do NOT assume the patient is stable just because they are currently conscious.
Do NOT allow them to drive or walk to the hospital — they may collapse suddenly.
seek: All TCA ingestions require immediate ER evaluation with continuous cardiac monitoring, even with no symptoms.

title: Caustic / Corrosive Ingestion
warn: ⛔ CHEMICAL BURNS FROM INSIDE — Acids and alkalis destroy the mouth, throat, and oesophagus. Do NOT induce vomiting — it causes a second pass of the burn.
steps: Call 112 or National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) immediately.
If the substance is on the skin or in the eyes, rinse with large volumes of water for at least 20 minutes.
For ingestion: give the patient small sips of water or milk (only if conscious) to dilute the substance.
Do NOT try to neutralize (e.g., do not give vinegar for alkali or baking soda for acid — the heat released worsens burns).
Keep the patient sitting upright.
Bring the container or its label to the ER.
If the patient becomes unconscious or stops breathing, begin CPR.
donot: Do NOT induce vomiting — it brings the corrosive back through the oesophagus, doubling the damage.
Do NOT try to neutralize the substance with household chemicals.
Do NOT give large quantities of fluids — just enough to dilute.
seek: All corrosive ingestions require immediate ER evaluation. Burns to the airway can cause fatal swelling within hours.

title: Cyanide Poisoning
warn: ⛔ CELLULAR ASPHYXIATION — Cells cannot use oxygen even if the blood is full of it. Death occurs within minutes. Often seen in house fire survivors.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Suspect cyanide in any patient who collapsed in a building fire, or who works in electroplating, mining, or chemical industries.
Move the patient to fresh air immediately if safe to do so.
Do NOT perform mouth-to-mouth rescue breathing — exhaled air from a cyanide patient can poison the rescuer. Use a bag-valve mask.
Begin CPR if the patient has no pulse.
If available and trained: administer Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) IV immediately — this is the specific antidote.
Provide 100% high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask.
Keep the patient warm and monitor for seizures.
donot: Do NOT perform mouth-to-mouth rescue breathing.
Do NOT enter a contaminated space without breathing protection.
Do NOT delay antidote administration waiting for lab confirmation.
seek: Absolute emergency requiring antidote administration and ICU admission. Do not wait for symptoms to worsen.

title: Methanol / Ethylene Glycol Poisoning
warn: ⛔ DELAYED DESTRUCTION — The patient may appear only mildly drunk at first, but will go blind and suffer fatal kidney/brain failure within 12–24 hours if untreated.
steps: Call 112 or National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) immediately. Even one mouthful of methanol can cause permanent blindness.
Note the time of ingestion and the exact substance swallowed — antifreeze, screen wash, windshield fluid.
Keep the patient conscious and talking.
If trained: fomepizole (4-MP) is the first-line antidote and blocks the metabolism of methanol into its toxic products.
In remote areas where fomepizole is unavailable, ethanol (oral alcohol) can be used as a bridge antidote — only under medical guidance.
Monitor vision carefully. Complaints of blurred vision or "seeing like looking through snow" are a critical sign.
donot: Do NOT wait for symptoms to worsen. The patient will seem "just drunk" until it is too late.
Do NOT induce vomiting.
Do NOT dismiss a patient who claims to have only had "a sip" — tiny amounts are lethal.
seek: Absolute emergency requiring antidote, haemodialysis, and ICU admission. Permanent blindness and death are preventable only with rapid treatment.

title: Benzodiazepine Overdose
warn: ⚠️ Dangerous sedation and respiratory depression, especially when combined with alcohol or opioids. The combination is far deadlier than either alone.
steps: Call 112 if the patient is unconscious, cannot be roused, or is breathing slowly.
Place in the recovery position if unconscious but breathing.
Keep the airway clear and monitor breathing continuously.
Ask about co-ingestion — did they also take alcohol, opioids, or other sleeping pills? This dramatically increases risk.
If trained and available: Flumazenil can reverse sedation but must be used with extreme caution (can precipitate fatal withdrawal seizures in dependent patients).
Begin CPR if breathing stops.
donot: Do NOT use Flumazenil in anyone who uses benzodiazepines regularly — it can cause life-threatening withdrawal seizures.
Do NOT assume the patient is safe because they appear to be sleeping peacefully.
Do NOT leave them unsupervised.
seek: Requires ER monitoring, especially if alcohol or other CNS depressants were also taken.

title: Stimulant Overdose (Cocaine / Amphetamine)
warn: ⚠️ Can cause heart attack, stroke, or seizure in young, otherwise healthy people. Hyperthermia (overheating) is a major killer.
steps: Call 112 immediately if the patient has chest pain, seizures, or is extremely confused or agitated.
Move the patient to a cool, quiet, calm environment — noise and stimulation worsen the crisis.
Cool the patient aggressively if they are very hot (fans, cool wet towels) — hyperthermia from stimulants can be fatal.
Keep the patient as calm as possible. Speak slowly and calmly.
Do not restrain aggressively — physical struggle dramatically increases body temperature and heart strain.
If the patient stops breathing or loses their pulse, begin CPR.
donot: Do NOT give beta-blockers (can cause paradoxical worsening of coronary artery spasm).
Do NOT restrain violently — excited delirium with restraint is a fatal combination.
Do NOT leave them alone if agitated or confused.
seek: Chest pain, stroke symptoms, seizures, or temperatures above 40°C (104°F) require immediate emergency care.

title: Salicylate (Aspirin) Overdose
warn: ⚠️ Chronic, low-level overdose in elderly patients is often missed. Early signs of tinnitus (ringing in ears) and rapid breathing are critical warnings.
steps: Call 112 or National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117). Note the amount taken and over what time period.
Keep the patient awake and talking — altered consciousness indicates severe toxicity.
Watch for rapid, deep breathing (Kussmaul breathing), ringing in ears, and extreme confusion.
Do NOT give bicarbonate of soda at home.
Bring the pill bottle to the ER.
If the patient becomes unconscious, begin CPR and call 112.
donot: Do NOT induce vomiting without specific instruction from National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117).
Do NOT give antacids or other medications at home.
Do NOT assume a small overdose is safe — aspirin has a very narrow therapeutic window in overdose.
seek: Requires ER evaluation for sodium bicarbonate infusion to alkalinize urine and potentially haemodialysis in severe cases.

title: Button Battery Ingestion
warn: ⛔ CHILD EMERGENCY — A button battery lodged in the oesophagus causes fatal chemical burns within 2 hours. Time is absolutely critical.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Do not wait for symptoms.
Note the time the battery was swallowed.

If the child can swallow and the battery has been in the oesophagus for less than 12 hours, give honey (1–2 teaspoons) every 10 minutes on the way to hospital — this coats the battery and slows burns. (Only for children over 1 year old).
Do NOT give food or drink other than honey.
Do NOT try to induce vomiting.
The child requires immediate X-ray and urgent endoscopic removal.
donot: Do NOT wait for symptoms. Burns begin immediately with no pain.
Do NOT give food or drink (except honey as above).
Do NOT induce vomiting — the battery can damage the airway on the way back up.
seek: Absolute emergency. The battery must be removed endoscopically within 2 hours of oesophageal lodgement to prevent fatal perforation.

title: Iron Tablet Overdose
warn: ⛔ DECEIVING RECOVERY — The patient may improve after initial vomiting, then enter sudden, severe shock and liver failure 6–24 hours later.
steps: Call 112 or National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) immediately. Note the number of tablets and the elemental iron content (mg per tablet).
Expect bloody vomiting and diarrhoea in the first phase.
Do NOT give milk or antacids — they do not effectively bind iron.
Keep the patient hydrated if they are conscious and able to swallow.
The specific antidote is Deferoxamine (IV infusion) — only available in hospital.
Bring the iron supplement bottle to the ER.
donot: Do NOT be reassured if the patient improves after initial vomiting — a "latent phase" of apparent recovery often precedes severe poisoning.
Do NOT induce vomiting at home (bloody vomit is already occurring).
Do NOT give milk or antacids.
seek: Requires serum iron levels, IV fluids, and potentially IV deferoxamine at an ER.

title: Mushroom Poisoning
warn: ⚠️ Death Cap mushroom (Amanita phalloides) causes NO symptoms for 6–24 hours, then sudden, irreversible liver failure. Other species cause rapid GI distress or hallucinations.
steps: Call 112 or National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) immediately.
Collect a sample or photograph of the mushroom if safe to do so.
Note the time of eating and the onset of symptoms.
If GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea) begin immediately: likely less deadly species.
If symptoms are delayed 6 or more hours: suspect Amanita species — absolute emergency even if the patient currently feels well.
Keep the patient hydrated with oral fluids if they can swallow.
Transport to ER with the mushroom sample.
donot: Do NOT wait for symptoms if you suspect Death Cap — treatment started before symptoms are the only way to prevent liver failure.
Do NOT rely on folk tests for mushroom identification (no reliable home tests exist).
Do NOT induce vomiting without National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) guidance.
seek: Delayed onset (6+ hours) mushroom poisoning is a liver failure emergency requiring ICU admission and potentially liver transplant.

title: Unknown Substance / Mixed Ingestion
warn: ⚠️ Multiple substances dramatically increase the risk of fatal interactions. Treat as critical until the substances are identified.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Collect ALL pill bottles, packets, and containers present and bring them to the ER — this is extremely valuable to the treating team.
Note the time of ingestion and any symptoms present.
Keep the patient awake and talking if possible.
Place in the recovery position if unconscious but breathing.
Begin CPR if breathing stops or pulse disappears.
Do not assume only one substance was taken.
donot: Do NOT induce vomiting unless specifically directed by National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117).
Do NOT give activated charcoal at home.
Do NOT leave the patient alone at any point.
seek: All suspected multi-drug ingestions require immediate ER evaluation. Always bring pill bottles and containers.

title: Household Chemical Exposure (Bleach, Ammonia, Cleaning Products)
warn: ⚠️ Mixing bleach and ammonia produces lethal chloramine gas. Even brief inhalation can cause chemical pneumonia hours later.
steps: Move the patient to fresh air immediately.
Call 112 if there is difficulty breathing, chest pain, or eye/skin burns.
For skin/eye contact: flush with large volumes of water for at least 20 minutes.
For inhalation: keep the patient calm and seated upright to ease breathing.
Open all windows and doors and evacuate others from the area.
Identify the chemicals involved and report them to emergency services.
Do NOT mix cleaning products at any point — the gas produced is toxic.
donot: Do NOT re-enter the room to get belongings until ventilated.
Do NOT induce vomiting for ingestion — chemical burns to the oesophagus will worsen.
Do NOT mix any chemical products to try to neutralize a spill.
seek: Any inhalation exposure with coughing, chest pain, or shortness of breath requires ER evaluation. Chemical pneumonitis can develop hours after apparent recovery.

title: Drug-Induced Hyperthermia (Serotonin Syndrome / NMS)
warn: ⚠️ High fever + muscle rigidity + altered mental state after starting or changing medications is a life-threatening emergency. Cooling is as important as any drug.
steps: Call 112. Note any recent medication changes, especially antidepressants, antipsychotics, or MDMA/ecstasy use.
Move the patient to a cool environment immediately.
Remove excess clothing and apply cool wet towels to armpits, neck, and groin.
Fan the patient aggressively while keeping them cool.
Keep the patient as calm and still as possible — muscle activity produces heat.
Begin CPR if the patient loses consciousness and stops breathing.
donot: Do NOT give additional medications without medical instruction.
Do NOT restrain the patient aggressively — struggling generates dangerous heat.
Do NOT assume the fever will come down on its own.
seek: Requires immediate ER cooling, IV benzodiazepines, and cyproheptadine (for serotonin syndrome) or bromocriptine/dantrolene (for NMS).

title: Food Poisoning (Severe / Bacterial)
warn: ⚠️ Botulism, E. coli O157 (especially in children), and Listeria can be fatal. Suspect a serious cause when neurological symptoms, bloody diarrhoea, or extreme weakness accompany food illness.
steps: Keep the patient hydrated — oral rehydration salts (ORS) are far better than plain water.
Rest the gut: small sips of fluid frequently rather than large amounts.
Call 112 or go to ER if there is: bloody diarrhoea, high fever over 38.5°C, signs of dehydration (sunken eyes, no urination for 8 hours), or any muscle weakness or vision changes (suggests botulism).
Note the food eaten and the time between eating and symptoms — report this to health authorities.
Do not share food with others until the source is identified.
donot: Do NOT take anti-diarrhoeal medications (e.g., Imodium) with bloody diarrhoea or high fever — can worsen bacterial infections.
Do NOT dismiss symptoms in infants, the elderly, or immunocompromised patients — dehydration is fatal in these groups.
Do NOT give antibiotics without medical guidance.
seek: Bloody stool, high fever, signs of dehydration, neurological symptoms, or symptoms in infants and elderly require immediate emergency care.

title: Digoxin / Cardiac Glycoside Toxicity
warn: ⚠️ Classic triad of nausea, visual disturbances (yellow/green halos), and bradycardia. Dangerously narrow therapeutic window — even a slight overdose can be fatal.
steps: Call 112. Note the patient's regular digoxin dose and any recent changes.
Have the patient rest completely — any exertion can trigger a fatal arrhythmia.
Ask about visual disturbances — seeing yellow/green halos around lights is a classic sign of toxicity.
Monitor pulse — a slow, irregular pulse indicates toxicity.
Bring the digoxin bottle to the ER.
The specific antidote is Digoxin-Specific Antibody Fragments (Digibind/DigiFab) — only available in hospital.
donot: Do NOT give any extra doses of digoxin.
Do NOT allow the patient to exert themselves.
Do NOT delay ER visit even if symptoms seem mild — arrhythmia can be sudden and fatal.
seek: Requires immediate ECG monitoring, electrolyte management (especially potassium), and potentially Digibind antidote at an ER.

title: Acetaminophen (Tylenol) Overdose
warn: ⛔ SILENT LIVER DESTRUCTION — Symptoms may not appear for 24-48 hours, but irreversible liver failure is actively occurring.
steps: Call National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) or 112 immediately upon discovering the overdose, even if the patient feels perfectly fine.
Determine exactly how much was taken and what time it was ingested. Bring the pill bottles to the ER.
Check the ingredients of any other cold/flu medicines the patient took, as many contain hidden acetaminophen.
If the patient is unconscious or seizing, begin CPR and clear the airway if they vomit.
donot: Do NOT wait for symptoms (like yellowing skin or right-sided abdominal pain) to appear; it is often too late by then.
Do NOT induce vomiting unless specifically instructed by National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117).
Do NOT let the patient sleep it off.
seek: Requires immediate ER evaluation for administration of the specific antidote (N-acetylcysteine / NAC) before liver damage becomes permanent.

title: Corrosive Liquid Ingestion (Bleach/Lye)
warn: ⛔ INTERNAL BURNS — Swallowing strong acids or bases instantly burns the mouth, throat, and stomach, risking a fatal rupture of the esophagus.
steps: Call 112 or National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) immediately.
If the patient is conscious, alert, and able to swallow normally, have them rinse their mouth out with water and spit it out.
Look for severe drooling, inability to swallow, or burns around the lips and mouth.
Keep the patient sitting upright to prevent the acid/base from refluxing back up into the throat or lungs.
Gather the exact container of the chemical swallowed.
donot: Do NOT induce vomiting under any circumstances (vomiting will burn the throat a second time and risks inhaling the chemical into the lungs).

Do NOT try to "neutralize" the chemical with milk, water, vinegar, or baking soda unless explicitly ordered by National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) (this can cause an exothermic reaction, boiling inside the stomach).
Do NOT give activated charcoal.
seek: Requires emergency transport. An endoscope will be used in the hospital to evaluate the extent of the internal burns.

title: Ethylene Glycol (Antifreeze) Poisoning
warn: ⛔ KIDNEY CRYSTALLIZATION — Antifreeze tastes sweet but breaks down into acids that crystallize inside the kidneys and brain.
steps: Call 112 or National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) immediately.
Recognize the three stages: 1. Appears heavily intoxicated (drunk) without alcohol odor. 2. Rapid breathing and racing heart. 3. Seizures and kidney failure.
Estimate the amount ingested. Even a few mouthfuls can be fatal.
Keep the patient safe if they are stumbling or confused.
Prepare for sudden cardiac arrest or seizures.
donot: Do NOT assume they are just drunk if they have had access to a garage or automotive chemicals.
Do NOT wait for the "drunk" phase to wear off; the next phase is fatal organ failure.
Do NOT induce vomiting.
seek: Requires immediate ER treatment. The antidote is Fomepizole or, ironically, pharmaceutical-grade intravenous ethanol to stop the breakdown of the poison.

title: Organophosphate (Pesticide) Poisoning
warn: ⛔ MASSIVE NERVOUS SYSTEM OVERLOAD — These chemicals (found in insecticides and nerve agents) cause every bodily fluid to leak uncontrollably.
steps: Protect yourself first. Do NOT touch the patient if they are covered in the chemical. Wear thick gloves and a mask.
Recognize SLUDGE syndrome: Salivation, Lacrimation (tears), Urination, Defecation, GI distress, Emesis (vomiting). The patient will literally be leaking from everywhere.
Call 112 immediately and state it is a pesticide/chemical exposure.
Move the patient to fresh air if inhaled.
If spilled on the skin, strip all clothing off the patient and wash them with massive amounts of soap and water.
donot: Do NOT perform mouth-to-mouth CPR if they ingested it or have it on their face; use a bag-valve-mask or do hands-only CPR to avoid poisoning yourself.
Do NOT bring contaminated clothing into the house or ambulance.
Do NOT delay calling EMS; the breathing muscles will eventually paralyze.
seek: Requires specific, heavy-duty antidotes (Atropine and Pralidoxime) administered by paramedics or ER staff.

title: Severe Alcohol Poisoning
warn: ⚠️ RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION & CHOKING — The brain centers controlling breathing and the gag reflex are shutting down.
steps: Try to wake the person up. If they cannot be roused by loud shouting or a firm sternal rub (rubbing your knuckles hard on their chest bone), call 112 immediately.
Check their breathing. If it is slower than 8 breaths per minute, or extremely irregular, it is a critical emergency.
Roll the person onto their side (the Recovery Position) and prop them so they cannot roll onto their back. This prevents them from choking to death on their own vomit.
Stay with the person continuously.
Keep them warm, as alcohol causes dangerous drops in body temperature.
donot: Do NOT leave them alone to "sleep it off." Their blood alcohol concentration can continue to rise even after they pass out as the stomach digests the alcohol.
Do NOT put them in a cold shower (risk of hypothermia and drowning).
Do NOT force them to drink coffee or eat food (choking hazard).
seek: Requires hospital observation, IV fluids, and potentially a breathing tube if respiratory failure occurs.

title: Tricyclic Antidepressant (TCA) Overdose
warn: ⛔ SUDDEN CARDIAC ARREST — Older antidepressants (like Amitriptyline) are highly toxic in overdose, causing rapid fatal heart arrhythmias and seizures.
steps: Call 112 immediately. The patient can deteriorate from awake and talking to seizing and pulseless in minutes.
Keep the patient completely at rest.
Look for signs of toxicity: extreme dry mouth, dilated pupils, confusion, rapid heart rate, and twitching.
Locate the pill bottle to tell EMS exactly what was taken.
Have an AED nearby if available, and be prepared to start CPR instantly.
donot: Do NOT assume they are safe if they seem fine 30 minutes after taking the pills.
Do NOT give them anything by mouth.
Do NOT induce vomiting (it can trigger an immediate seizure).
seek: Absolute emergency. Requires continuous EKG monitoring and Sodium Bicarbonate IV pushes to protect the heart.

title: Severe Stimulant Overdose (Cocaine/Methamphetamine)
warn: ⛔ CARDIOVASCULAR COLLAPSE — Massive surges in adrenaline cause blood vessels to clamp shut, risking immediate heart attack, stroke, or lethal overheating.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Inform the dispatcher of the suspected drug to ensure proper medical response.
Ensure your own safety; the patient may be severely agitated, paranoid, or combative (excited delirium).
If safe to do so, move them to a quiet, dimly lit environment to reduce sensory stimulation.
Monitor their temperature. If they are sweating profusely and feel extremely hot, begin cooling them with ice packs to the neck, armpits, and groin.
Monitor for chest pain or signs of a stroke (FAST).
donot: Do NOT physically restrain the patient if they are struggling (fighting restraints severely worsens muscle breakdown and raises body temperature to lethal levels).
Do NOT argue with them if they are paranoid or hallucinating; agree and reassure them.
Do NOT leave them alone.
seek: Requires ER administration of sedatives (Benzodiazepines) to calm the brain and lower the heart rate, plus active cooling.

title: Methanol Poisoning
warn: ⛔ BLINDNESS AND ORGAN FAILURE — Found in improper homemade alcohol, windshield washer fluid, and solvents. The body converts it into formaldehyde and formic acid.
steps: Call 112 or National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) immediately if suspected.
Look for the hallmark symptom: The patient complains of blurred vision, "snowstorm" vision, or sudden blindness, along with severe abdominal pain and vomiting.
These symptoms can be delayed 12-24 hours after ingestion.
Keep the patient calm and safe, especially if their vision is failing.
Bring any remaining suspect liquid to the hospital.
donot: Do NOT assume it is a standard hangover if they complain of severe visual changes.
Do NOT induce vomiting.
Do NOT delay treatment waiting for symptoms to pass.
seek: Requires immediate ER treatment with Fomepizole or IV Ethanol, and often emergency dialysis to remove the acid from the blood and save the optic nerve.

title: Cyanide Poisoning
warn: ⛔ CELLULAR SUFFOCATION — Cyanide stops cells from using oxygen. The blood has oxygen, but the body literally suffocates at the cellular level in minutes.
steps: Evacuate the area immediately. Most common exposures are smoke inhalation from burning plastics/synthetics in house fires, or industrial chemical spills.
Call 112 immediately.
If the patient collapsed in an enclosed space (like a jewelry workshop or chemical lab), DO NOT enter without Hazmat gear.
If the patient is safe to touch and unresponsive, begin CPR. (Use a bag-valve-mask; do NOT do mouth-to-mouth).
Notice any smell of "bitter almonds" on the breath, though many people genetically cannot smell it.
donot: Do NOT become a secondary victim by rushing into a toxic gas environment.
Do NOT perform mouth-to-mouth rescue breaths.
Do NOT delay calling EMS; death occurs very rapidly.
seek: Requires the immediate administration of specific Cyanide Antidote Kits (Hydroxycobalamin or Sodium Thiosulfate) by paramedics or ER.

title: Iron Supplement Overdose
warn: ⛔ CORROSIVE AND TOXIC — Iron pills eat through the stomach lining and cause massive cellular shock. Highly lethal to toddlers.
steps: Call 112 or National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) immediately. Adult prenatal vitamins or iron supplements look like candy to children.
Watch for Phase 1: Severe vomiting (often bloody), diarrhea, and abdominal pain within 6 hours.
Beware of Phase 2: A "latent period" where the child suddenly seems better (6-24 hours). This is a trap; the iron is quietly destroying the liver and cellular metabolism.
Bring the bottle to the ER to calculate the exact elemental iron dose.
Keep the patient NPO (nothing by mouth).
donot: Do NOT assume the danger has passed just because the child stops vomiting after a few hours.
Do NOT give activated charcoal (it does NOT bind to heavy metals like iron and is completely useless here).
Do NOT induce vomiting.
seek: Requires abdominal X-rays (iron pills show up on X-rays) and administration of a specific chelating agent (Deferoxamine) that binds the iron and turns urine a "vin rosé" color.

title: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma
warn: ⛔ IMMINENT BLINDNESS — Fluid in the eye cannot drain, causing a massive, rapid spike in pressure that crushes the optic nerve.
steps: Recognize the sudden onset of severe, agonizing eye pain accompanied by a severe headache, nausea, and vomiting.
Check the patient’s vision: they often report blurred vision or seeing rainbow-colored halos around lights.
Look at the eye: it will appear red, and the pupil may be mid-dilated and unreactive to light.
Call 112 or go to the nearest ER immediately.
Keep the patient resting quietly in a supine (flat) position if possible, as this can sometimes slightly ease pressure.
donot: Do NOT assume it is a migraine just because of the headache and nausea.
Do NOT put a patch over the eye (darkness dilates the pupil, which worsens the fluid blockage).
Do NOT wait until morning to see an eye doctor.
seek: Requires immediate emergency administration of pressure-lowering eye drops and IV medications, followed by laser surgery.

title: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (Eye Stroke)
warn: ⛔ RETINAL DEATH — A blood clot blocks the main artery to the retina. You have roughly 90 to 120 minutes to restore blood flow before permanent blindness.
steps: Acknowledge the classic symptom: Sudden, completely painless loss of vision in one eye (like a curtain falling over the eye).
Call 112 immediately. Time is as critical as a brain stroke.
Have the patient breathe into a paper bag (this increases CO2 in the blood, which can dilate blood vessels and potentially dislodge the clot).
Gently massage the closed eye: press firmly for 10 seconds, then release for 5 seconds. Repeat. This sudden change in pressure can sometimes pop the clot loose.
Keep the patient lying flat to maximize blood flow to the head.
donot: Do NOT wait to see if vision returns on its own.
Do NOT let the patient drive.
Do NOT press so hard during eye massage that you cause severe pain.
seek: Requires immediate stroke-protocol evaluation in an ER to attempt clot-busting or anterior chamber paracentesis (draining eye fluid to drop pressure).

title: Retinal Detachment
warn: ⚠️ TISSUE SEPARATION — The light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye pulls away from its blood supply.
steps: Ask the patient about warning signs: a sudden massive increase in "floaters" (dark specks/webs), flashes of light in their peripheral vision, or a dark shadow creeping across their vision.
Have the patient restrict their eye and head movements as much as possible.
Have them close both eyes (since eyes move together) and rest quietly.
Transport to an ER with ophthalmology capabilities or an emergency eye clinic immediately.
donot: Do NOT allow the patient to read, look at their phone, or look around the room.
Do NOT apply any pressure to the eyes.
Do NOT assume it is a normal part of aging if the floaters or flashes appear suddenly and abundantly.
seek: Requires urgent surgical reattachment (laser, freezing, or pneumatic retinopexy) within 24-72 hours to preserve central vision.

title: Orbital Cellulitis
warn: ⛔ DEEP INFECTION — A bacterial infection deep inside the eye socket. It can rapidly spread to the brain or cause permanent blindness.
steps: Observe for a red, extremely swollen eyelid accompanied by a high fever.
Check eye movement: Have the patient look up, down, left, and right. If moving the eye is severely painful or restricted, or if the eye is bulging outward (proptosis), it is an emergency.
Call 112 or go to the ER immediately.
Keep the patient calm and sitting slightly upright.
donot: Do NOT confuse this with a simple stye or "pink eye" (conjunctivitis usually does not cause pain with eye movement, bulging, or high fever).
Do NOT try to pop or drain any swelling.
Do NOT delay medical care; the infection is millimeters from the brain.
seek: Requires immediate hospital admission for IV antibiotics and a CT scan of the orbits and sinuses.

title: Hyphema
warn: ⚠️ INTERNAL EYE BLEEDING — Blood pools in the front chamber of the eye (between the cornea and iris), usually from blunt trauma.
steps: Notice a visible pool of blood covering the lower part of the colored part of the eye (iris).
Have the patient sit upright or prop their head up at least 45 degrees. This allows gravity to pull the blood down, keeping it out of the visual axis and away from drainage canals.
Place a rigid shield (like a paper cup) over the eye to prevent accidental rubbing or bumping.
Keep the patient extremely quiet and calm to prevent blood pressure spikes that could cause a secondary, worse bleed.
donot: Do NOT let the patient lie flat on their back.
Do NOT give aspirin, ibuprofen, or naproxen for pain (they thin the blood and worsen bleeding; use acetaminophen instead).
Do NOT apply a pressure patch or bandage that touches the eyelid.
seek: Requires ophthalmology evaluation to monitor internal eye pressure and check for other trauma to the globe.

title: Orbital Blowout Fracture
warn: ⚠️ MUSCLE ENTRAPMENT — The thin bone at the bottom of the eye socket breaks, and the eye muscles can drop into the sinus and get stuck.
steps: Occurs after blunt force to the eye (e.g., a baseball or fist).
Check for entrapment: Ask the patient to look up. If the injured eye cannot look up and they experience double vision, the muscle is trapped in the broken bone.
Apply a cold compress gently to the surrounding cheek/eyebrow (not directly on the eyeball) to reduce swelling.
Instruct the patient to absolutely NOT blow their nose (this forces air from the sinuses into the eye socket, causing it to swell massively).
donot: Do NOT let the patient blow their nose or hold their breath and bear down.
Do NOT apply any direct pressure to the eyeball itself.
Do NOT force the eyelids open if they are swollen shut.
seek: Requires a CT scan to identify the fracture. Surgery is needed if the muscle is entrapped to prevent permanent double vision.

title: Corneal Ulcer (Keratitis)
warn: ⚠️ CORNEAL DESTRUCTION — An open sore on the cornea, often caused by sleeping in contact lenses or bacterial/fungal infections. Can eat through the eye.
steps: If the patient wears contact lenses, have them remove the lens IMMEDIATELY and save it in a case (doctors can culture it to identify the bacteria).
Look for a small white or gray spot on the normally clear part of the eye.
The patient will experience severe pain, feeling like something is stuck in the eye, and intense light sensitivity (photophobia).
Have the patient wait in a dark room or wear dark sunglasses.
Go to an ER or urgent eye clinic.
donot: Do NOT put the contact lens back in.
Do NOT use leftover antibiotic or steroid eye drops from a previous infection (steroid drops will cause a fungal or viral ulcer to rapidly worsen and perforate the eye).
Do NOT rub the eye.
seek: Requires specialized, highly concentrated antibiotic/antifungal eye drops compounded by a pharmacy, taken every hour around the clock.

title: Corneal Foreign Body
warn: ⚠️ RUST RING RISK — Metal fragments embedded in the cornea begin to rust within hours, causing a chemical burn to the eye tissue.
steps: Do NOT let the patient rub their eye, as this will scratch the cornea further.
Attempt to flush the eye with a sterile saline wash or clean tap water for 10-15 minutes.
If the object is visible on the white of the eye (sclera), you can try to gently brush it away with a moist cotton swab.
If the object is on the colored part of the eye (cornea) or embedded, DO NOT try to remove it.
Tape a paper cup or rigid shield over the eye to prevent rubbing, and transport to a doctor.
donot: Do NOT use tweezers, toothpicks, or any hard objects to dig at the eye.
Do NOT attempt to remove a piece of metal, glass, or an object that is stuck fast.
Do NOT use tap water if you are in a region where amoebic infections (Acanthamoeba) in the water supply are a known risk.
seek: An eye doctor will use a specialized tool (spud) or a tiny drill (Algerbrush) to remove the object and any rust rings under magnification.

title: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL)
warn: ⛔ NERVE DAMAGE — Unexplained, rapid loss of hearing in one ear (usually over a period of 72 hours or less). The inner ear is failing.
steps: Acknowledge the symptom: The patient wakes up deaf in one ear, or hears a loud "pop" followed by ringing and deafness.
Rule out obvious causes like a visible wax plug or recent underwater swimming/flying.
Treat this as a true medical emergency, not a casual annoyance to be checked next week.
Go to the ER or an ENT specialist immediately.
donot: Do NOT assume it is just earwax or fluid and wait a week for it to clear up.
Do NOT put cotton swabs or ear drops into the ear.
Do NOT ignore associated symptoms like dizziness, vertigo, or facial numbness.
seek: There is a very strict 1-to-2 week window to treat this with high-dose oral or injected steroids to save the hearing. After that, the deafness is permanent.

title: Live Insect in the Ear
warn: ⚠️ PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTRESS & SCRATCHING — A live insect will panic, buzz loudly, and scratch the eardrum, causing severe pain and distress.
steps: Keep the patient calm. The noise is terrifying, but usually not life-threatening.
Take the patient into a dark room and shine a flashlight near the outside of the ear. Sometimes the bug will walk toward the light.
If the bug does not come out, tilt the patient’s head so the affected ear is pointing UP.
POUR warm mineral oil, baby oil, or olive oil into the ear canal to suffocate the insect and float it to the top.
Once the buzzing stops, tip the head over to let the oil and bug drain out.
donot: Do NOT use tweezers or cotton swabs (you will anger the insect, making it sting/bite, or push it deeper into the eardrum).
Do NOT use oil if the patient has ear tubes (tympanostomy tubes) or a known hole in their eardrum.
Do NOT try to flush it with water (some bugs swell up when wet).
seek: If the oil trick fails or you only get part of the bug out, see an ENT or go to urgent care for professional extraction.

title: Ruptured Eardrum (Tympanic Membrane Perforation)
warn: ⚠️ INFECTION GATEWAY — A hole in the eardrum from pressure changes, loud noises, infections, or poking with a cotton swab.
steps: Recognize the signs: Sudden sharp ear pain that rapidly decreases, followed by clear, bloody, or pus-filled drainage from the ear.
The patient may report ringing in the ear (tinnitus) or hearing loss.
Place a dry, sterile cotton ball loosely in the outer ear to catch drainage.
Keep the ear completely dry. When showering, coat a cotton ball in petroleum jelly and place it in the outer ear to block water.
donot: Do NOT put any ear drops or liquids into the ear (they will enter the middle ear and cause severe infection or vertigo).
Do NOT blow the nose forcefully.
Do NOT stick a Q-tip inside to clean up the blood.
seek: Most heal on their own in a few weeks, but an ENT must evaluate it to ensure no middle ear bones are broken and prescribe safe, non-ototoxic antibiotics if infected.

title: Mastoiditis
warn: ⚠️ SKULL INFECTION — An untreated middle ear infection spreads into the porous mastoid bone directly behind the ear.
steps: Look behind the ear: The skin over the mastoid bone will be red, swollen, hot, and extremely tender to the touch.
Notice if the swelling pushes the entire outer ear forward and downward.
Check for fever and throbbing, persistent ear pain.
Go to the ER immediately, especially if this occurs in a child.
donot: Do NOT ignore a worsening ear infection that starts causing pain behind the ear.
Do NOT rely on over-the-counter pain meds to treat the underlying cause.
Do NOT wait to see if it improves on its own; it can spread to the brain or cause meningitis.
seek: Requires CT scan, IV antibiotics, and potentially a mastoidectomy (surgical removal of the infected bone).

title: Auricular Hematoma (Cauliflower Ear)
warn: ⚠️ CARTILAGE DEATH — Blood pools between the ear cartilage and skin. Cartilage has no blood supply of its own; it dies quickly if separated from the skin.
steps: Identify the injury: A blunt blow to the ear (common in wrestling/MMA) causes a painful, swollen, doughy, purple bulge on the outer ear.
Apply an ice pack to the ear immediately to reduce swelling (15 mins on, 15 mins off).
Apply firm, even pressure to the ear with a bandage.
Go to an ER, urgent care, or ENT specialist within hours.
donot: Do NOT ignore it, assuming it is just a bruise. If left undrained, the cartilage dies and shrivels into a permanent "cauliflower" deformity.
Do NOT try to drain it yourself with an unsterile needle (high risk of severe cartilage infection).
Do NOT return to contact sports without headgear.
seek: A doctor must drain the blood (incision and drainage) and tightly bolster/sew pressure pads onto the ear to prevent the blood from pooling again.

title: Posterior Epistaxis (Severe Nosebleed)
warn: ⚠️ ARTERIAL BLEEDING — Unlike a normal nosebleed, a posterior bleed comes from a large artery deep in the nose and will not stop with simple pinching.
steps: Have the patient sit upright and lean SLIGHTLY FORWARD.
Pinch the soft, fleshy part of the nose (not the bony bridge) firmly against the face for 15 solid minutes without letting go to check.
If blood is pouring down the back of their throat despite leaning forward and pinching, or if it is flowing heavily from both nostrils, it is likely a posterior bleed.
Call 112 or go to the ER immediately.
Have the patient spit out any blood into a bowl. Swallowed blood will cause severe vomiting.
donot: Do NOT tilt the head back (blood will flow into the airway and stomach, causing choking and vomiting).
Do NOT pack the nose with dry tissue or cotton (it acts like a wick, and pulling it out tears the clot).
Do NOT lay the patient flat.
seek: Requires ER management. Doctors will use a specialized inflatable balloon catheter (like a Rapid Rhino) inserted deep into the nasal cavity to tamponade the bleeding artery.

title: Septal Hematoma
warn: ⚠️ SADDLE NOSE DEFORMITY — Blood pools inside the wall between the nostrils after trauma. It starves the nasal cartilage, causing the nose to permanently collapse.
steps: Examine the nose after any facial trauma (even a few days later).
Look inside both nostrils with a flashlight.
If you see a soft, cherry-red or purple, grape-like swelling bulging from the center wall (septum) that blocks the airway, it is a hematoma.
Ask the patient if they have worsening nasal congestion and pain that doesn't match the initial injury.
Go to the ER or an ENT immediately.
donot: Do NOT assume a blocked nose after a punch is just swelling from a broken bone.
Do NOT pop or pierce the bulge yourself.
Do NOT wait a week to see if the swelling goes down.
seek: Requires urgent surgical drainage by an ENT to save the septal cartilage and prevent a permanent "saddle nose" facial deformity.

title: Nasal Foreign Body (Button Battery or Magnet)
warn: ⚠️ TISSUE BURN / NECROSIS — A button battery in the moist environment of the nose creates an electrical current, burning through the septum in under 2 hours.
steps: Determine what the child put in their nose. If it is a button battery or two magnets, treat it as an absolute emergency.

If it is a soft object (like a bead or pea) and the child is cooperative, try the "Mother's Kiss": Close the clear nostril, place your mouth entirely over the child's open mouth, and blow a sharp, quick puff of air to shoot the object out.
If it is a battery, magnet, or the Mother's Kiss fails, go to the ER immediately.
Keep the child breathing through their mouth.
donot: Do NOT use tweezers to try and grab a round, hard object (you will squeeze it deeper into the airway).
Do NOT flush the nose with water (if it is a bean or seed, it will swell and get stuck tighter).
Do NOT wait to see if a battery will fall out on its own.
seek: Button batteries require immediate removal by an ENT or ER doctor to prevent a permanent hole from burning through the nasal septum.

title: Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy)
warn: ⛔ AIRWAY COMPROMISE — A massive pocket of pus forms behind the tonsil, threatening to push the airway shut or rupture into the lungs.
steps: Look for the classic triad: 1. A severely worsening sore throat (usually worse on one side). 2. Difficulty opening the mouth (trismus). 3. A muffled, garbled "hot potato" voice (like talking with hot food in the mouth).
Have the patient open their mouth and look with a flashlight: If the dangling thing in the back (uvula) is pushed far to one side by a massive swelling, it is an abscess.
Observe for drooling (inability to swallow saliva).
Go to the ER immediately.
donot: Do NOT assume it is just severe strep throat if they cannot open their mouth or swallow their own spit.
Do NOT try to pop the abscess with a sharp object at home (if it ruptures uncontrollably, they can aspirate the pus and choke).
Do NOT lay the patient flat.
seek: Requires emergency needle aspiration or incision and drainage by a doctor to remove the pus, along with IV antibiotics.

title: Ludwig’s Angina
warn: ⛔ RAPID AIRWAY CLOSURE — A massive, rapidly spreading bacterial infection under the floor of the mouth, usually originating from an infected lower tooth.
steps: Look for extreme swelling under the chin and the floor of the mouth (it will feel hard and "woody", not squishy).
Check the tongue: The swelling pushes the tongue UP and BACK, blocking the throat.
Observe for drooling, inability to swallow, fever, and breathing difficulty.
Call 112 immediately. Keep the patient sitting upright.
Prepare for an impending loss of airway.
donot: Do NOT ignore severe toothaches, especially in the lower jaw.
Do NOT force the patient to lie down or lean back for an exam.
Do NOT give them food or water.
seek: Absolute emergency requiring emergency airway management (often an awake tracheostomy), broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and surgical drainage of the neck.

title: Pharyngeal Foreign Body (Fish Bone)
warn: ⚠️ ESOPHAGEAL PERFORATION RISK — Sharp objects lodged in the throat can pierce the pharynx or esophagus, leading to deep neck infections.
steps: Ask the patient to point exactly to where they feel the object. (If it is high in the throat, they will point to the neck; if lower, they will point to the chest).
Look inside the mouth with a bright light; occasionally the bone is visible sticking into a tonsil.
If the patient is drooling, having difficulty breathing, or spitting up blood, call 112.
If they can breathe fine but have severe pain when swallowing, go to the ER or an ENT.
donot: Do NOT try to push the bone down by eating large chunks of dry bread or sticky rice (this old wives' tale often drives the sharp bone deeper into the tissue).
Do NOT stick your fingers blindly down their throat to fish it out.
Do NOT induce vomiting (it will tear the throat on the way back up).
seek: Requires evaluation by an ENT or GI doctor, often using a flexible fiberoptic scope to safely locate and extract the sharp object.

title: Retropharyngeal Abscess
warn: ⛔ HIDDEN AIRWAY THREAT — A pocket of pus forms deep in the tissues at the very back of the throat (between the throat and the spine). Most common in young children.
steps: Observe the child: They will have a high fever, difficulty swallowing, drooling, and a distinctly stiff neck (they will refuse to bend their neck forward or look side to side).
They may have stridor (a high-pitched whistling sound when breathing in).
Notice their posture: They often hold their head tilted back and to one side to keep the airway open.
Call 112 or go to the pediatric ER immediately.
Keep the child calm and upright.
donot: Do NOT mistake the stiff neck for meningitis without ruling out this abscess first.
Do NOT force the child to tilt their head forward to look at their throat (this can close off the compromised airway entirely).
Do NOT use a tongue depressor to look down their throat.
seek: Requires an emergency CT scan of the neck and immediate surgery to drain the abscess in an operating room, plus IV antibiotics.

title: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS)
warn: ⛔ LETHAL ALLERGIC REACTION — A severe reaction (usually to a medication) that causes the top layer of skin to die and peel off. Affects <10% of the body surface.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This is a medical emergency treated similarly to a severe burn.
Identify and STOP any new medications the patient started recently (especially antibiotics, anti-seizure meds, or NSAIDs).
Look for the classic early signs: flu-like symptoms followed by a painful red/purple rash that spreads and blisters.
Check the mouth, eyes, and genitals for painful blisters or bleeding (mucosal involvement is a hallmark sign).
Keep the patient warm, as skin loss causes rapid heat loss.
donot: Do NOT give the patient any over-the-counter painkillers or fever reducers (they might be the cause of the reaction).
Do NOT pop the blisters or peel the dead skin away.
Do NOT apply any adhesive bandages (they will rip the fragile skin off).
seek: Requires immediate transport to a Burn Center or ICU for specialized wound care, pain management, and fluid resuscitation.

title: Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)
warn: ⛔ MASSIVE SKIN LOSS — The most severe form of SJS, where more than 30% of the body’s skin blisters and peels off in large sheets.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Mortality rates are very high due to massive infection and dehydration risks.
Treat the patient exactly like a major 3rd-degree burn victim.
Cover exposed, raw skin loosely with a clean, dry, sterile sheet to prevent airborne infection.
Keep the environment incredibly warm to prevent fatal hypothermia.
Gather all pill bottles in the house to help doctors identify the offending drug.
donot: Do NOT apply creams, ointments, or wet dressings to the raw skin.
Do NOT attempt to move the patient by grabbing their arms or legs (the skin will literally slide off).
Do NOT delay EMS transport.
seek: Absolute emergency requiring a specialized Burn Unit for IV fluids, prophylactic antibiotics, and pain control.

title: Necrotizing Fasciitis (Flesh-Eating Disease)
warn: ⛔ RAPID TISSUE DEATH — Bacteria release toxins that destroy skin and underlying muscle fascia at a rate of an inch per hour.
steps: Look for a minor cut or scrape that is surrounded by redness, swelling, and pain that is severely out of proportion to the injury.
Watch for the skin turning purple, black, or developing fluid-filled blisters (bullae).
Gently press the skin: if you feel a crackling sensation like bubble wrap underneath (crepitus), gas-producing bacteria are destroying the tissue.
Draw a line around the red area with a pen and mark the time to track the rapid spread.
Go to the ER immediately.
donot: Do NOT assume it is a simple spider bite or rash, especially if the patient has a high fever or is vomiting.
Do NOT wait until the next morning to see if it improves.
Do NOT apply heating pads.
seek: Requires emergency surgery to slice open the skin and cut away the dead tissue (debridement), plus massive IV antibiotics.

title: Purpura Fulminans (Meningococcemia)
warn: ⛔ LETHAL BACTERIAL TOXIN — Bacteria in the blood cause massive clotting and bleeding into the skin, leading to rapid limb death and organ failure.
steps: Recognize the warning signs: Sudden high fever, lethargy, and the appearance of tiny red pinpricks (petechiae) that rapidly grow into large, dark purple, bruise-like patches.
Perform the "Glass Test": Press a clear drinking glass firmly against the purple rash. If the rash does NOT fade or turn white under pressure, it is a critical medical emergency.
Call 112 immediately. This can kill a healthy person within 12-24 hours.
Protect yourself (wear a mask and wash hands) as the underlying bacteria is highly contagious.
donot: Do NOT wait to see if the fever breaks with Tylenol/Motrin.
Do NOT dismiss the rash as simple bruising.
Do NOT let the patient exert themselves.
seek: Requires immediate, aggressive IV antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, and ICU admission.

title: Severe Angioedema
warn: ⚠️ AIRWAY CLOSURE RISK — Massive, rapid swelling deep under the skin, usually affecting the face, lips, tongue, or throat.
steps: Assess the airway immediately. Ask the patient to speak and swallow.
If their voice becomes hoarse, or they feel a "lump in their throat," the swelling is reaching the airway. Call 112 immediately.
If it is an allergic reaction and an EpiPen is available, use it immediately.
Check if they recently started a new blood pressure medication (ACE inhibitors like Lisinopril are a common cause, even years after starting).
Keep the patient sitting upright to ease breathing.
donot: Do NOT lay the patient flat on their back.
Do NOT assume an antihistamine (like Benadryl) will work fast enough if their throat is tightening.
Do NOT ignore swelling of the tongue, even if it seems minor initially.
seek: Requires ER evaluation for epinephrine, IV steroids, and airway monitoring.

title: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS)
warn: ⛔ EPIDERMAL DETACHMENT — A staph infection releases a toxin that breaks the bonds holding children’s skin together, making it look like they were dipped in boiling water.
steps: Primarily affects infants and children under 5.
Look for an initial crusty infection (often around the nose/mouth or diaper area), followed by a sudden high fever and bright red skin over the whole body.
Check for Nikolsky’s Sign: The top layer of the skin slips off easily when rubbed gently with a finger, leaving a raw, red, weeping surface.
Call 112 or go to the pediatric ER immediately.
Handle the child extremely gently to prevent further skin sloughing.
donot: Do NOT pick at the skin or pop any fluid-filled blisters.
Do NOT dress the child in tight clothing.
Do NOT apply steroid creams (this is a bacterial toxin, not eczema).
seek: Requires hospitalization, IV antibiotics to kill the staph bacteria, and burn-like wound care.

title: Facial Erysipelas
warn: ⚠️ BRAIN PROXIMITY — A superficial but intense bacterial infection of the skin on the face. High risk of spreading to the eyes or brain.
steps: Look for a bright red, swollen, raised, and highly painful plaque on the face (often across the nose and cheeks in a "butterfly" pattern).
Notice the distinct, sharp border between the red infected skin and the normal skin.
Check for systemic symptoms: Patients often develop a very high fever, chills, and shaking before the rash even appears.
Go to the ER or urgent care immediately.
Elevate the head of the bed to reduce facial swelling.
donot: Do NOT confuse this with a simple sunburn or lupus rash (the sudden high fever and extreme tenderness point to infection).
Do NOT squeeze or press hard on the affected area.
Do NOT apply makeup or cosmetic creams to the area.
seek: Requires prompt oral or IV antibiotics to prevent the infection from tracking into the delicate veins that lead to the brain.

title: Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS)
warn: ⛔ SEPTIC SHOCK — A bacterial toxin causes massive organ failure, accompanied by a very specific skin rash.
steps: Recognize the clinical triad: 1. Sudden high fever. 2. Dangerously low blood pressure (dizziness/fainting). 3. A widespread red rash that looks exactly like a severe sunburn.
Identify potential sources: Recent surgery, an infected wound, or leaving a tampon/menstrual cup in for a prolonged period.
Remove the tampon or any wound packings immediately if present.
Call 112 immediately. The patient will deteriorate into shock rapidly.
Lay the patient flat and elevate their legs to maintain blood flow to the brain.
donot: Do NOT assume it is just the flu with a fever rash.
Do NOT give the patient anything to eat or drink.
Do NOT leave the patient alone if they feel faint.
seek: Requires ICU admission for massive fluid resuscitation, blood pressure support medications, and IV antibiotics.

title: Pemphigus Vulgaris
warn: ⚠️ SEVERE BLISTERING — An autoimmune disease where the body attacks its own skin cells, causing large, flaccid blisters that burst easily and become infected.
steps: Identify the signs: Painful sores usually start in the mouth (making swallowing agonizing) and then spread to the skin as large, soft blisters.
Treat the open sores like burns. Cover them with loose, non-stick, sterile dressings.
If the patient has trouble swallowing, stick to cool, soft foods or liquids if they must eat, but ER evaluation is preferred.
Look for signs of severe dehydration, as fluid weeps constantly from the open sores.
Go to the ER or contact a dermatologist immediately if this is a new onset.
donot: Do NOT rub the skin; even light friction can cause the top layer of skin to slide off (positive Nikolsky sign).
Do NOT apply tape to the skin.
Do NOT use harsh mouthwashes or eat spicy/acidic foods.
seek: Requires heavy immunosuppressants (high-dose steroids, Rituximab) and specialized wound care to prevent lethal sepsis.

title: DRESS Syndrome
warn: ⚠️ HIDDEN ORGAN DAMAGE — Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms. A delayed, severe allergic reaction that attacks internal organs beneath a widespread rash.
steps: Take a careful history: Did the patient start a new medication (especially anti-seizure meds or antibiotics) 2 to 8 weeks ago?
Look for the hallmark triad: A widespread, itchy red rash, severe facial swelling, and a high fever.
Watch for signs of liver or kidney inflammation: yellowing of the eyes/skin (jaundice) or decreased urination.
Stop the suspected medication immediately.
Go to the Emergency Room.
donot: Do NOT assume the rash is harmless because the drug was started weeks ago (DRESS is famous for its long delay).
Do NOT ignore facial swelling accompanying a full-body rash.
Do NOT wait for a scheduled doctor's appointment if fever is present.
seek: Requires hospitalization, systemic steroids, and blood work to monitor for acute liver failure and heart inflammation.

title: Erythroderma (Exfoliative Dermatitis)
warn: ⛔ TOTAL BODY INFLAMMATION — Over 90% of the skin turns bright red, thickens, and scales. Causes massive heat, fluid, and protein loss leading to heart failure.
steps: Recognize the severity: The entire body looks intensely sunburned, feels hot to the touch, and sheds scales constantly.
Check for shivering. Despite feeling hot to the touch, the patient cannot regulate their temperature and will suffer from severe hypothermia.
Wrap the patient in warm blankets to maintain their core temperature.
Monitor for swelling in the lower legs and shortness of breath (the heart has to pump massively harder to supply all the inflamed skin, causing high-output heart failure).
Go to the ER immediately.
donot: Do NOT apply cold compresses all over the body (this will trigger lethal hypothermia).
Do NOT ignore a rapidly racing heart in these patients.
Do NOT assume it is just a bad eczema flare if more than 90% of the body is suddenly involved.
seek: Requires hospital admission to correct fluid/electrolyte imbalances, regulate body temperature, and treat the underlying cause.

title: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus
warn: ⚠️ BLINDNESS THREAT — Shingles (reactivated chickenpox virus) occurring on the face, specifically threatening the optic nerve and cornea.
steps: Observe for a painful, blistering rash that occurs ONLY on one side of the forehead, scalp, and eye area (it will not cross the midline of the face).
Check for Hutchinson’s Sign: If there is a blister on the very tip or side of the nose, the virus has tracked along the nerve that also supplies the eye. This is an absolute red flag.
The patient will often complain of severe, burning, electric nerve pain in that area days before the rash appears.
Go to the ER or an ophthalmologist immediately.
donot: Do NOT let the patient rub their eyes.
Do NOT apply over-the-counter steroid creams to the eye or the rash (steroids can worsen viral eye infections to the point of rupture).
Do NOT delay treatment (antiviral meds must be started within 72 hours).
