seek: Requires immediate prescription oral antiviral medication (Acyclovir/Valacyclovir) and a thorough eye exam to prevent permanent blindness.

title: Eczema Herpeticum
warn: ⚠️ VIRAL SPREAD — The Herpes Simplex Virus (cold sore virus) infects skin that is already compromised by eczema, spreading rapidly across the body.
steps: Look for a sudden, severe worsening of an existing eczema rash.
Identify the classic lesion: Clusters of tiny, uniform, fluid-filled blisters that burst and leave circular, "punched-out" scabs.
Check for systemic symptoms: The patient will usually have a high fever, swollen lymph nodes, and feel generally unwell.
Particularly dangerous in infants and children.
Go to the pediatric ER or urgent care immediately.
donot: Do NOT kiss or let anyone with an active cold sore near a child with severe eczema.
Do NOT apply steroid creams to these new punched-out blisters (it will suppress the immune system and let the virus spread faster).
Do NOT send the child to school/daycare (highly contagious).
seek: Requires immediate systemic antiviral medications (Acyclovir) to prevent the virus from spreading to the brain or eyes.

title: Fournier’s Gangrene
warn: ⛔ LETHAL GENITAL INFECTION — A rare but extremely aggressive flesh-eating infection of the perineum and genitals. High mortality rate if delayed.
steps: Recognize the symptoms: Sudden, excruciating pain, swelling, and redness in the genital or anal region.
Watch for systemic collapse: The patient will quickly develop a high fever, sweating, confusion, and a racing heart.
Note any foul-smelling drainage or dark/black patches of skin in the affected area.
Call 112 or go to the ER immediately. Time is measured in minutes and hours.
Most common in elderly men, diabetics, or immunocompromised individuals.
donot: Do NOT delay going to the hospital out of embarrassment (this is a common and deadly mistake).
Do NOT try to treat it at home with sitz baths or antibacterial creams.
Do NOT hide the symptom of agonizing genital pain from the triage nurse.
seek: Requires immediate, aggressive surgical debridement (cutting away the dead tissue) by a urologist/surgeon and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.

title: Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (RMSF)
warn: ⛔ LETHAL TICK DISEASE — A bacterial infection from a tick bite that damages the lining of blood vessels throughout the body, causing them to leak.
steps: Ask about recent outdoor activity in wooded or grassy areas (even if they didn't notice a tick bite).
Watch for the classic early signs: Sudden high fever, severe headache, and muscle aches.
Look for the hallmark rash (usually appears on days 3-5): Small, flat, pink, non-itchy spots that start on the WRISTS, FOREARMS, and ANKLES, and spread inward to the trunk.
As it worsens, the rash turns into dark purple pinpricks (petechiae) indicating bleeding under the skin.
Go to the ER immediately if this specific rash pattern appears with a fever.
donot: Do NOT wait for the rash to appear to seek medical help if they have a fever and a known tick bite.
Do NOT ignore a rash that starts on the palms of the hands or soles of the feet (this is highly specific to RMSF and a few other serious diseases).
Do NOT squeeze a tick if you find one attached; remove it gently with tweezers.
seek: Requires immediate administration of Doxycycline. Delaying antibiotics past the 5th day of symptoms massively increases the risk of death.

title: Cutaneous Anthrax
warn: ⚠️ TOXIC SPORES — Caused by handling infected animals, wool, or hides. The bacteria produce toxins that cause a highly distinct, necrotic skin ulcer.
steps: Identify the classic lesion: It starts as an itchy bump, blisters, and within days turns into a completely PAINLESS ulcer with a pitch-black center (an eschar).
Notice the surrounding skin: It is usually massively swollen and surrounded by smaller blisters.
Ask the patient about their occupation or hobbies (farming, veterinary work, handling imported animal hides/drums).
Cover the wound with a dry, sterile bandage to prevent spreading the spores.
Go to the ER immediately and explicitly state your suspicion of anthrax.
donot: Do NOT touch the wound with bare hands.
Do NOT attempt to scrape or remove the black scab.
Do NOT assume it is a spider bite if it is completely painless (spider bites hurt; anthrax ulcers do not).
seek: Requires a 60-day course of specific antibiotics (like Ciprofloxacin or Doxycycline). Usually fully curable if treated before the bacteria enter the bloodstream.

title: Bullous Pemphigoid (Severe Flare)
warn: ⚠️ WIDESPREAD BLISTERS — An autoimmune disease primarily affecting the elderly, causing deep, tense blisters that do not rupture easily.
steps: Recognize the patient profile: Usually over the age of 60.
Look for the lesions: Intensely itchy, red hives that evolve into large, tight, fluid-filled blisters (often on the lower abdomen, thighs, or armpits).
Unlike Pemphigus Vulgaris, these blisters are tough and do not pop easily, and they rarely affect the mouth.
If the blisters pop, treat them with sterile, non-stick dressings to prevent infection.
Seek medical evaluation if a large portion of the body is covered.
donot: Do NOT pop the blisters purposefully (the intact skin protects against infection).
Do NOT scrub the skin while bathing.
Do NOT ignore signs of infection (yellow pus, increasing redness, fever) in burst blisters.
seek: Requires evaluation by a dermatologist or ER to start potent topical or oral corticosteroids and prevent secondary bacterial infections.

title: Acute Generalized Exanthematous Pustulosis (AGEP)
warn: ⚠️ RAPID PUSTULAR REACTION — A rare drug reaction where thousands of tiny, non-infected pus-filled bumps rapidly erupt over a red, swollen rash.
steps: Ask about new medications: This almost always happens within 1 to 3 days of starting a new antibiotic (like Penicillin or Macrolides).
Look for the hallmark sign: A bright red rash that suddenly develops dozens or hundreds of pinpoint white/yellow pustules (usually starting in the armpits or groin).
Check for a fever, which is almost always present.
Stop the suspected antibiotic immediately.
Go to an urgent care or ER for diagnosis.
donot: Do NOT try to pop or scrub the pustules away.
Do NOT apply thick ointments or occlusive dressings over the rash.
Do NOT assume it is a widespread bacterial infection; the "pus" here is actually sterile white blood cells reacting to the drug.
seek: Usually resolves quickly once the offending drug is stopped, but a doctor must confirm the diagnosis and provide alternative antibiotics if needed.

title: Erythema Multiforme Major
warn: ⚠️ TARGET LESIONS & MUCOSA — An immune reaction (often to the Herpes virus or Mycoplasma pneumonia) causing bullseye-shaped spots and severe mucosal blistering.
steps: Identify the classic rash: Looks like a literal target or bullseye (a dark center, surrounded by a pale ring, surrounded by a red ring).
Check where it starts: Usually appears on the backs of the hands, palms, and feet, then moves toward the torso.
CRITICAL CHECK: Look inside the mouth, eyes, and genital area. If there are painful blisters or raw ulcers there, it is "Major" and an emergency.
Monitor for difficulty breathing or swallowing.
Go to the ER if mucous membranes are involved or if the patient is in severe pain.
donot: Do NOT ignore mouth pain or eye redness accompanying a rash.
Do NOT administer new, unprescribed over-the-counter medications.
Do NOT let the patient become dehydrated if mouth pain prevents drinking.
seek: Requires hospital evaluation for fluid support, pain control, and to rule out the more severe Stevens-Johnson Syndrome.

title: Severe Cellulitis with Systemic Toxicity
warn: ⚠️ BLOOD POISONING THREAT — A common bacterial skin infection that escapes local control and begins sending bacteria into the bloodstream.
steps: Look at the affected area (usually a lower leg): It will be red, swollen, hot to the touch, and very tender.
Look for Red Streaks: If you see red lines tracking up the skin away from the infection toward the lymph nodes, the infection is spreading rapidly (lymphangitis).
Check for systemic signs: High fever, chills, dizziness, confusion, or a racing heart.
Draw a line with a pen around the red border to show doctors if it is expanding.
Elevate the limb to reduce swelling and pain.
donot: Do NOT attempt to squeeze or drain the skin (cellulitis is deep in the tissue, there is no pus to pop; squeezing spreads the bacteria).
Do NOT wait to see a primary doctor in two days if red streaks or a high fever develop.
Do NOT wear tight socks, shoes, or compression garments over the active infection.
seek: Requires immediate IV antibiotics in the ER. If left untreated, it will quickly progress to life-threatening sepsis.

title: Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH)
warn: ⛔ MASSIVE BLOOD LOSS — The uterus fails to contract after delivery, allowing the placental wound to bleed uncontrollably.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This is the leading cause of maternal mortality.
Perform a Fundal Massage: Find the top of the uterus (fundus) near the mother's navel. Massage it vigorously and deeply with a cupped hand until it feels as firm as a grapefruit.
Have the mother breastfeed the baby immediately if possible (this naturally releases oxytocin, which causes the uterus to contract).
Keep the mother lying flat and elevate her legs to treat for shock.
Encourage the mother to empty her bladder if she can, as a full bladder prevents the uterus from clamping down.
donot: Do NOT stop massaging the uterus just because the mother complains of pain (the massage is saving her life).
Do NOT pack the vagina with towels or gauze to stop the bleeding.
Do NOT let the mother stand up or walk to the bathroom.
seek: Requires immediate IV fluids, synthetic oxytocin (Pitocin), and emergency OB/GYN intervention.

title: Eclampsia (Maternal Seizure)
warn: ⛔ SEIZURE DURING/AFTER PREGNANCY — Severe high blood pressure leads to a sudden, life-threatening seizure, depriving both mother and baby of oxygen.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Ease the mother to the floor. Protect her head with something soft.
Roll her onto her LEFT side (Recovery Position). This keeps her airway clear and prevents the heavy uterus from crushing the main blood vessels returning to her heart.
Clear the area of sharp or hard objects.
Note the exact time the seizure started and how long it lasts.
donot: Do NOT attempt to hold the mother down or stop the convulsions.
Do NOT put anything in her mouth.
Do NOT assume she is safe just because she delivered the baby days ago (postpartum eclampsia can occur weeks after birth).
seek: Requires immediate emergency transport for IV Magnesium Sulfate to stop the seizures, and rapid delivery of the baby if still pregnant.

title: Placental Abruption
warn: ⛔ INTERNAL HEMORRHAGE — The placenta prematurely tears away from the uterine wall, suffocating the baby and causing massive internal bleeding for the mother.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Time is critical for fetal survival.
Recognize the classic signs: Sudden, severe, constant abdominal pain, a stomach that feels rock-hard (rigid) to the touch, and dark red vaginal bleeding (though bleeding may be hidden inside).
Lay the mother on her LEFT side to maximize blood flow to the baby.
Treat the mother for shock (keep her warm, administer oxygen if trained and equipped).
Provide constant reassurance.
donot: Do NOT lay the mother flat on her back.
Do NOT allow her to eat or drink anything (she will need an emergency C-section).
Do NOT ignore a pregnant woman complaining of severe abdominal pain after a car accident or fall, even if she has no visible bleeding.
seek: Requires an absolute emergency C-section and massive blood transfusions.

title: Placenta Previa (Bleeding)
warn: ⚠️ BLOCKED EXIT — The placenta is covering the cervix. Cervical dilation causes the placenta to tear and bleed profusely.
steps: Recognize the classic sign: Sudden, painless, bright red vaginal bleeding in the second or third trimester.
Call 112 or transport the mother to the hospital immediately.
Have the mother lie down on her left side and rest completely.
Keep track of roughly how much blood is being lost (e.g., how many pads are soaked).
Keep the mother completely calm.
donot: Do NOT insert anything into the vagina (no tampons, no fingers).
Do NOT allow the mother to do any physical activity.
Do NOT perform a vaginal exam under any circumstances (you can puncture the placenta and cause catastrophic hemorrhage).
seek: Requires ultrasound diagnosis and hospital bed rest. The baby must be delivered via C-section if the placenta covers the cervix.

title: Umbilical Cord Prolapse
warn: ⛔ FETAL CHOKING — The umbilical cord drops through the cervix before the baby. The baby's head then crushes the cord, cutting off its own oxygen supply.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This usually happens right after the mother’s "water breaks."
If you see the umbilical cord coming out of the vagina, DO NOT push it back in.
Position the mother IMMEDIATELY into the Knee-Chest position (kneeling, with her chest flat on the floor and her buttocks highest in the air).
Alternatively, use an exaggerated Sims position (lying on left side with hips elevated on thick pillows).
If you are a trained medical provider, insert a sterile, gloved hand into the vagina and gently push the baby's head UP and OFF the cord. Keep your hand there until the C-section.
donot: Do NOT attempt to push the cord back into the uterus (it will spasm and cut off blood flow).
Do NOT let the mother push or bear down.
Do NOT pull on the cord.
seek: Requires a hyper-emergency C-section (often within minutes) to save the baby from brain damage or death.

title: Shoulder Dystocia
warn: ⛔ BABY TRAPPED — The baby's head is delivered, but the shoulders get stuck behind the mother's pelvic bone. The baby cannot breathe.
steps: Call 112 if delivering outside a hospital.
Recognize the "Turtle Sign": The baby’s head delivers, but then retracts tightly back against the mother’s perineum.
Perform the McRoberts Maneuver: Have two helpers sharply and firmly push the mother’s knees as far back toward her own ears as possible. (This flattens her pelvis).
Apply Suprapubic Pressure: A helper must push firmly down and toward the baby's face just ABOVE the mother's pubic bone to pop the shoulder loose.
Encourage the mother to push only when instructed.
donot: Do NOT pull forcefully on the baby’s head or neck (you will permanently tear the spinal nerves/brachial plexus).
Do NOT push on the top of the uterus (fundal pressure); this wedges the shoulder in tighter.
Do NOT panic, but act rapidly (you have roughly 5 minutes to free the baby).
seek: Requires specific obstetrical maneuvers by a trained provider. Often results in the need for newborn resuscitation.

title: Uterine Rupture
warn: ⛔ UTERUS TEARS OPEN — The wall of the uterus tears during labor, spilling the baby and massive amounts of blood into the mother's abdomen.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This is highest risk for mothers attempting a Vaginal Birth After C-Section (VBAC).
Recognize the signs: The mother complains of a sudden, sharp, tearing pain that is completely different from a contraction.
Contractions may suddenly stop entirely.
The baby's parts may suddenly be easily felt through the skin of the stomach.
Treat the mother for profound shock (lie her on her left side, keep warm).
donot: Do NOT wait to see if contractions restart.
Do NOT attempt to feel for the baby’s position by aggressively pressing on the abdomen.
Do NOT let the mother eat or drink.
seek: Absolute surgical emergency requiring a crash C-section to save the baby and a hysterectomy or uterine repair to save the mother.

title: Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy
warn: ⛔ MASSIVE INTERNAL BLEEDING — A fertilized egg grows in the fallopian tube until it bursts. The leading cause of maternal death in the first trimester.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Suspect this in any woman of childbearing age with sudden, severe, one-sided lower abdominal pain and a missed period.
Ask about "referred shoulder pain" (blood pooling in the abdomen irritates the diaphragm, causing sharp pain in the tip of the shoulder).
Monitor for signs of shock: pale skin, dizziness, fainting, racing heart.
Lay the patient flat and elevate her legs slightly to maintain blood flow to the brain.
Keep her warm.
donot: Do NOT ignore severe one-sided abdominal pain in early pregnancy, assuming it is just "growing pains."
Do NOT give pain medication or food/drink.
Do NOT assume she is not pregnant just because she had some light spotting (ectopics often cause spotting).
seek: Requires immediate emergency surgery to stop the bleeding and remove the ruptured fallopian tube.

title: Severe Pre-eclampsia
warn: ⚠️ ORGAN DAMAGE IMMINENT — Dangerously high blood pressure in pregnancy damaging the liver, kidneys, and brain. The precursor to seizures.
steps: Acknowledge red-flag symptoms in a pregnant woman (usually 20+ weeks): A severe, pounding headache that won't go away, seeing spots/flashing lights, and severe pain in the upper right stomach.
Check for sudden, extreme swelling in the face and hands (not just the feet).
Go to the Emergency Room or Labor & Delivery immediately.
Keep the mother in a quiet, dark environment (bright lights and noise can trigger a seizure).
Have her rest on her left side.
donot: Do NOT ignore a severe headache in the 3rd trimester, assuming it is just stress or dehydration.
Do NOT tell her to just take Tylenol and lie down.
Do NOT let her drive herself to the hospital.
seek: Requires hospitalization, IV blood pressure medications, Magnesium Sulfate, and likely induction of labor (delivery is the only cure).

title: HELLP Syndrome
warn: ⛔ TOXIC PREGNANCY COMPLICATION — Hemolysis (breaking down blood), Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelet count. A severe variant of pre-eclampsia.
steps: Call 112 or go to the ER immediately.
Watch for the hallmark symptom: Severe, unrelenting pain just under the right rib cage or in the center of the upper stomach (this is the liver swelling/bleeding).
Look for nausea, vomiting, extreme fatigue, and easy bruising/bleeding.
Treat as a critical emergency; the liver can rupture or the mother can stroke.
Keep the mother strictly on bed rest on her left side.
donot: Do NOT mistake the upper abdominal pain for simple heartburn or indigestion (a deadly, common mistake).
Do NOT massage the upper right abdomen.
Do NOT wait for a scheduled OB appointment.
seek: Requires ICU/L&D admission for blood transfusions, steroids, and emergency delivery of the baby, regardless of gestational age.

title: Amniotic Fluid Embolism (AFE)
warn: ⛔ SUDDEN MATERNAL ARREST — Amniotic fluid enters the mother’s bloodstream during labor or birth, causing an anaphylactic-like shock and sudden heart stoppage.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This usually occurs during intense labor or immediately after delivery.
Recognize the sudden onset: The mother suddenly gasps for air, turns blue, complains of a sense of doom, and rapidly loses consciousness and pulse.
Begin CPR immediately if she is pulseless and unresponsive.

CRITICAL DIFFERENCE: During CPR, a helper MUST physically push the pregnant belly entirely to the LEFT side (Left Uterine Displacement). If the heavy uterus crushes the vena cava, CPR compressions will not circulate any blood.
Prepare to use an AED as soon as it arrives.
donot: Do NOT perform CPR with the pregnant mother lying perfectly flat on her back without moving the uterus out of the way.
Do NOT stop CPR.
Do NOT delay calling for advanced life support.
seek: Highest level emergency. Requires massive ICU intervention, blood products, and perimortem C-section (if undelivered) to save the baby and aid maternal CPR.

title: Vasa Previa (Ruptured)
warn: ⛔ FETAL EXSANGUINATION — The baby’s blood vessels cross the cervix unprotected. When the mother’s "water breaks," the baby’s blood vessels snap.
steps: Call 112 IMMEDIATELY. The blood being lost belongs to the baby, not the mother. A baby has very little blood volume and can bleed to death in minutes.
Recognize the event: The mother’s water breaks, and it is immediately followed by dark or bright red, painless vaginal bleeding.
Keep the mother completely flat and still.
Elevate her hips if possible.
Provide oxygen to the mother if trained (this maximizes oxygen to the baby).
donot: Do NOT mistake this for normal "bloody show" (which is mucus-like and scant). Vasa Previa bleeding is liquid blood pouring out when the water breaks.
Do NOT allow the mother to sit on the toilet or bear down.
Do NOT delay transport.
seek: Requires a hyper-emergency crash C-section and immediate blood transfusions for the newborn.

title: Uterine Inversion
warn: ⛔ UTERUS TURNS INSIDE OUT — Following delivery, the uterus completely collapses in on itself and protrudes from the vagina. Causes instant, profound shock.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Recognize the sign: A large, red, bleeding mass suddenly bulges out of the vagina shortly after the baby is born, accompanied by massive maternal blood pressure drop.
If the placenta is still attached to the inverted uterus, DO NOT attempt to peel it off (this will cause fatal bleeding).
Treat the mother for profound shock: lie her flat, elevate her legs, and keep her warm.
Apply moist, sterile dressings to the exposed uterine tissue if possible.
donot: Do NOT ever pull forcefully on the umbilical cord to try and deliver the placenta (this is the #1 cause of uterine inversion).
Do NOT attempt to push the uterus back inside unless you are a trained obstetric provider.
Do NOT give oxytocin until the uterus is put back into place.
seek: Requires a doctor to manually punch the uterus back into place under general anesthesia, or emergency abdominal surgery.

title: Chorioamnionitis (Intra-amniotic Infection)
warn: ⚠️ INFECTION IN THE WOMB — Bacteria infect the amniotic fluid and membranes, putting both mother and baby at risk for deadly sepsis.
steps: Look for the signs during labor or after the water breaks: Maternal fever (>100.4°F/38°C), a racing heart rate in the mother or baby, and a tender, painful uterus even between contractions.
Notice the fluid: The amniotic fluid may be yellow, cloudy, or have a foul odor.
Go to the hospital immediately if the water broke at home and these symptoms appear.
Keep the mother hydrated and monitor her temperature.
donot: Do NOT try to treat a fever in labor at home.
Do NOT take a bath if the water has broken.
Do NOT engage in any sexual intercourse after the water has broken (introduces bacteria directly to the baby).
seek: Requires IV antibiotics during labor and immediate evaluation of the newborn for sepsis after delivery.

title: Retained Placenta
warn: ⚠️ FAILED DETACHMENT — The placenta fails to deliver within 30 minutes of the baby. It acts as a sponge, keeping the blood vessels open and bleeding.
steps: If giving birth outside a hospital, wait calmly. The placenta usually delivers within 5-30 minutes.
Encourage the mother to breastfeed the baby immediately (nipple stimulation causes the uterus to contract and expel the placenta).
Have the mother squat or sit upright to use gravity.
If the placenta has not delivered after 30-45 minutes, or if she begins bleeding heavily, call 112.
Keep the umbilical cord clamped or tied off.
donot: Do NOT pull on the umbilical cord to yank the placenta out (you will cause a uterine inversion or snap the cord, making it harder for a doctor to retrieve).
Do NOT aggressively massage the uterus BEFORE the placenta is out, unless she is actively hemorrhaging.
Do NOT cut the cord if you don't have sterile equipment (leave baby attached until EMS arrives).
seek: Requires a doctor to perform a manual extraction (reaching into the uterus to peel it off) or a surgical D&C to remove the tissue and stop bleeding.

title: Imminent Preterm Labor (<37 Weeks)
warn: ⚠️ EARLY ARRIVAL — Labor begins before the baby's lungs and brain are fully developed. Every hour the baby stays inside counts.
steps: Recognize the signs: Regular contractions (more than 4 in an hour) before 37 weeks, constant low backache, or a sudden feeling of heavy pressure in the pelvis.
Have the mother stop whatever she is doing, lie down on her left side, and drink 2-3 large glasses of water (dehydration can trigger false labor).
If the contractions do not stop after an hour of resting and hydrating, or if her water breaks, call 112 or go to L&D immediately.
Check for any bleeding or change in vaginal discharge.
donot: Do NOT wait to see if the contractions get painfully strong (preterm labor is often less painful than full-term labor initially).
Do NOT let the mother take a hot bath.
Do NOT delay going to a hospital with a Level III NICU.
seek: Requires medications (tocolytics) to stop contractions and steroid injections to rapidly mature the baby’s lungs before birth.

title: Septic Abortion / Infected Miscarriage
warn: ⛔ TOXIC INFECTION — Following a miscarriage or abortion, tissue remains inside the uterus and becomes severely infected, risking lethal sepsis.
steps: Observe for red flags in the days following a pregnancy loss: High fever, chills, severe abdominal pain, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge.
Call 112 or go to the ER immediately if the patient looks pale, confused, or has a racing heart (signs of systemic septic shock).
Keep the patient laying down and resting.
Gather information about when the pregnancy loss occurred and any procedures performed.
donot: Do NOT ignore a fever after a miscarriage, assuming it is just grief or a normal cold.
Do NOT use tampons or insert anything into the vagina.
Do NOT rely on over-the-counter pain meds; the infection must be removed.
seek: Requires immediate IV antibiotics and an emergency D&C (Dilation and Curettage) to surgically empty and clean the uterus.

title: Severe Hyperemesis Gravidarum
warn: ⚠️ STARVATION & DEHYDRATION — Extreme, unrelenting morning sickness that prevents the mother from keeping any food or liquid down, threatening her kidneys and the baby's growth.
steps: Assess for severe dehydration: Dark urine, not urinating for 8+ hours, dizziness upon standing, and extreme weakness.
If she cannot keep even a sip of water down for 12-24 hours, take her to the ER or urgent care.
Have her try sucking on ice chips or popsicles rather than drinking a full glass of water.
Keep her environment free of strong smells and entirely dark and quiet to reduce nausea.
donot: Do NOT dismiss it as "just normal morning sickness" if she is losing weight or unable to urinate.
Do NOT force her to eat large meals or "push through it."
Do NOT give her unprescribed anti-nausea medications or herbs.
seek: Requires IV fluids, IV vitamins (specifically Thiamine), and prescription antiemetics (like Zofran) in a hospital setting.

title: Decreased Fetal Movement
warn: ⚠️ FETAL DISTRESS WARNING — A significant drop in the baby's normal kicking or moving is often the first and only warning sign that the baby is struggling for oxygen.
steps: If the mother notices the baby is unusually quiet, perform a "Kick Count" immediately.
Have the mother drink something very cold or very sweet (like orange juice) and lie down on her left side in a quiet room.
Focus purely on the baby. Count every movement (kick, flutter, roll).
If the mother does NOT feel 10 movements within 2 hours, go to Labor & Delivery immediately.
Trust the mother’s intuition; if she feels something is wrong, get checked.
donot: Do NOT use an at-home fetal doppler to check for a heartbeat (a dying baby will still have a heartbeat until the very end; lack of movement is the warning sign).
Do NOT wait until tomorrow if the baby stops moving tonight.
Do NOT let anyone dismiss her concerns as "the baby is just running out of room." (Babies do not stop moving at the end of pregnancy).
seek: Requires an immediate Non-Stress Test (NST) and biophysical ultrasound at the hospital to check the baby's oxygen and fluid levels.

title: Imminent Breech Delivery (Out of Hospital)
warn: ⚠️ HEAD TRAPPED RISK — The baby is coming buttocks or feet first. The largest part (the head) comes last and can easily get trapped by the cervix, cutting off the cord.
steps: Call 112 immediately. Inform them the mother is pushing and the baby is breech.
Position the mother with her buttocks at the very edge of a bed, legs supported by helpers.
Let the baby deliver spontaneously up to the belly button. DO NOT PULL ON THE BABY.
Once the body is out, support the baby's body with a towel, letting it hang slightly downward to encourage the head to enter the pelvis.

If the head does not deliver within 3 minutes of the body, or if the baby is trying to breathe, place your fingers in the vagina and push the vaginal wall away from the baby’s face to create an airway until EMS arrives.
donot: Do NOT pull the baby by the legs or body (you will cause the head to extend back and get permanently wedged in the pelvis).
Do NOT try to push the baby back inside.
Do NOT panic if the baby is bruised or blue upon delivery (breech babies often are).
seek: Requires extreme emergency obstetric skills or a C-section if caught before delivery. High risk for newborn resuscitation.

title: Acute Suicidal Crisis
warn: ⛔ IMMEDIATE THREAT TO LIFE — The person has a plan, intent, and the means to end their life.
steps: Ask directly and clearly: "Are you thinking about killing yourself?" (Asking does NOT plant the idea).
If they say yes, ask if they have a plan and the means to do it right now.
Remove any lethal means immediately (pills, firearms, knives, ropes) if it is safe for you to do so.
Call 112, a local crisis response team, or iCall: 9152987821 or Vandrevala Foundation Helpline: 1860-2662-345 (24×7) immediately.
Stay with the person continuously. Do not leave them alone for a second, not even to go to the bathroom.
Listen without judgment. Acknowledge their pain without trying to "fix" it instantly.
donot: Do NOT promise to keep their suicidal thoughts a secret.
Do NOT argue with them about the value of life or tell them they have "so much to live for" (this causes guilt and shuts them down).
Do NOT leave them alone under any circumstances.
seek: Requires immediate emergency psychiatric evaluation in a secure hospital unit.

title: Acute Psychotic Episode
warn: ⛔ BREAK FROM REALITY — The person is experiencing intense hallucinations (seeing/hearing things) or delusions (false, fixed beliefs).
steps: Maintain a calm, low-pitched voice. Move slowly and predictably.
Reduce environmental stimuli (turn off the TV, dim the lights, ask bystanders to leave).
Validate their feelings of fear or distress without validating the delusion itself (e.g., "I don't hear the voices, but I can see how terrified you are.").
Give them plenty of physical space. Do not corner them.
Call 112 or a mobile crisis unit if they become a danger to themselves or others.
donot: Do NOT argue with their delusions or try to logic them out of it (it is a biological reality to their brain).
Do NOT play along with the delusion (do not pretend to see the hallucinations).
Do NOT touch them without explicit warning and permission.
seek: Requires emergency psychiatric care for antipsychotic medication and stabilization.

title: Severe Panic Attack
warn: ⚠️ MIMICS A HEART ATTACK — The physical symptoms are incredibly real and terrifying to the patient, often leading them to believe they are dying.
steps: Move the person to a quiet, less crowded space if possible.
Speak in short, simple, reassuring sentences: "You are having a panic attack. It is temporary. You are safe."
Guide them through Box Breathing: Inhale for 4 seconds, hold for 4, exhale for 4, hold for 4.
Use the 5-4-3-2-1 Grounding Technique: Ask them to name 5 things they see, 4 they can touch, 3 they hear, 2 they smell, and 1 they taste.
If they complain of severe chest pain that radiates, or if it is their first panic attack, call 112 to rule out a cardiac event.
donot: Do NOT tell them to "just calm down" or "it is all in your head."
Do NOT have them breathe into a paper bag (this can be dangerous if they are actually having a heart attack or asthma attack).
Do NOT shake them or grab their shoulders.
seek: If grounding techniques fail after 20-30 minutes, or if physical symptoms worsen, seek ER evaluation to rule out medical emergencies.

title: Acute Manic Episode
warn: ⚠️ IMPULSIVITY AND AGITATION — Extreme, boundless energy often paired with severe lack of sleep, grandiose delusions, and highly reckless behavior.
steps: Decrease stimulation heavily (quiet room, low lights, minimal conversation).
Set clear, firm, but non-confrontational boundaries regarding safety.
Try to restrict access to car keys, credit cards, or large sums of money if they are engaging in destructive, impulsive behaviors.
Offer high-calorie, easy-to-eat foods and fluids, as they often forget to eat or cannot sit still long enough to do so.
Contact their psychiatrist, family members, or emergency services.
donot: Do NOT argue with their grandiose claims or try to match their intense energy.
Do NOT engage in long, drawn-out conversations (their racing thoughts will escalate).
Do NOT attempt to physically restrain them unless there is an immediate threat to life.
seek: Often requires voluntary or involuntary psychiatric hospitalization for medication adjustment (mood stabilizers/antipsychotics).

title: PTSD Flashback / Dissociation
warn: ⚠️ RELIVING TRAUMA — The patient is psychologically transported back to a traumatic event. They may not recognize you or their current surroundings.
steps: Do NOT touch the person. Touching someone in a flashback can trigger a violent, defensive reflex.
Speak in a calm, clear, and consistent voice.
Orient them to the present: "My name is [Name]. It is the year 2026. You are in Kolkata. You are safe now."
Encourage grounding: "Can you feel the chair underneath you? Can you feel the floor under your feet?"
Give them physical space and ensure nobody blocks their exit path from the room.
donot: Do NOT sneak up behind them or make sudden loud noises.
Do NOT ask for details about the trauma during the crisis.
Do NOT tell them "it’s over" if they are actively hallucinating the threat; instead, focus on grounding them to the current physical room.
seek: Follow up with their trauma therapist. Emergency services are only needed if they become a danger to themselves or others during the episode.

title: Active Non-Suicidal Self-Injury (NSSI)
warn: ⛔ ACCIDENTAL LETHALITY RISK — While the intent may be to relieve emotional pain rather than die, severe cuts or burns can easily become accidentally lethal.
steps: Address the physical injury first. Apply direct pressure to any bleeding wounds using clean cloths or sterile gauze.
Remove any remaining sharp objects or hazardous materials from the immediate area.
Maintain an absolutely neutral, non-judgmental, and calm demeanor.
If the bleeding is arterial (spurting), deep, or won't stop after 10 minutes of pressure, call 112 immediately.
Offer them a safe alternative coping mechanism if they are still feeling the urge (e.g., holding ice cubes tightly, snapping a rubber band on the wrist).
donot: Do NOT act horrified, disgusted, or angry at the self-harm (this drastically increases their shame and emotional pain).
Do NOT demand that they promise "never to do it again" in the middle of a crisis.
Do NOT force them to show you all their scars.
seek: Requires medical attention for suturing/wound care, followed by psychiatric assessment to address the underlying distress.

title: Postpartum Psychosis
warn: ⛔ EXTREME RISK TO INFANT AND MOTHER — A rare but highly lethal psychiatric emergency occurring days or weeks after childbirth, involving severe delusions about the baby.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This is an absolute, time-critical medical emergency.
Ensure the infant’s safety immediately. Gently and calmly separate the baby from the mother by having another trusted adult take over childcare in another room.
Do not accuse the mother of being a "bad mom"; validate that she is exhausted and unwell.
Stay with the mother continuously. The risk of sudden suicide or infanticide is incredibly high, even if she seems calm one minute.
Listen for bizarre beliefs regarding the infant (e.g., believing the baby is a demon or that the baby needs to be "saved" from the world).
donot: Do NOT leave the mother alone with the infant under any circumstances until she is cleared by a psychiatrist.
Do NOT dismiss bizarre statements as simple "baby blues" or normal sleep deprivation.
Do NOT argue with her delusions.
seek: Requires immediate emergency psychiatric hospitalization. It is highly treatable, but deeply dangerous while active.

title: Substance-Induced Psychosis
warn: ⛔ UNPREDICTABLE VIOLENCE RISK — Hallucinogens or severe stimulant abuse (methamphetamine) causing intense paranoia, extreme physical strength, and agitation.
steps: Ensure your own safety first. Keep a clear path to the door and do not let the patient get between you and the exit.
Call 112 and inform them of suspected drug use so EMS and law enforcement are prepared.
Keep your hands visible, speak softly, and avoid sudden movements.
Reduce all environmental stimulation (turn off music, ask crowds to disperse).
Do not attempt to orient them to reality if they are heavily intoxicated; simply reassure them that they are safe and the feeling will wear off.
donot: Do NOT corner the person or attempt to physically restrain them (stimulant-induced psychosis can grant extreme, dangerous adrenaline strength).
Do NOT argue with their paranoia (e.g., if they think the FBI is outside, do not mock them).
Do NOT shine flashlights in their face.
seek: Requires chemical sedation (e.g., Benzodiazepines/Haloperidol) by EMS or ER staff to calm the brain and protect the heart.

title: Delirium Tremens (Severe Alcohol Withdrawal)
warn: ⛔ FATAL SEIZURE RISK — Occurs 48-72 hours after the last drink in severe alcoholics. The nervous system goes into massive overdrive.
steps: Call 112 immediately. DTs have a high mortality rate without medical intervention.
Recognize the signs: Profuse sweating, severe full-body tremors, racing heart, and terrifying visual/tactile hallucinations (e.g., seeing bugs crawling on the walls or under the skin).
Keep the patient in a well-lit, quiet room (shadows can worsen hallucinations).
Reassure the patient constantly that they are safe and experiencing withdrawal.
Prepare for a sudden seizure (clear the area, protect their head).
donot: Do NOT treat severe alcohol withdrawal at home "cold turkey." It requires medical supervision.
Do NOT restrain the patient if they are reacting to hallucinations.
Do NOT give them a "sip of alcohol" to calm them down once DTs have started; they need IV medication.
seek: Requires ICU admission for heavy IV Benzodiazepine protocols to suppress the nervous system and prevent fatal seizures.

title: Catatonia
warn: ⚠️ TRAPPED IN THE BODY — The person is awake but completely unresponsive, mute, and physically rigid. They are highly aware of their surroundings but physically paralyzed by psychiatric distress.
steps: Speak to the person normally. Explain what you are doing before you do it (e.g., "I am going to check your pulse now"). They can hear and understand you perfectly.
Check for waxy flexibility: If you gently lift their arm, they may leave it exactly in that bizarre, gravity-defying posture.
Ensure they are sitting or lying in a safe, comfortable position to prevent muscle cramps or bedsores.
Call 112 or contact their psychiatric provider.
Monitor their hydration and temperature.
donot: Do NOT talk about them as if they aren't in the room (they will remember everything you say).
Do NOT try to forcefully bend their rigid limbs.
Do NOT assume they are faking or just being stubborn.
seek: Requires ER evaluation to rule out neuroleptic malignant syndrome, followed by specific psychiatric treatment (often Lorazepam or ECT).

title: Acute Homicidal Ideation
warn: ⛔ IMMINENT THREAT TO OTHERS — The patient expresses a clear, specific plan and intent to kill or severely harm another person.
steps: Prioritize your own safety. If the person has a weapon or is actively violent, evacuate the area immediately.
If they are calm but making the threat: Call 112 or local law enforcement immediately.
If you are a medical/mental health professional, initiate "Duty to Warn" protocols to notify the police and the intended victim.
Keep a safe distance, maintain a calm voice, and do not make sudden moves.
Listen to their grievances without validating the violence (e.g., "I hear how incredibly angry you are at them, but I want to keep everyone safe today.").
donot: Do NOT attempt to physically disarm or restrain the person yourself.
Do NOT argue with them about the morality of murder.
Do NOT keep a specific, credible death threat a secret under the guise of "privacy."
seek: Requires immediate police intervention and involuntary psychiatric hold (e.g., 5150) to protect the public and the patient.

title: BPD Emotional Dysregulation Crisis
warn: ⚠️ EMOTIONAL THIRD-DEGREE BURN — The patient is experiencing emotional pain that is so intense it feels physically intolerable, often triggered by perceived abandonment.
steps: Use extreme validation. Acknowledge that their pain is real and overwhelming: "It makes sense that you are hurting this much right now."
Remain a constant, calm presence. Do not walk away or threaten to leave them during the peak of the crisis (this triggers absolute terror).
Encourage TIPP distress tolerance skills: Temperature (hold ice or splash cold water on face), Intense exercise (do 20 jumping jacks), Paced breathing, Paired muscle relaxation.
Assess for self-harm or suicidal intent, which is highly common during these spikes.
Speak in a warm, low, steady voice.
donot: Do NOT tell them they are "overreacting" or being dramatic (their emotional baseline is chemically different).
Do NOT threaten to leave or abandon them to "teach them a lesson."
Do NOT try to logically problem-solve the situation until they are emotionally regulated.
seek: If suicidal or engaging in severe self-harm, seek ER care. Otherwise, bridge to their Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) provider.

title: Psychogenic Non-Epileptic Seizures (PNES)
warn: ⚠️ PSYCHOLOGICAL OVERLOAD — Looks exactly like a grand mal seizure, but is caused by severe psychological stress/trauma, not abnormal brain electricity.
steps: Treat it physically like a real seizure to be safe: ease them to the floor, clear the area of hard objects, and place something soft under their head.
Unlike true epilepsy, the patient’s eyes are often forced tightly shut, and their head may thrash side-to-side (rather than rigid twitching).
Speak calmly and comfortingly to them during the event (they may be semi-aware of their surroundings).
Do not loudly announce "It's just a fake seizure" to bystanders (it is an involuntary, terrifying conversion of trauma, not "faking").
Call 112 if it is their first seizure or if it lasts longer than 5 minutes.
donot: Do NOT hold them down or try to stop the movements.
Do NOT put anything in their mouth.
Do NOT perform sternal rubs or inflict pain to "test" if it is real.
seek: Requires neurological evaluation to officially rule out epilepsy, followed by trauma-focused psychotherapy (CBT/EMDR).

title: Severe Depressive Stupor (Gravely Disabled)
warn: ⛔ IMMINENT NEGLECT RISK — The depression is so severe the patient has lost the physical will or ability to eat, drink, or use the restroom for days.
steps: Assess their physical state: Are they severely dehydrated? Have they not eaten in days? Are there bedsores or hygiene hazards?
Bring small, easy-to-consume calories directly to them (e.g., a protein shake with a straw, a glass of water).
Use gentle, directive statements rather than questions (e.g., "Here is some water, please take a sip" rather than "Do you want water?").
If they absolutely refuse to eat, drink, or move, call 112 or a mobile crisis team.
Treat them with profound gentleness; they are crushed under psychological weight.
donot: Do NOT tell them to "snap out of it" or "just go outside for a walk."
Do NOT try to aggressively cheer them up or minimize their despair.
Do NOT leave them in a state of severe dehydration assuming they will eat when hungry (the survival instinct is suppressed).
seek: Requires hospitalization for IV fluids, nutrition, and urgent psychiatric intervention (often ECT or rapid-acting antidepressants).

title: Acute Anorexia Nervosa Crisis
warn: ⛔ CARDIAC COLLAPSE RISK — Severe malnutrition leads to dangerous electrolyte imbalances, causing the heart muscle to waste away and beat dangerously slow.
steps: Assess for immediate medical danger: fainting upon standing, extreme cold intolerance, blue fingernails, or a highly irregular/slow pulse.
Call 112 immediately if the patient loses consciousness, complains of chest pain, or has a heart rate under 40 bpm.
Keep the patient sitting or lying down to reduce strain on the heart.
Avoid commenting on their body, weight, or the physical evidence of their disease.
Maintain a calm, compassionate demeanor.
donot: Do NOT try to force them to eat a massive meal right now (this can trigger Refeeding Syndrome, a fatal shift in electrolytes).
Do NOT argue with the "Eating Disorder Voice" (e.g., if they say they are fat, do not engage in a debate about their weight).
Do NOT praise them for looking "so thin."
seek: Requires immediate medical stabilization in a hospital, followed by highly specialized inpatient eating disorder treatment.

title: Dissociative Fugue / Severe Amnesia
warn: ⚠️ COMPLETE IDENTITY LOSS — A rare psychological reaction to extreme trauma where the person forgets who they are and wanders far from home.
steps: Approach the person calmly. They are likely highly confused but may seem outwardly normal until questioned.
Ask basic orientation questions gently: "Can you tell me your name? Do you know what city we are in?"
If they do not know who they are, call 112 or local law enforcement.
Keep them in a safe, contained, and warm environment while waiting for authorities.
Reassure them: "It’s okay that you don't remember right now. We are going to help you stay safe."
donot: Do NOT interrogate them aggressively or act suspicious of them.
Do NOT let them continue wandering off.
Do NOT overwhelm them with loud noises or large crowds.
seek: Requires medical evaluation to rule out a brain injury, stroke, or tumor, followed by psychiatric care to uncover the trauma.

title: Acute Paranoia / Persecutory Delusions
warn: ⚠️ INTENSE TERROR — The person genuinely believes they are being hunted, poisoned, or monitored by malevolent forces.
steps: Be totally transparent. Explain exactly what you are doing before you do it (e.g., "I am going to reach into my pocket to get my phone").
Keep your hands visible and empty.
Do not whisper to others in the room or pass notes (this massively escalates paranoia).
Offer pre-packaged, sealed food or water if they need it (they may believe open food is poisoned).
Focus on their underlying emotion: "It sounds terrifying to feel like people are watching you. You are safe in this room with me."
donot: Do NOT laugh at their conspiracies or call them crazy.
Do NOT try to prove them wrong with logic (e.g., pointing out there are no cameras).
Do NOT block their exit or trap them in a small room.
seek: Requires psychiatric evaluation. If they become aggressive out of "self-defense," involve a mobile crisis unit.

title: Intermittent Explosive Episode (Acute Rage)
warn: ⚠️ BLIND RAGE — A sudden, disproportionate outburst of violent rage, throwing objects, screaming, and physical aggression, followed by deep remorse.
steps: Ensure scene safety immediately. Move children, vulnerable people, and hazardous objects out of the room.
Give the person massive amounts of physical space.
Have ONLY ONE person speak to them (multiple voices escalate the confusion and anger).
Use a calm, monotone, low-volume voice.
Give simple, clear directives: "I need you to step back. Put the chair down. We are going to talk, but you need to sit down first."
donot: Do NOT yell back or try to assert dominance.
Do NOT order them to "calm down" (this usually incites further rage).
Do NOT stand directly in front of them face-to-face (stand at a slight angle to appear less confrontational).
seek: If they cannot de-escalate and begin harming people or property, call law enforcement/EMS. Follow up with anger management/psychotherapy.

title: Acute Agoraphobia Crisis
warn: ⚠️ PARALYZING FEAR OF ENVIRONMENT — The person is trapped in an environment (a crowd, public transport, or outside their home) and is completely paralyzed by panic.
steps: Acknowledge their terror. They feel entirely unsafe in the current environment.
Offer to be their "shield" or "anchor." Ask if you can link arms or walk closely beside them to help them navigate out of the triggering space.
Create a small bubble of calm. Stand slightly in front of them to block their view of a massive crowd.
Give them a single, small focus point (e.g., "Just look at the back of my jacket. Follow my jacket to the exit.").
Move them to a quiet, enclosed space (like a restroom or an empty hallway) to regroup.
donot: Do NOT force them to "face their fears" by abandoning them in the crowd (flooding is a dangerous tactic during a crisis).
Do NOT physically drag them.
Do NOT draw unnecessary attention to them from bystanders.
seek: Requires long-term exposure therapy and Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). Emergency transport is rarely needed unless physical symptoms mimic a heart attack.

title: Acute Traumatic Grief / Shock
warn: ⚠️ PSYCHOLOGICAL SHOCK — The immediate aftermath of receiving catastrophic news (e.g., sudden death of a child or spouse). The brain cannot process the reality.
steps: Provide a safe, private, and quiet environment immediately.
Anticipate profound physical reactions: vomiting, fainting, screaming, wailing, or absolute silent catatonia.
Stay with them. Do not leave them alone. Be a silent, grounding presence.
Ensure they do not injure themselves if they thrash or collapse.
Offer basic physical comforts (a blanket, a glass of water, tissues) without demanding they use them.
Help them contact a trusted family member or friend to come be with them.
donot: Do NOT offer platitudes like "They are in a better place," "Everything happens for a reason," or "I know how you feel." (These are deeply unhelpful).
Do NOT tell them to be strong or stop crying.
Do NOT force them to make complex decisions immediately.
seek: Requires immediate psychological first aid and support from family/community. Medication (short-term sedatives) may be prescribed by a doctor if they become a danger to themselves.

title: Avulsed Tooth (Knocked-Out Adult Tooth)
warn: ⛔ TIME SENSITIVE — You have a 30 to 60-minute window to save the tooth. The root cells die rapidly if dry.
steps: Find the tooth immediately.
Pick the tooth up ONLY by the chewing surface (the crown). NEVER touch the root (the pointy part), as this kills the cells needed for reattachment.
If the tooth is dirty, rinse it for no more than 10 seconds in cold milk or sterile saline. Do NOT scrub it.
Attempt to gently push the tooth back into its socket in the gums immediately. Have the patient bite down softly on a gauze pad to hold it in place.
If you cannot put it back in the socket, place the tooth in a small container of cold MILK, or have the patient hold it inside their cheek (if they are old enough not to swallow it).
Go to a dentist or ER immediately.
donot: Do NOT put the tooth in plain water (water swells and bursts the root cells).
Do NOT scrub the tooth or wipe it off with a shirt/tissue.
Do NOT try to re-implant a baby tooth (primary tooth) in a young child, as it can damage the adult tooth growing underneath.
seek: Requires an emergency dentist to splint the tooth to the adjacent teeth within the hour.

title: Acute Dental Abscess
warn: ⚠️ SEVERE INFECTION — A pocket of pus at the root of the tooth. Can spread to the jawbone, neck, or brain if ignored.
steps: Look for a pimple-like bump on the gums, severe throbbing pain, facial swelling, or a foul taste in the mouth.
Have the patient rinse their mouth with mild, warm saltwater (1/2 teaspoon salt in 8oz water) to help draw the pus to the surface.
Apply a cold compress to the OUTSIDE of the cheek to reduce swelling.
Take over-the-counter pain medication like Ibuprofen if there are no contraindications.
Call a dentist immediately for an emergency appointment.
donot: Do NOT attempt to pop the abscess with a needle or pin at home.
Do NOT put aspirin directly on the gums (it will cause a severe chemical burn).
Do NOT apply a warm compress to the outside of the face (heat draws the infection outward into the facial tissues).
seek: Requires professional drainage by a dentist and prescription antibiotics. If swelling reaches the eye or under the jaw, go to the ER.

title: Severe Pulpitis (Unrelenting Toothache)
warn: ⚠️ NERVE INFLAMMATION — The nerve inside the tooth is dying or severely inflamed, causing agonizing, continuous pain that prevents sleep.
steps: Floss gently around the painful tooth to ensure no food particles are wedged and causing gum pressure.
Rinse the mouth thoroughly with warm water.
Take an over-the-counter anti-inflammatory (like Ibuprofen) to reduce nerve swelling, rather than just Acetaminophen.
Keep the head elevated when lying down to reduce blood pressure in the head and tooth.
Avoid extremely hot, cold, or sweet foods.
donot: Do NOT ignore the pain if it suddenly stops completely (this often means the nerve has entirely died, and a massive abscess is about to form).
Do NOT place painkillers directly against the tooth.
Do NOT use topical numbing gels (like Orajel) excessively, as they can cause rare but dangerous blood oxygen issues (methemoglobinemia) in large amounts.
seek: Requires a dentist to perform a root canal or extraction to remove the dying nerve.

title: Post-Extraction Hemorrhage
warn: ⚠️ UNCONTROLLED BLEEDING — The blood clot fails to form or is dislodged after a tooth is pulled, leading to continuous bleeding.
steps: Fold a clean piece of gauze into a thick square, place it directly over the bleeding socket, and have the patient bite down with FIRM, continuous pressure for 45 minutes.
If bleeding persists after 45 minutes, replace the gauze with a moistened ordinary black tea bag. (The tannic acid in black tea helps constrict blood vessels and form a clot).
Bite firmly on the tea bag for another 30-45 minutes.
Have the patient sit upright and avoid physical exertion.
donot: Do NOT rinse the mouth, spit forcefully, or use a straw (the suction will rip the new clot right out).
Do NOT lie flat.
Do NOT smoke, as the suction and chemicals prevent clotting.
seek: If heavy, bright red bleeding continues after using a tea bag, contact the oral surgeon or go to the ER.

title: Alveolar Osteitis (Dry Socket)
warn: ⚠️ EXPOSED BONE — The blood clot falls out of an extraction site prematurely (usually 3-5 days after extraction), exposing the jawbone and nerves to air.
steps: Recognize the signs: Severe, dull, throbbing pain radiating to the ear or eye that starts several days AFTER a tooth extraction.
Look into the socket: It will look empty, dry, and white (bone) rather than having a dark red clot.
Rinse gently with warm saltwater to clear any food debris out of the open hole.
Take over-the-counter pain medications.
Call the dentist or oral surgeon who performed the extraction.
donot: Do NOT poke around in the socket with a toothpick or finger.
Do NOT aggressively swish mouthwash.
Do NOT smoke (smoking is the #1 cause of dry socket).
seek: The dentist will pack the socket with a medicated, soothing paste (often containing clove oil/eugenol) that provides almost instant pain relief.

title: Fractured Tooth with Pulp Exposure
warn: ⚠️ NERVE EXPOSURE — The tooth is broken so deeply that the pink/red nerve center (pulp) is visible and bleeding. Extremely painful and prone to instant infection.
steps: If the piece of the tooth that broke off is intact, save it in a container of milk or saline (the dentist can sometimes re-bond it).
Rinse the mouth gently with warm water to clean the area.
If the nerve is exposed and bleeding, have the patient bite gently on a clean piece of moist gauze.
Apply a cold compress to the outside of the face to manage swelling from the trauma.
Avoid breathing cold air through the mouth, which will cause agonizing pain.
donot: Do NOT apply topical pain gels directly to an exposed nerve.
Do NOT chew on that side of the mouth.
Do NOT brush the broken surface of the tooth.
seek: Requires immediate emergency dental care for a root canal and crown to save the remainder of the tooth.

title: Luxated Tooth (Extruded or Intruded)
warn: ⚠️ DISPLACED TOOTH — Trauma has pushed the tooth deeper into the gums (intruded), pulled it partially out (extruded), or pushed it sideways.
steps: Apply a cold compress to the outside of the cheek/lips to reduce trauma swelling.
If the tooth is pushed out or sideways, you may attempt to use VERY light finger pressure to reposition it back to its normal alignment, but ONLY if it moves easily.
Have the patient bite down very softly on a gauze pad to hold it in place.
If it is pushed deep into the gum (intruded), do NOT try to pull it out.
Go to a dentist immediately.
donot: Do NOT force the tooth if it will not move easily.
Do NOT let the patient wiggle the tooth with their tongue or fingers.
Do NOT try to pull an intruded baby tooth back out (it can damage the adult tooth bud above it).
seek: A dentist must evaluate the surrounding bone for fractures and splint the tooth in its correct position while it heals.

title: Pericoronitis (Infected Wisdom Tooth)
warn: ⚠️ TRAPPED BACTERIA — The gum flap over a partially erupted wisdom tooth becomes severely infected, causing extreme pain and difficulty opening the mouth.
steps: Look for severe swelling, redness, and pus in the very back of the mouth where the wisdom tooth is coming in.
Have the patient rinse vigorously with warm saltwater to try to flush debris out from under the gum flap.
If the patient has a curved plastic syringe (monojet), fill it with warm water and gently flush UNDER the gum flap.
If they cannot open their mouth more than a few fingers wide (trismus), the infection is spreading to the chewing muscles.
Call a dentist immediately.
donot: Do NOT apply a heating pad to the outside of the jaw.
Do NOT try to cut or lift the gum flap yourself.
Do NOT ignore it if swallowing becomes difficult.
seek: Requires professional flushing, antibiotics, and usually the extraction of the offending wisdom tooth once the infection cools down.

title: TMJ Dislocation (Locked Jaw)
warn: ⚠️ JOINT OUT OF SOCKET — The lower jaw has popped too far forward (often from a wide yawn) and cannot close. The patient will be stuck with their mouth wide open.
steps: Keep the patient calm. Panic makes the jaw muscles spasm tighter, making it harder to fix.
Apply warm compresses to the jaw muscles (cheeks) to help them relax.
Support the lower jaw gently, but do not force it shut.
Have the patient try to relax their jaw completely and gently slide the jaw backward, not just upward.
If it will not reduce (pop back), go to the ER or an oral surgeon.
donot: Do NOT try to forcefully push the chin upward to close the mouth (this pushes the bone into the wrong part of the skull).
Do NOT stick your fingers into their mouth without wrapping your thumbs in thick gauze (when the jaw pops back, it snaps shut violently and can bite your fingers).
Do NOT let them attempt wide yawning immediately after it is fixed.
seek: A doctor will perform a specific manual reduction, pushing DOWN on the back molars and back on the chin to slip the joint back into place.

title: Mandibular (Jaw) Fracture
warn: ⛔ BONE BREAK & AIRWAY RISK — A broken jaw changes the bite and can cause the tongue to block the airway if the bone collapses backward.
steps: Call 112 or go to the ER immediately following severe facial trauma.
Ask the patient to bite down gently. If they report their teeth "don't fit together right anymore" (malocclusion), the jaw is almost certainly broken.
Look for bleeding from around the teeth, a numb lower lip/chin, or a visible step/deformity in the gums.
If the patient is having trouble breathing, have them lean completely forward to keep blood and the tongue out of the throat.
Manually support the lower jaw with your hands to keep it still.
donot: Do NOT lay the patient flat on their back if they are bleeding from the mouth.
Do NOT wrap a bandage tightly around the head and jaw (if they vomit, they will choke to death).
Do NOT let them try to talk or chew.
seek: Requires emergency maxillofacial surgery, often involving wiring the jaw shut or inserting titanium plates.

title: Deep Soft Tissue Laceration (Tongue/Lip)
warn: ⚠️ HEAVY BLEEDING — The mouth has a massive blood supply, so even small cuts on the tongue or lips will bleed profusely and look terrifying.
steps: Clean the area gently with a mild saltwater rinse.
Use a clean piece of gauze or a wet tea bag to apply firm, direct pressure to the bleeding area for 15-20 minutes.
Apply a cold compress or ice cube wrapped in cloth to the OUTSIDE of the lip/cheek to reduce swelling.
If it is a tongue laceration, pinch the tongue with the gauze to apply pressure to both sides of the cut.
If bleeding does not stop after 20 minutes of continuous pressure, go to the ER.
donot: Do NOT pull the gauze away every 2 minutes to check if it has stopped bleeding.
Do NOT swallow large amounts of blood (have the patient lean forward and spit it out to prevent vomiting).
Do NOT put unprescribed ointments inside the mouth.
seek: Deep cuts that gap open, cross the border of the lip (vermilion border), or do not stop bleeding require stitches.

title: Chemical Burn on Gums (e.g., Aspirin Burn)
warn: ⚠️ TISSUE NECROSIS — Placing an aspirin directly against a painful tooth causes the acidic pill to severely burn and kill the gum tissue, turning it stark white.
steps: Immediately remove the pill or chemical from the mouth.
Rinse the mouth thoroughly with copious amounts of water or a mild saltwater solution to wash away the acid.
The white, dead tissue will eventually slough off, leaving a raw, painful ulcer.
Treat the resulting ulcer with over-the-counter topical numbing gels (like Orajel) applied directly to the sore.
Take pain relievers ORALLY (swallow them) for the underlying toothache.
donot: Do NOT ever place aspirin or any other pill directly against the gums.
Do NOT peel the white, dead skin off forcefully.
Do NOT eat acidic or spicy foods while the burn heals.
seek: The burn will heal over 1-2 weeks, but the patient still needs to see a dentist for the original toothache that caused them to attempt the home remedy.

title: Orthodontic Wire Puncture
warn: ⚠️ SOFT TISSUE IRRITATION — A broken or shifted braces wire stabs deeply into the cheek or gums, causing severe ulcers.
steps: Locate the end of the poking wire.
Use a cotton swab or the eraser end of a pencil to gently try and push the wire flat against the tooth.
If it won't move, dry the wire and the tooth completely with a tissue, and cover the sharp end with orthodontic wax.
If you do not have wax, a small piece of sugarless chewing gum can be used temporarily.
If the wire has pierced completely through the cheek, leave it and go to the orthodontist.
donot: Do NOT attempt to cut the wire yourself unless absolutely necessary (if you must, use clean nail clippers, but hold the cut end so it is not swallowed).
Do NOT try to pull the wire out of the brackets.
Do NOT use sticky candies instead of wax.
seek: See the orthodontist as soon as possible to have the wire clipped or replaced.

title: Primary Tooth Intrusion (Toddler Tooth Pushed In)
warn: ⚠️ ADULT TOOTH RISK — A toddler falls on their face and the baby front tooth is shoved completely up into the gums, disappearing from sight.
steps: Keep the child calm and apply a cold compress to the swollen lip/gum.
Check the mouth carefully. The tooth may be pushed entirely into the gum socket, or it may have been knocked out and swallowed/inhaled.
Have the child bite gently on a clean, wet washcloth to control bleeding.
Call a pediatric dentist immediately.
Watch for signs of breathing difficulty, which indicates the tooth may have been aspirated into the lungs.
donot: Do NOT try to grab the tooth with tweezers or pull it back down.
Do NOT panic if you cannot see the tooth; it is often safely hidden inside the gum.
Do NOT let the child chew on hard toys or pacifiers.
seek: An X-ray is required to ensure the baby tooth was not pushed into the developing adult tooth bud. Most intruded baby teeth will re-erupt on their own over several months.

title: Foreign Object Wedged in Gums
warn: ⚠️ GUM ABSCESS RISK — Something (often a popcorn kernel or fingernail) gets wedged deep under the gumline, causing massive inflammation and localized bone loss.
steps: Attempt to gently remove the object using dental floss. Tie a small knot in the floss and pull it through the space to try and snag the object.
Use a water flosser (Waterpik) on a low setting to try and flush it out.
Rinse vigorously with warm saltwater.
If it causes severe, throbbing pain and swelling, an abscess is forming around the object.
donot: Do NOT dig aggressively under the gums with a metal pin, needle, or sharp toothpick.
Do NOT ignore it if it hurts to chew on that side.
Do NOT leave it in; the body will attack it, destroying the surrounding jawbone in the process.
seek: A dentist can easily numb the area and use specialized instruments to flush and remove the object in minutes.

title: Cracked Tooth Syndrome
warn: ⚠️ MICRO-FRACTURE — A microscopic crack runs through the tooth. The classic symptom is a sharp, shocking pain specifically when RELEASING a bite.
steps: Identify the trigger: The pain usually happens when chewing something hard or chewy (like a bagel or nuts).
Avoid chewing on that side of the mouth entirely.
Avoid extremely hot or cold foods, as the crack exposes the nerve to temperature changes.
Take over-the-counter pain relievers if the tooth aches constantly.
Call a dentist to schedule an evaluation.
donot: Do NOT continue "testing" the tooth by biting hard things to see if it still hurts.
Do NOT wait until the tooth splits completely in half (at which point it must be extracted).
Do NOT use temporary filling material from the drugstore; it won't fix a structural crack.
seek: Requires a dental crown to hold the cracked pieces together. If the crack has reached the nerve, a root canal will also be needed.

title: Lost Crown or Large Filling
warn: ⚠️ TOOTH VULNERABILITY — The underlying tooth is now exposed to bacteria and temperature, and is structurally very weak.
steps: Find the crown or filling if possible. Save a crown in a safe place, as the dentist can often recement it.
If the tooth is extremely sensitive, you can apply a small amount of over-the-counter dental cement or orthodontic wax over the exposed tooth.
If you have the crown, you can clean it and temporarily stick it back on using a tiny dab of toothpaste or denture adhesive. (This is only for aesthetics/comfort).
Keep the area clean by brushing very gently.
Call your dentist for an appointment.
donot: Do NOT use superglue or any household glues to put the crown back on (it is toxic and will destroy the tooth).
Do NOT chew sticky or hard foods on that side.
Do NOT swallow the crown if you sleep with it temporarily re-attached (take it out at night).
seek: A dentist needs to clean the tooth and use permanent dental cement to re-attach the crown.

title: Odontogenic Sinusitis (Tooth Root in Sinus)
warn: ⚠️ SINUS PERFORATION — The roots of the upper back teeth extend into the sinus cavity. A dental infection can burst into the sinus, or an extraction can leave a permanent hole.
steps: Watch for symptoms: Severe pain in the upper back teeth that gets worse when bending over or walking down stairs.
Check for foul-tasting, yellowish discharge coming from one nostril, or a chronic bad smell in the nose.
If this occurs immediately after having an upper tooth pulled, the patient may notice air or liquids passing from their mouth into their nose.
Instruct the patient not to blow their nose, use a straw, or sneeze with their mouth closed (this blows the hole wider).
Go to a dentist or ENT.
donot: Do NOT blow the nose forcefully.
Do NOT ignore a one-sided sinus infection that doesn't respond to normal cold medicine.
Do NOT smoke or vape.
seek: Requires specific antibiotics and often surgical closure of the hole (fistula) by an oral surgeon.

title: Broken Denture Causing Tissue Laceration
warn: ⚠️ CHRONIC ULCERATION — Wearing a cracked or sharply broken denture will quickly slice through the gum tissue, causing massive ulcers.
steps: Remove the broken denture from the mouth immediately and do not wear it.
Rinse the mouth with warm saltwater to clean the cuts/ulcers.
Use an over-the-counter oral numbing gel on the sore gums.
Gather all pieces of the broken denture to bring to the dentist.
Switch to a soft-food diet until the appliance is fixed.
donot: Do NOT attempt to glue the denture back together with Superglue or Gorilla Glue (these glues are toxic and ruin the acrylic, making it impossible for the lab to fix).
Do NOT continue wearing the broken denture "just to eat."
Do NOT try to file down the sharp edges with a nail file.
seek: Take the appliance to a dentist. They can send it to a lab for a professional, seamless acrylic repair.

title: Retained Root Tip Infection
warn: ⚠️ BURIED INFECTION — A piece of a tooth root breaks off during an extraction and is left in the bone, becoming infected months or years later.
steps: Recognize the signs: A small, painful bump or chronic bad taste in an area where a tooth was pulled a long time ago.
Sometimes small, sharp bone fragments (bone spicules) work their way out naturally, but a true root tip will cause a throbbing abscess.
Rinse with warm saltwater.
Take over-the-counter pain relievers.
Make an appointment with an oral surgeon.
donot: Do NOT try to dig the root tip out with tweezers.
Do NOT ignore chronic swelling in an edentulous (toothless) area.
Do NOT wear a denture over the swollen area.
seek: Requires an X-ray to locate the fragment and a minor surgical procedure to retrieve the infected root tip.

title: Sepsis / Septic Shock
warn: ⛔ SYSTEMIC SHOCK — The body's extreme response to an infection damages its own tissues and organs. Every hour delays increases mortality by 8%.
steps: Watch for the TIME criteria: Temperature (higher or lower than normal), Infection (signs of a procedure/wound), Mental decline (confused/sleepy), Extremely ill ("I feel like I might die").
Call 112 immediately if the patient has an infection and suddenly becomes confused, has a racing heart, or is breathing rapidly.
Lay the patient flat and elevate their legs to keep blood flowing to the core organs.
Keep the patient warm if they are shivering.
Have their medical history and recent infection history ready for EMS.
donot: Do NOT assume it is just the flu if they have extreme weakness or confusion.
Do NOT wait to see if oral antibiotics kick in if they are showing signs of shock.
Do NOT let the patient stand up (blood pressure may be dangerously low).
seek: Requires immediate ICU admission for massive IV fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.

title: Bacterial Meningitis
warn: ⛔ RAPIDLY LETHAL — Inflammation of the brain and spinal cord linings. Can cause death or permanent brain damage within 24 hours.
steps: Call 112 immediately if a high fever is paired with a stiff neck (unable to touch chin to chest) and a severe headache.
Look for a dark purple/red pinpoint rash. Perform the "Glass Test": Press a clear drinking glass firmly against the rash. If it does not fade under pressure, it is a critical emergency.
Keep the patient in a dark, quiet room (they will likely be very sensitive to light).
Isolate the patient and wear a mask; it is highly contagious via respiratory droplets.
donot: Do NOT give ibuprofen/acetaminophen and wait for the fever to break if the neck is stiff.
Do NOT share drinks, utensils, or get close to the patient's face without a mask.
Do NOT delay EMS transport.
seek: Requires an emergency lumbar puncture (spinal tap) and immediate, aggressive IV antibiotics.

title: Rabies Exposure
warn: ⛔ 100% FATAL IF UNTREATED — Once neurological symptoms of rabies appear, the disease is universally fatal. Prevention immediately after exposure is the only cure.
steps: WASH THE WOUND IMMEDIATELY and aggressively with soap and running water for at least 15 uninterrupted minutes (this physically washes away the virus).
Apply a virucidal antiseptic like povidone-iodine if available.
If the bite was from a wild animal (especially a bat, raccoon, skunk, or stray dog), go to the ER immediately.
Note: If you wake up and find a bat in your bedroom, assume you were bitten and go to the ER (bat bites are tiny and painless).
Call animal control to safely capture the animal for testing if possible.
donot: Do NOT stitch or glue the wound closed unless absolutely medically necessary for massive bleeding (leaving it open reduces rabies risk).
Do NOT wait to see if the animal acts "rabid".
Do NOT delay going to the ER.
seek: Requires a series of Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) vaccines and Rabies Immune Globulin injected directly around the wound.

title: Tetanus (Lockjaw)
warn: ⚠️ SEVERE NEUROTOXIN — Bacteria from soil/dust enter a wound and produce a toxin that causes agonizing, uncontrollable muscle spasms and bone fractures.
steps: PREVENTION: Clean all puncture wounds, cuts, or animal bites thoroughly with soap and water immediately.
If the patient experiences stiffness in the jaw (inability to open the mouth), neck stiffness, or difficulty swallowing days/weeks after a cut, call 112.
Keep the patient in a dark, completely quiet room (even sudden loud noises or bright lights can trigger violent, whole-body muscle spasms).
Monitor airway and breathing constantly.
donot: Do NOT ignore deep puncture wounds, especially from objects outdoors or in dirt.
Do NOT stimulate the patient unnecessarily if they are spasming.
Do NOT attempt to force their mouth open.
seek: Requires ICU care, Tetanus Immune Globulin (TIG), muscle relaxants, and often mechanical ventilation until the toxin wears off.

title: Severe Malaria (Cerebral Malaria)
warn: ⛔ PARASITIC EMERGENCY — Red blood cells become infected and sticky, blocking blood vessels in the brain and other organs.
steps: Suspect in anyone with a high, cyclical fever who has traveled to a malaria-endemic region in the past year.
Watch for critical signs: extreme confusion, seizures, extreme lethargy, dark urine, or difficulty breathing.
Go to the Emergency Room immediately; inform triage immediately of the patient's travel history.
If the patient has a seizure, place them in the recovery position and protect their head.
donot: Do NOT assume it is just a traveler's stomach bug or the flu.
Do NOT delay treatment waiting for a doctor's appointment; severe malaria can kill within 24 hours of symptom onset.
Do NOT let the patient become severely dehydrated.
seek: Requires immediate IV antimalarial drugs (like Artesunate) and blood transfusions if anemia is severe.

title: Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever
warn: ⛔ VASCULAR LEAKAGE — A severe complication of Dengue where blood vessels leak plasma and blood fails to clot, leading to rapid shock.
steps: Recognize the danger phase: Often occurs 3-7 days after symptoms start, right as the fever begins to drop.
Watch for warning signs: severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums/nose, vomiting blood, or extreme fatigue/restlessness.
Call 112 or go to the ER immediately if these signs appear.
Keep the patient laying down and strictly resting.
Provide oral rehydration salts (ORS) if they are awake and can swallow, to replace leaked fluids.
donot: Do NOT give Aspirin, Ibuprofen, or Naproxen (these worsen bleeding risk; use Acetaminophen for fever/pain).
Do NOT assume the patient is getting better just because the fever went away (this is when the hemorrhagic phase starts).
Do NOT allow physical exertion.
seek: Requires emergency hospitalization for careful IV fluid replacement and blood pressure monitoring.

title: Cholera
warn: ⚠️ MASSIVE FLUID LOSS — An intestinal infection causing such profuse, watery diarrhea that a person can die from dehydration in mere hours.
steps: Recognize the classic sign: Painless, profuse "rice-water" diarrhea (looks like cloudy water) and vomiting.
HYDRATE IMMEDIATELY: Provide Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) continuously. The patient must drink as much as they are losing.
If ORS is unavailable, mix 1 liter of clean water with 6 level teaspoons of sugar and 1/2 level teaspoon of salt.
Seek medical care urgently, especially if the patient stops urinating, has sunken eyes, or cannot keep fluids down.
Wash your hands aggressively to prevent spreading the bacteria.
donot: Do NOT give anti-diarrheal medications (like Imodium); the bacteria must be flushed out of the system.
Do NOT use contaminated water to mix the rehydration salts.
Do NOT wait to see if it stops on its own.
seek: Requires massive fluid replacement (often via IV in severe cases) and antibiotics to shorten the duration of the illness.

title: Viral Hemorrhagic Fever (Ebola/Marburg/Lassa)
warn: ⛔ EXTREME BIOHAZARD — Highly lethal viruses causing systemic hemorrhage and multi-organ failure. Contact with bodily fluids is strictly prohibited.
steps: Suspect if high fever, severe weakness, and unexplained bleeding (from eyes, gums, IV sites) occur after travel to an outbreak region.
ISOLATE THE PATIENT IMMEDIATELY in a separate room. Close the door.
Do NOT touch the patient or any of their bodily fluids, clothing, or bedding without full-body Hazmat/PPE gear.
Call 112 immediately. Inform the dispatcher of the travel history and suspected hemorrhagic fever so EMS can arrive in bio-containment gear.
Keep a log of anyone who came into contact with the patient.
donot: Do NOT perform CPR or mouth-to-mouth if the patient stops breathing (you will contract the virus).
Do NOT clean up vomit, blood, or diarrhea without specialized biohazard protocols.
Do NOT bring the patient to a crowded ER waiting room without calling ahead.
seek: Requires transport to a specialized biocontainment hospital unit for isolation, fluid support, and experimental antivirals.

title: Inhalation Anthrax
warn: ⛔ LETHAL TOXIN — Inhaled spores multiply in the lungs and lymph nodes, releasing deadly toxins that cause massive internal bleeding and shock.
steps: Suspect in cases of suspected bioterrorism or occupational exposure (handling animal hides/wool) followed by severe flu-like symptoms that rapidly progress to severe shortness of breath.
Call 112 immediately. The disease progresses from a mild cough to severe respiratory collapse in 24-48 hours.
Keep the patient sitting upright to ease breathing.
Administer oxygen if available.
Decontaminate: If a white powder exposure just occurred, remove the patient's clothing, place it in a plastic bag, and wash the patient with soap and water.
donot: Do NOT assume it is a standard cold if symptoms rapidly worsen into extreme breathing difficulty and shock.
Do NOT shake out clothing covered in suspicious powders (this aerosolizes the spores).
Do NOT delay seeking antibiotics.
