seek: Requires immediate emergency care for IV antibiotics (Ciprofloxacin/Doxycycline), Anthrax Antitoxin, and mechanical ventilation.

title: Botulism
warn: ⛔ DESCENDING PARALYSIS — A neurotoxin (often from improperly canned food) that paralyzes the body from the head down, eventually stopping the lungs.
steps: Look for the classic early signs: Double vision, blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, and difficulty swallowing.
Watch for the progression: Weakness moves down to the shoulders, arms, and finally the chest and legs.
Call 112 immediately. This is a life-threatening emergency.
Keep the patient sitting upright if they are struggling to swallow, to prevent choking on saliva.
Monitor breathing constantly. Be prepared to perform CPR with rescue breaths if the diaphragm paralyzes.
donot: Do NOT let the patient eat or drink anything (they will aspirate/choke).
Do NOT wait to see if the symptoms pass.
Do NOT throw away the suspected food source (health departments need it for testing).
seek: Requires immediate administration of Botulinum Antitoxin and often mechanical ventilation in the ICU for weeks/months.

title: Pneumonic Plague
warn: ⛔ EXTREMELY CONTAGIOUS & FATAL — The lung-based version of the plague. It spreads person-to-person through the air and can kill within 24 hours of symptom onset.
steps: Suspect if a patient develops sudden high fever, severe weakness, and a rapidly worsening pneumonia with watery, bloody sputum (coughing up blood).
ISOLATE THE PATIENT immediately. Wear a tight-fitting mask (N95) and gloves.
Call 112 immediately and inform them of the severe bloody pneumonia so EMS wears protective gear.
Keep the patient resting and upright to help with breathing.
Anyone who has been in close contact with the patient must be evaluated for prophylactic antibiotics.
donot: Do NOT stay in the same room without an N95 mask.
Do NOT assume coughing up watery blood is just a severe chest cold.
Do NOT delay treatment; antibiotics must be given within 24 hours of first symptoms to prevent death.
seek: Requires isolation in a hospital and immediate IV antibiotics (Streptomycin or Gentamicin).

title: Diphtheria
warn: ⛔ AIRWAY OBSTRUCTION — Bacteria produce a toxin that creates a thick, leathery, gray pseudomembrane over the throat and tonsils, physically choking the patient.
steps: Look inside the mouth: If you see a thick, tough, gray coating over the back of the throat and tonsils, accompanied by severe swelling of the neck ("bull neck"), it is a medical emergency.
Call 112 immediately.
Keep the patient as calm as possible to reduce oxygen demand.
Keep them sitting upright.
Prepare for an emergency loss of airway.
donot: Do NOT try to scrape or peel the gray membrane off (it will bleed profusely, release more toxin into the bloodstream, and swell the airway further).
Do NOT force the patient to lie flat.
Do NOT delay EMS; the airway can close entirely at any moment.
seek: Requires immediate Diphtheria Antitoxin (DAT), antibiotics, and often a surgical airway (tracheostomy) if the membrane blocks the throat.

title: Severe Influenza (ARDS complication)
warn: ⚠️ VIRAL PNEUMONIA — The flu virus attacks the lungs so severely that they fill with fluid, stopping oxygen from reaching the blood.
steps: Watch for warning signs in a flu patient: Sudden worsening of shortness of breath, inability to speak in full sentences, or chest pain with every breath.
Check skin color: If the lips, nail beds, or face turn blue or gray, oxygen levels are critically low.
Call 112 or go to the ER immediately.
Keep the patient seated upright.
If they have prescribed inhalers for asthma/COPD, assist them in using them.
donot: Do NOT assume that because it is "just the flu" it cannot be fatal.
Do NOT give Aspirin to children or teenagers with the flu (risk of Reye's Syndrome).
Do NOT lay the patient flat if they are struggling to breathe.
seek: Requires hospitalization for oxygen therapy, IV antiviral medications, and potentially mechanical ventilation.

title: Severe COVID-19 (Silent Hypoxia)
warn: ⛔ SILENT HYPOXIA — Blood oxygen drops to dangerously low levels without the patient feeling typically "breathless" until they suddenly collapse.
steps: Monitor oxygen levels with a home pulse oximeter if available. If oxygen consistently reads below 90%, go to the ER.
Watch for sudden confusion, inability to wake up, blueish lips/face, or severe pressure in the chest.
Call 112 immediately if these emergency warning signs appear.
Have the patient rest on their STOMACH (proning) if they are awake and struggling to breathe, as this opens up the back of the lungs.
Keep the patient isolated.
donot: Do NOT trust that the patient is "fine" just because they are talking; rely on the pulse oximeter or objective signs like blue lips.
Do NOT let them exert themselves (even walking to the bathroom can cause oxygen to plummet).
Do NOT ignore sudden leg pain or unilateral swelling (high risk of blood clots/DVT).
seek: Requires ER evaluation for supplemental oxygen, corticosteroids (Dexamethasone), and anti-coagulants.

title: Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome
warn: ⛔ RAPID LUNG FAILURE — Inhaling dust from infected rodent droppings causes a flu-like illness that suddenly shifts to massive fluid leaking into the lungs.
steps: Suspect if the patient was recently cleaning out an old barn, shed, or cabin with mouse droppings.
Early symptoms are fatigue, fever, and muscle aches (especially in thighs/hips).
LATE STAGE (Emergency): 4-10 days later, sudden, severe shortness of breath occurs, feeling like a tight band around the chest as lungs fill with fluid.
Call 112 immediately. The patient can drown in their own fluids within hours.
Keep the patient seated upright and provide oxygen if trained.
donot: Do NOT sweep or vacuum dry rodent droppings (always spray with bleach/water first to prevent aerosolizing the virus).
Do NOT delay going to the ER once breathing difficulty starts.
Do NOT lay the patient flat.
seek: Requires immediate ICU admission for intubation and oxygen therapy. There is no specific cure, only supportive care.

title: Gas Gangrene (Clostridial Myonecrosis)
warn: ⛔ EXTREME MUSCLE NECROSIS — Bacteria (usually Clostridium) introduced via deep trauma thrive in low-oxygen environments, destroying muscle and producing gas.
steps: Look at the wound: It will be extremely painful, swollen, and the skin may turn pale, then bronze, then dark purple/black.
Smell the wound: Gas gangrene produces a distinct, incredibly foul, sweet/rotting odor.
Press the skin gently: You will feel a crackling sensation (crepitus) due to the gas bubbles trapped under the skin.
Check for signs of shock: High heart rate, low blood pressure, pale skin.
Call 112 or go to the ER immediately.
donot: Do NOT tightly close or bandage deep, dirty puncture wounds at home (these bacteria thrive when sealed away from oxygen).
Do NOT ignore severe pain that is out of proportion to the original wound.
Do NOT delay transport; toxins spread rapidly to the heart.
seek: Absolute surgical emergency requiring wide debridement (cutting away dead muscle), high-dose IV antibiotics, and Hyperbaric Oxygen therapy.

title: Leptospirosis (Weil's Disease)
warn: ⚠️ ORGAN FAILURE — Bacteria spread via animal urine in water/soil. Severe cases cause liver and kidney failure simultaneously.
steps: Assess history: Did the patient recently swim in a freshwater lake, wade through floodwaters, or do an obstacle mud-run?
Watch for the severe phase: Yellowing of the skin/eyes (jaundice), severe muscle aches (especially calves/back), red eyes without pus, and decreased urination.
Go to the Emergency Room if the patient develops jaundice, cannot urinate, or starts coughing up blood.
Keep the patient hydrated if they are conscious and not vomiting.
donot: Do NOT assume it is standard hepatitis if they have severe muscle aches and red eyes.
Do NOT ignore symptoms if they occur 1-2 weeks after a flooding event.
Do NOT let the patient take Ibuprofen (can worsen kidney damage and bleeding).
seek: Requires hospitalization for IV Penicillin or Doxycycline, and potentially dialysis for kidney failure.

title: Yellow Fever (Toxic Phase)
warn: ⛔ HEMORRHAGIC ORGAN FAILURE — After a brief remission, the virus attacks the liver and kidneys, causing massive internal bleeding and yellowing of the skin.
steps: Assess history: Travel to tropical areas of Africa or South America without a Yellow Fever vaccination.
Watch for the "Toxic Phase": The patient improves for 24 hours, then suddenly develops high fever, severe jaundice (yellow skin/eyes), and bleeding from the mouth, nose, or eyes.
Recognize the hallmark sign: Vomiting dark, black, digested blood ("coffee-ground" vomit).
Call 112 immediately.
Keep the patient laying down to manage shock from blood loss.
donot: Do NOT give Aspirin, Ibuprofen, or any NSAIDs (these drastically increase the bleeding risk).
Do NOT assume the patient is cured during the brief remission phase.
Do NOT delay emergency care.
seek: Requires intensive supportive care in a hospital for blood loss, kidney failure, and liver damage.

title: West Nile Encephalitis
warn: ⚠️ NEUROINVASIVE VIRUS — A mosquito-borne virus that crosses into the brain, causing swelling, paralysis, and coma, primarily in the elderly.
steps: Watch for neurological symptoms: A severe headache and high fever progressing to neck stiffness, disorientation, tremors, or convulsions.
Check for sudden muscle weakness or acute flaccid paralysis (sudden inability to move an arm or leg).
Go to the Emergency Room immediately if confusion or paralysis occurs.
Keep the patient safe from falling if they are experiencing tremors or weakness.
Provide supportive comfort.
donot: Do NOT mistake severe confusion in an elderly patient during summer months for simple dementia or a UTI without ruling this out.
Do NOT let the patient walk unassisted.
Do NOT delay seeking a medical evaluation.
seek: Requires an ER evaluation (lumbar puncture/MRI) and supportive hospital care. There is no specific antiviral treatment.

title: Typhoid Fever (Intestinal Perforation)
warn: ⛔ BOWEL RUPTURE — In the 3rd week of untreated Typhoid, the infected intestinal wall can burst open, spilling feces into the abdomen.
steps: Suspect in someone with a prolonged, gradually increasing high fever, severe stomach pain, and a rash of flat, rose-colored spots.
EMERGENCY SIGN: The patient suddenly experiences agonizing, sharp abdominal pain, and the stomach becomes rigid and board-like to the touch.
The patient will rapidly pale, sweat profusely, and their blood pressure will drop (septic shock).
Call 112 immediately.
Keep the patient strictly NPO (nothing by mouth).
donot: Do NOT give the patient any food, water, or pain medication by mouth (the bowel has a hole in it).
Do NOT apply a heating pad to the rigid abdomen.
Do NOT delay surgery.
seek: Absolute surgical emergency to repair the hole in the intestine and wash out the abdominal cavity, plus IV antibiotics.

title: Measles (Complicated / Encephalitis)
warn: ⚠️ EXTREMELY CONTAGIOUS & DANGEROUS — The virus can cause severe pneumonia or cross into the brain, causing deadly encephalitis.
steps: Look for the sequence: High fever, cough, runny nose, and red watery eyes. Look inside the mouth for "Koplik spots" (tiny white dots on the inner cheek).
3-5 days later, a red, blotchy rash erupts starting at the hairline/face and moving downward.
EMERGENCY SIGNS: Call 112 if the patient develops extreme difficulty breathing, turns blue, or suddenly becomes confused, lethargic, or starts having seizures (signs of encephalitis).
Isolate the patient immediately in a separate room with the door closed.
donot: Do NOT bring the patient into a crowded doctor's waiting room (Measles lingers in the air for 2 hours after the patient leaves). Call ahead so they can prepare isolation.
Do NOT ignore a returning fever after the rash has peaked.
Do NOT give Aspirin to a child.
seek: Requires ER evaluation for complications. Vitamin A may be administered to children to reduce severity.

title: Severe C. difficile (Toxic Megacolon)
warn: ⛔ COLON EXPLOSION RISK — After antibiotic use, bad bacteria take over the gut, causing the colon to rapidly widen, paralyze, and threaten to burst.
steps: Identify the history: The patient recently took a course of antibiotics and developed severe, foul-smelling, watery diarrhea.
EMERGENCY SIGN: The diarrhea suddenly stops, but the patient's abdomen becomes massively swollen, hard, and extremely painful.
Watch for systemic shock: High fever, racing heart, confusion, and lethargy.
Go to the Emergency Room immediately.
Keep the patient NPO (nothing by mouth).
donot: Do NOT give anti-diarrheal medications (like Imodium) to someone with antibiotic-associated diarrhea (this causes the toxins to build up and triggers Toxic Megacolon).
Do NOT ignore a swollen, hard belly in someone who recently had severe diarrhea.
Do NOT give laxatives or enemas.
seek: Requires hospital admission for specific antibiotics (Oral Vancomycin/Fidaxomicin) and potential emergency surgery to remove the colon if it is about to burst.

title: Japanese Encephalitis
warn: ⚠️ NEUROLOGICAL DEVASTATION — A viral brain infection spread by mosquitoes in rural Asia. High mortality and long-term brain damage rates.
steps: Suspect in someone who has recently traveled to rural/agricultural areas of Asia without vaccination.
Watch for the rapid onset of high fever, headache, and vomiting.
The critical phase follows quickly: Mental status changes, severe neck stiffness, spastic paralysis, and frequent seizures.
Call 112 or transport to the ER immediately.
If seizing, roll to the side and protect the airway.
donot: Do NOT delay medical care assuming it is just a traveler's flu.
Do NOT attempt to give oral fluids if the patient is confused or seizing.
Do NOT leave the patient alone.
seek: Requires intensive care in a hospital for seizure management, airway protection, and pressure relief on the brain.

title: Poliovirus (Acute Flaccid Paralysis)
warn: ⛔ SPINAL CORD DESTRUCTION — The virus destroys motor neurons, causing sudden, irreversible paralysis that can reach the muscles controlling breathing.
steps: Look for the classic sign: A child or unvaccinated adult suddenly develops asymmetric weakness (e.g., one leg becomes entirely floppy and paralyzed).
Assess breathing: If the paralysis moves upward to the chest, the patient will struggle to take a deep breath or speak.
Call 112 immediately if there is any difficulty breathing or swallowing.
Keep the paralyzed limbs supported and comfortable.
Keep the patient completely calm.
donot: Do NOT attempt to forcefully exercise or stretch the paralyzed limb (the nerve is dead, not asleep).
Do NOT let the patient eat or drink if they sound hoarse or are struggling to swallow.
Do NOT delay emergency transport.
seek: Requires immediate ER evaluation and potentially mechanical ventilation (the modern "iron lung") if respiratory muscles fail.

title: Acute HIV Infection (Severe Seroconversion)
warn: ⚠️ IMMUNE SYSTEM BATTLE — 2 to 4 weeks after exposure, the body mounts a massive response as the virus rapidly replicates, sometimes causing severe neurological symptoms.
steps: Acknowledge severe, prolonged flu-like symptoms (fever, swollen lymph nodes, sore throat) paired with a rash on the trunk.
EMERGENCY: Seek immediate care if the patient develops signs of aseptic meningitis (severe headache, stiff neck, light sensitivity) or severe confusion.
If the patient knows they had a high-risk exposure recently, inform the doctors so they can run an HIV RNA test (antibody tests will still be negative).
Keep the patient hydrated and resting.
donot: Do NOT ignore a severe, prolonged "flu" that includes a rash and neurological symptoms.
Do NOT engage in unprotected sex or share needles (the patient is highly infectious during this acute stage due to massive viral load).
Do NOT rely on standard rapid HIV tests during this window.
seek: Requires an ER or specialized clinic for diagnosis, symptom management, and rapid initiation of Antiretroviral Therapy (ART).

title: Severe MERS / SARS
warn: ⛔ LETHAL RESPIRATORY SYNDROMES — Coronaviruses with highly lethal profiles. MERS is particularly dangerous, often causing simultaneous ARDS and acute kidney failure.
steps: Suspect MERS if the patient recently traveled to the Middle East or had contact with camels, and develops fever, cough, and severe shortness of breath.
Isolate the patient immediately. Wear an N95 mask.
Call 112 if the patient is struggling to breathe or turning pale/blue.
Inform EMS of the travel/exposure history immediately.
Keep the patient seated upright.
donot: Do NOT allow the patient to use public transportation or sit in an open ER waiting room.
Do NOT use nebulizer treatments at home (this aerosolizes the virus, spreading it to everyone in the room).
Do NOT delay seeking oxygen support.
seek: Requires isolation in an intensive care unit, mechanical ventilation, and dialysis if kidneys fail.

title: Nipah Virus Encephalitis
warn: ⛔ RAPID COMA — A highly lethal virus transmitted by fruit bats or pigs. It causes severe respiratory illness that rapidly progresses to fatal encephalitis.
steps: Suspect in regions with known outbreaks (e.g., South Asia) or after consuming raw date palm sap contaminated by bats.
Watch for fever, headache, and cough that rapidly deteriorates (within 24-48 hours) into severe confusion, drowsiness, and coma.
Call 112 immediately. The progression is exceptionally fast.
If the patient loses consciousness, place them in the recovery position.
Isolate the patient (it can spread person-to-person).
donot: Do NOT leave the patient alone.
Do NOT attempt to give them food or water once confusion or drowsiness begins.
Do NOT touch their bodily fluids.
seek: Requires immediate ICU admission for life support. There are no specific drugs or vaccines; care is purely supportive.

title: Tick-Borne Encephalitis (TBE)
warn: ⚠️ BIPHASIC BRAIN INFECTION — The virus causes a mild flu, seems to disappear, and then returns days later with a devastating attack on the brain and spinal cord.
steps: Assess history: A tick bite in wooded areas of Europe or Asia, or consuming unpasteurized dairy in those regions.
Recognize the Biphasic pattern: Phase 1 is a mild summer flu. The patient feels better for a few days. Phase 2 hits with high fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and confusion.
Watch for upper body paralysis (especially arms and breathing muscles).
Go to the Emergency Room immediately during the second phase.
Provide comfort and dark/quiet environment.
donot: Do NOT assume they are cured after the first "flu" phase goes away.
Do NOT delay medical care if they develop arm weakness or a stiff neck.
Do NOT squeeze ticks when removing them.
seek: Requires hospital admission for management of brain swelling and respiratory support.

title: Lassa Fever
warn: ⛔ HEMORRHAGIC SHOCK — Spread by the Mastomys rat in West Africa. Causes severe bleeding, fluid leaking into the lungs, and permanent deafness.
steps: Suspect if symptoms arise 1-3 weeks after travel to West Africa.
Early symptoms: Gradual weakness, fever, and a severely sore throat.
CRITICAL STAGE: Look for facial swelling, fluid in the lungs (gasping), bleeding from the mouth/nose, and dangerously low blood pressure.
Call 112 immediately, state the travel history, and isolate the patient.
Keep the patient laying flat to manage shock.
donot: Do NOT handle the patient's blood, urine, or saliva without full PPE.
Do NOT mistake the severe sore throat for simple strep throat if accompanied by bleeding or facial swelling.
Do NOT delay transport to a bio-secure facility.
seek: Requires isolation and administration of the antiviral drug Ribavirin as early as possible in the illness course.

title: Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM)
warn: ⛔ >97% FATALITY RATE — The "brain-eating amoeba" (Naegleria fowleri) enters through the nose while swimming in warm freshwater and rapidly destroys brain tissue.
steps: Assess the exact history: Did the patient swim, dive, or use a Neti pot with warm, unchlorinated freshwater in the last 1-9 days?
Watch for sudden, severe frontal headache, fever, nausea, and vomiting.
As it attacks the brain, look for a stiff neck, altered mental status, hallucinations, and seizures.

Go to the ER immediately and explicitly tell the doctor about the freshwater exposure in the nose (this disease is incredibly rare and often misdiagnosed as bacterial meningitis until it is too late).
Keep the patient safe during seizures or hallucinations.
donot: Do NOT use tap water in a Neti pot or sinus rinse (always use boiled or distilled water).
Do NOT delay going to the ER; death typically occurs within 5 days of symptoms starting.
Do NOT withhold the swimming history from the doctors.
seek: Requires an immediate induced coma and an experimental cocktail of drugs (including Miltefosine) administered directly into the spinal fluid.

title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
warn: ⛔ FATAL ACID BUILDUP — The body cannot use sugar for energy due to a lack of insulin, so it rapidly burns fat, releasing toxic blood acids (ketones).
steps: Recognize the classic signs: Excessive thirst, frequent urination, nausea, vomiting, and extreme fatigue.
Check breathing: Look for Kussmaul respirations (deep, rapid, labored breathing) and breath that smells like fruity nail polish remover.
Test blood sugar and ketones if a meter is available (blood sugar is usually >250 mg/dL, but can be lower).
Call 112 or go to the ER immediately if the patient is vomiting, confused, or struggling to breathe.
If conscious and able to swallow, have them drink water to help flush ketones.
donot: Do NOT attempt to treat severe DKA at home with large doses of insulin (dropping blood sugar too fast without IV fluids can cause fatal brain swelling).
Do NOT give sugary fluids.
Do NOT assume they just have a stomach bug if they are vomiting continuously.
seek: Requires immediate ICU admission for carefully calculated IV insulin drips, massive fluid replacement, and potassium monitoring.

title: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS)
warn: ⛔ MASSIVE DEHYDRATION & COMA — Blood sugar spikes to extreme levels (often >600 mg/dL), turning the blood into a thick syrup and draining water from the brain.
steps: Identify the patient profile: Most common in elderly patients with Type 2 diabetes who have an underlying infection or illness.
Watch for symptoms developing over days/weeks: Profound thirst, extreme urination that eventually stops, high fever, and worsening confusion or hallucinations.
Check for signs of severe dehydration (dry mouth, sunken eyes, skin that stays "tented" when pinched).
Call 112 immediately if the patient is severely confused, seizing, or unarousable.
Keep the patient safe from falls if they are disoriented.
donot: Do NOT give sugary foods or drinks.
Do NOT delay calling EMS; HHS has a higher mortality rate than DKA due to the extreme dehydration and age of typical patients.
Do NOT leave the patient alone.
seek: Requires emergency hospital admission for aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (often liters of fluid are needed) and slow IV insulin.

title: Severe Hypoglycemia (Insulin Shock)
warn: ⛔ IMMEDIATE BRAIN STARVATION — Blood sugar drops so low the brain shuts down. Can cause permanent brain damage, seizures, or death within minutes.
steps: If the patient is unconscious, having a seizure, or unable to swallow safely: DO NOT put food or liquid in their mouth.
Locate and administer Glucagon IMMEDIATELY if available (nasal spray or injection). Inject into the thigh or buttocks.
Call 112 immediately after administering Glucagon, or if you do not have it.
Roll the patient onto their side (recovery position) to prevent choking if they vomit.
If the patient wakes up and can swallow safely, give them fast-acting carbs (juice, regular soda) followed by a protein snack.
donot: Do NOT inject insulin (this will kill them).
Do NOT put fingers, spoons, or hard candy in the mouth of an unconscious or seizing diabetic.
Do NOT assume they will stay awake once revived with Glucagon; it wears off and blood sugar can crash again.
seek: Requires emergency transport for IV Dextrose (D50) if Glucagon fails or is unavailable. Hospital observation is needed to prevent recurrence.

title: Infected Diabetic Foot Ulcer
warn: ⚠️ LIMB & LIFE THREAT — Poor blood flow and nerve damage allow minor cuts to become deep, necrotic infections that spread to the bone.
steps: Examine the foot: Look for an open sore (ulcer) with surrounding redness, swelling, or foul-smelling drainage.
Check for systemic signs of infection: high fever, chills, confusion, or a racing heart (signs of sepsis).
If the tissue around the ulcer is turning black (necrosis/gangrene), go to the ER immediately.
Keep the foot elevated and completely offload all weight from it.
Cover the wound loosely with a dry, sterile dressing.
donot: Do NOT let the patient walk on the affected foot.
Do NOT soak the foot in hot water or apply heating pads (nerve damage means they cannot feel if they are being burned).
Do NOT ignore a foul smell coming from the shoes or socks.
seek: Requires immediate medical evaluation, deep tissue cultures, IV antibiotics, and likely surgical debridement to save the limb.

title: Acute Charcot Foot (Neuropathic Arthropathy)
warn: ⚠️ STRUCTURAL COLLAPSE — Severe nerve damage prevents the patient from feeling micro-fractures in their foot bones. The arch completely collapses, destroying the foot.
steps: Recognize the early signs: One foot suddenly becomes red, very swollen, and hot to the touch, often without any known trauma.
Ask the patient if it hurts; due to neuropathy, they may feel little to no pain despite massive bone damage.
Compare the affected foot to the normal foot.
Take ALL weight off the foot immediately. Make the patient use crutches or a wheelchair.
Go to the ER or urgent care for X-rays.
donot: Do NOT mistake this for simple cellulitis or a gout flare without getting an X-ray to check the bones.
Do NOT allow the patient to walk on the foot (every step crushes the broken bones further into a "rocker-bottom" deformity).
Do NOT apply heat.
seek: Requires immediate and total immobilization in a specialized cast (CROW boot or total contact cast) for months to allow the bones to fuse properly.

title: Euglycemic Diabetic Ketoacidosis (euDKA)
warn: ⚠️ HIDDEN ACID BUILDUP — A dangerous form of DKA where the blood is highly acidic and toxic, but the blood sugar level appears completely normal.
steps: Identify the risk: Often triggered by SGLT2 inhibitor medications (like Jardiance, Farxiga, Invokana), fasting, or low-carb diets in diabetics.
Watch for DKA symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, lethargy, abdominal pain, and heavy breathing.
Check blood sugar: It may be normal or only slightly elevated (<250 mg/dL), which gives a false sense of security.
Check urine or blood for KETONES. If ketones are high and the patient is vomiting, it is an emergency.
Go to the ER immediately.
donot: Do NOT dismiss the patient’s symptoms just because their blood sugar reading is normal.
Do NOT let the patient continue taking their SGLT2 inhibitor if they are vomiting or unable to eat.
Do NOT try to manage this at home with rest.
seek: Requires ER evaluation to test blood pH levels. Treatment is the same as classic DKA (IV fluids and insulin), despite the normal blood sugar.

title: Diabetic Vitreous Hemorrhage
warn: ⚠️ SIGHT THREATENING — Fragile, abnormal blood vessels in the eye (caused by prolonged high blood sugar) burst and fill the inside of the eye with blood.
steps: Acknowledge the symptoms: The patient experiences a sudden, massive onset of dark "floaters," cobwebs, or a complete red/dark wash over their vision in one eye.
This is completely painless.
Have the patient sit perfectly upright. Elevating the head allows gravity to settle the blood at the bottom of the eye, clearing the line of sight.
Have them limit their physical activity and eye movements.
Go to an ER with ophthalmology services or an emergency eye clinic.
donot: Do NOT let the patient lie flat on their back.
Do NOT let them lift heavy objects, bend over, or strain (which spikes pressure in the eye vessels).
Do NOT give them aspirin or ibuprofen.
seek: Requires urgent evaluation by a retinal specialist. It may clear on its own over months, or require emergency laser surgery or a vitrectomy.

title: Severe Gastroparesis Flare
warn: ⚠️ DEHYDRATION & SUGAR CRASH — Nerve damage paralyzes the stomach. Food rots instead of digesting, causing violent vomiting and unpredictable blood sugar spikes/crashes.
steps: Recognize the flare: Severe nausea, a feeling of being completely full after a few bites, severe bloating, and vomiting undigested food eaten hours or days ago.
Monitor blood sugar closely: Because food is not digesting normally, insulin taken for a meal will cause severe hypoglycemia before the food ever reaches the intestines.
If the patient cannot keep liquids down for more than 12-24 hours, seek medical attention.
Have them sip electrolyte fluids extremely slowly.
donot: Do NOT force the patient to eat solid, high-fiber, or high-fat foods (these are impossible for a paralyzed stomach to pass).
Do NOT administer full doses of meal-time insulin if they are vomiting or unable to digest.
Do NOT ignore symptoms of severe dehydration.
seek: Requires ER admission for IV hydration, IV antiemetics, and careful IV blood sugar management until the stomach begins moving again.

title: Emphysematous Pyelonephritis (EPN)
warn: ⛔ NECROTIZING KIDNEY INFECTION — A severe, life-threatening infection almost exclusively found in diabetics, where bacteria destroy kidney tissue and produce gas inside the organ.
steps: Recognize the red flags: Severe pain in the flank (lower back/side), high fever, chills, nausea, and severe lethargy.
Check for a sudden, unexplained spike in blood sugar levels (infections cause severe insulin resistance).
The patient will rapidly deteriorate into septic shock (confusion, low blood pressure, racing heart).
Call 112 or go to the ER immediately.
Keep the patient lying down and resting.
donot: Do NOT assume severe lower back pain with a fever is just a pulled muscle or a standard UTI.
Do NOT give ibuprofen (can worsen acute kidney injury).
Do NOT delay EMS transport.
seek: Requires an emergency CT scan, massive IV antibiotics, and often emergency surgical drainage or removal of the kidney (nephrectomy) to save the patient's life.

title: Diabetic Autonomic Neuropathy (Severe Syncope)
warn: ⚠️ FALL AND HEAD TRAUMA RISK — Diabetes damages the autonomic nerves that control blood pressure and heart rate, preventing the body from adjusting when standing up.
steps: Recognize the event: The patient stands up and immediately experiences severe dizziness, tunnel vision, and fainting (Orthostatic Hypotension).
Lay the patient flat on their back immediately and elevate their legs to return blood to the brain.
Check their blood sugar to ensure the fainting wasn't actually caused by hypoglycemia (a crucial distinction).
Once they wake up, have them remain lying down for several minutes, then slowly sit up before attempting to stand again.
Ensure they drink a large glass of water, as dehydration worsens this condition severely.
donot: Do NOT prop the fainting patient up in a chair (they must lie flat so the heart doesn't have to pump against gravity to reach the brain).
Do NOT let them walk to the bathroom if they are feeling dizzy.
Do NOT ignore it if it results in a head strike during the fall.
seek: If the fainting was accompanied by chest pain, or if they struck their head, go to the ER. Otherwise, requires follow-up with a cardiologist for blood pressure regulation.

title: Minor Laceration (Clean Cut)
warn: ⚠️ Edges are clean and straight, but it requires proper cleaning to prevent infection.
steps: Wash your own hands before treating the wound.
Apply direct pressure with a clean cloth until bleeding stops (usually 5-10 minutes).
Rinse the wound gently but thoroughly under cool running tap water to remove dirt.
Wash around the wound with mild soap, avoiding getting soap directly into the deep cut.
Apply a thin layer of antibiotic ointment (like Polysporin) and cover with a sterile bandage.
Change the bandage daily or whenever it gets wet or dirty.
donot: Do NOT use hydrogen peroxide, rubbing alcohol, or iodine inside the wound (they damage healthy tissue and delay healing).
Do NOT blow on the wound (mouths harbor bacteria).
Do NOT pick at the scab as it heals.
seek: See a doctor if the wound becomes red, hot, swollen, or starts draining pus after a few days.

title: Deep / Gaping Laceration
warn: ⚠️ TISSUE SEPARATION — If the wound edges do not easily fall together, or if you can see yellow fat/muscle, it requires sutures (stitches).
steps: Apply firm, direct pressure with a sterile gauze or clean cloth until bleeding stops.
If blood soaks through, place another cloth on top; do not remove the first one.
Rinse briefly with clean water if grossly dirty, but do not scrub.
If you have Steri-Strips (butterfly closures) and are trained, you can use them to pull the edges together temporarily.
Keep the injured area elevated above the heart to reduce throbbing and bleeding.
donot: Do NOT apply tourniquets for standard lacerations unless there is spurting, massive arterial bleeding.
Do NOT pour chemicals or ointments deep into a gaping wound.
Do NOT wait until the next day to get stitches (most doctors will not stitch a wound older than 12-24 hours due to infection risk).
seek: Requires ER or urgent care for professional cleaning, suturing, and a potential tetanus booster.

title: Severe Abrasion (Road Rash)
warn: ⚠️ HIGH INFECTION RISK — Abrasions cover a large surface area and often grind dirt, asphalt, and bacteria deep into the skin layers.
steps: Wash your hands and put on gloves if available.
Rinse the abrasion under copious amounts of clean running water.
Gently use a clean, soft washcloth or gauze to lightly scrub away loose dirt and debris (this will be painful but is necessary).
Apply a thick layer of antibiotic ointment or petroleum jelly to keep the wound moist.
Cover with a non-adherent (Telfa) pad and wrap with a gauze roll.
donot: Do NOT leave dirt or gravel embedded in the skin ("tattooing" will occur if the skin heals over the dirt).
Do NOT let the abrasion dry out and form a massive hard scab (moist wounds heal twice as fast and scar less).
Do NOT apply standard woven gauze directly to the raw wound (it will stick and rip the new skin off when removed).
seek: If you cannot get all the dirt out, or if the abrasion covers a massive area, seek medical help for professional debridement and numbing.

title: Deep Puncture Wound
warn: ⚠️ BACTERIA TRAP — Puncture wounds do not bleed much, which means they do not wash themselves out. They trap bacteria deep in the tissue.
steps: Encourage the wound to bleed slightly by applying gentle pressure around the hole (this helps flush out bacteria).
Wash the surface of the skin with soap and water.
Do not attempt to probe or dig into the hole.
Apply a sterile bandage.
Check the patient’s tetanus vaccination history (must be within the last 5 years for a dirty puncture).
donot: Do NOT plug the hole with ointments, creams, or tight closures (the wound must heal from the bottom up to prevent abscesses).
Do NOT soak the wound in water (this can introduce new bacteria).
Do NOT ignore it if it was caused by a dirty object (soil, rusty metal, teeth).
seek: Go to urgent care or the ER for a tetanus shot and potential prophylactic antibiotics. Punctures through shoes pose a high risk for Pseudomonas infections.

title: Animal Bite (Dog/Cat/Wild)
warn: ⚠️ RABIES & SEVERE INFECTION RISK — Cat bites are especially dangerous as their sharp teeth inject bacteria deep into joints and tendons.
steps: If the bite is bleeding heavily, apply direct pressure to stop it first.
If bleeding is minor, WASH the wound immediately and continuously for 10-15 minutes under running water with plenty of soap. This is the #1 way to prevent rabies and infection.
Cover with a sterile bandage.
Identify the animal if safely possible (e.g., ask the owner for vaccination records, or note the wild animal’s location for animal control).
donot: Do NOT try to catch or kill a wild, aggressive animal yourself.
Do NOT use superglue or butterfly strips to close an animal bite at home (closing it traps the bacteria and guarantees an abscess).
Do NOT assume a small puncture from a cat is harmless.
seek: ALL animal bites breaking the skin require medical evaluation for antibiotics (like Augmentin) and a rabies risk assessment.

title: Human Bite
warn: ⚠️ EXTREME INFECTION RISK — The human mouth harbors highly aggressive bacteria. Bites often occur on the knuckles during fights ("fight bite").
steps: Wash the wound vigorously with soap and warm water for at least 5 minutes.
Apply direct pressure to stop any bleeding.
Apply a sterile dressing.
Immobilize the affected area (especially if it is a hand).
Go to the emergency room or urgent care.
donot: Do NOT put your mouth on the wound to suck out blood.
Do NOT try to close the wound with tape or glue.
Do NOT lie to the doctor about how the injury happened (doctors need to know it was a human tooth to prescribe the correct antibiotics).
seek: Requires professional medical cleaning, X-rays (to check for tooth fragments in the knuckle), and specific antibiotics to prevent joint destruction.

title: Skin Avulsion (Skin Flap)
warn: ⚠️ FRAGILE TISSUE — A flap of skin is torn loose but remains partially attached. Common in the elderly due to paper-thin skin.
steps: Control bleeding with direct, gentle pressure.
Clean the wound area gently with sterile saline or clean running water.
If the skin flap is still viable and not grossly contaminated, gently unroll it and lay it flat back over the wound bed (this acts as a natural biological bandage).
Cover with a non-adherent dressing (Telfa) or petroleum-jelly-coated gauze.
Secure the dressing gently (use a gauze wrap or cohesive bandage, NOT sticky tape on the skin).
donot: Do NOT cut or tear the skin flap off.
Do NOT apply strong adhesive tape directly to the fragile skin surrounding the wound.
Do NOT scrub the exposed tissue underneath the flap.
seek: Seek medical care if the flap is dirty, turning black/purple (dying), or if it requires sutures to hold it in place.

title: Partial Digit Amputation
warn: ⚠️ PRESERVE THE TISSUE — A portion of a finger or toe is severed but still hanging on by a thread of skin or tendon.
steps: Call 112 or go directly to the ER.
Apply direct pressure to the stump/wound base to stop bleeding. Elevate the hand/foot.
Gently align the severed piece back into its normal anatomical position if possible.
Wrap the entire digit snugly (but not tourniquet-tight) in bulky sterile gauze.
Splint the finger/hand to prevent any movement that could tear the remaining tissue.
Apply an ice pack to the OUTSIDE of the bulky dressing to keep it cool.
donot: Do NOT pull or twist the hanging piece of tissue.
Do NOT apply ice directly to the skin (it will cause frostbite and kill the remaining viable tissue).
Do NOT soak the finger in water.
seek: Requires immediate evaluation by a hand surgeon or plastic surgeon for microvascular repair.

title: Infected Wound (Abscess / Cellulitis)
warn: ⚠️ SEPSIS THREAT — The wound has bypassed local healing and is actively breeding bacteria, threatening to enter the bloodstream.
steps: Recognize the signs of infection: Increasing pain, spreading redness, swelling, warmth, and thick yellow/green pus.
Look for danger signs: Red streaks traveling from the wound toward the heart, or the patient developing a fever and chills.
If there is an obvious pocket of pus (abscess) pointing at the skin, apply a warm, moist compress to encourage it to drain.
Keep the affected limb elevated to reduce throbbing and swelling.
donot: Do NOT squeeze, pop, or cut an abscess open yourself (you can push the bacteria deeper into the bloodstream).
Do NOT apply leftover antibiotic creams and hope it goes away if a fever or red streaks are present.
Do NOT ignore a wound that smells foul.
seek: Requires a doctor to formally incise and drain (I&D) the abscess and prescribe oral or IV antibiotics.

title: Embedded Splinter / Glass Shard
warn: ⚠️ RETAINED FRAGMENTS — Objects left in the skin will cause a localized infection (granuloma) as the body tries to wall it off.
steps: Wash the area with soap and water.
If the end of the splinter is protruding, sterilize a pair of tweezers with rubbing alcohol and pull the splinter out exactly in the same angle it went in.
If it is entirely under the skin, you can sterilize a needle, gently prick the skin over the end of the splinter, and lift it to expose the tip for the tweezers.
Once removed, wash again, apply antibiotic ointment, and bandage.
If it is glass and you cannot easily see/grab it, leave it alone.
donot: Do NOT squeeze the skin around the splinter (this can break it into smaller pieces or drive it deeper).
Do NOT dig deeply into the flesh with a needle or knife.
Do NOT ignore wood or organic matter splinters (they carry fungi and bacteria and must be removed).
seek: See a doctor if the splinter is deep, near a joint, under a fingernail, or if it is glass that you cannot completely remove.

title: Subungual Hematoma (Smashed Fingernail)
warn: ⚠️ PRESSURE BUILDUP — Blood pools under the rigid fingernail, causing intense, agonizing throbbing pain due to the lack of space.
steps: Immediately apply an ice pack and elevate the hand above the heart to minimize initial swelling and bleeding.
Assess the finger: If the finger is deformed, cannot bend, or has a cut involving the nail bed, go to urgent care.
If the pain is unbearable due to pressure, a doctor can perform "trephination" (melting a tiny hole through the nail to let the blood squirt out, providing instant relief).
donot: Do NOT attempt to melt a hole in the nail at home with a hot paperclip (this old trick frequently causes deep infections or burns the nail bed permanently).
Do NOT try to pull the nail off.
Do NOT ignore it if the blood covers more than 50% of the nail.
seek: See a doctor if pain is unmanageable, the nail is torn, or you suspect the bone underneath is broken (tuft fracture).

title: Fishhook Impalement
warn: ⚠️ BARBED THREAT — The barb on a fishhook acts like a harpoon; pulling it backward tears the flesh aggressively.
steps: Keep the patient calm and immobilize the body part.

If the hook is superficially embedded, use the "String Yank" method: Tie a piece of fishing line to the curve of the hook. Press down hard on the eye (shank) of the hook to disengage the barb, then yank the string firmly and quickly parallel to the skin.
Alternatively, if the point is near the surface, push the point completely THROUGH the skin, use wire cutters to snip the barb off, and then back the smooth hook out.
Wash the wound thoroughly.
donot: Do NOT simply yank the hook backward without disengaging or cutting the barb.
Do NOT attempt home removal if the hook is in the face, eye, joint, or deeply embedded in muscle.
Do NOT leave the wound uncleaned (lake/ocean water harbors aggressive bacteria).
seek: Seek medical help if home removal fails, if the hook is near the eye, or for a tetanus booster and antibiotics.

title: Scalp Laceration
warn: ⚠️ DECEPTIVE BLEEDING — The scalp has a massive blood supply. Even tiny cuts will bleed profusely, often making the injury look much worse than it is.
steps: Apply firm, direct pressure with a clean cloth or gauze. You may need to press hard against the skull to stop the bleeding.
Hold pressure continuously for 15 minutes without peeking.
While holding pressure, assess the patient for signs of a concussion or traumatic brain injury (confusion, vomiting, loss of consciousness).
If the bleeding stops, part the hair to assess the cut. If it is gaping or longer than a half-inch, it needs closure.
donot: Do NOT apply extreme pressure if you suspect the skull underneath is fractured or dented.
Do NOT wash the wound vigorously if you cannot stop the bleeding.
Do NOT tie hair across the wound to close it yourself.
seek: Requires ER evaluation for staples/stitches to close the scalp, and a neurological exam to rule out brain injury.

title: Oral Laceration (Lip / Tongue Bite)
warn: ⚠️ AIRWAY & SWELLING RISK — The mouth bleeds heavily and heals quickly, but severe swelling of the tongue can threaten the airway.
steps: Have the patient sit up and lean their head slightly forward so blood drains out of the mouth, not down the throat.
Rinse the mouth gently with cool water to identify where the bleeding is coming from.
Pinch the bleeding lip firmly with gauze, or press gauze directly onto the bleeding part of the tongue.
Apply a cold pack or have the patient suck on an ice cube or popsicle to constrict blood vessels and reduce swelling.
donot: Do NOT let the patient swallow large amounts of blood (it causes severe vomiting).
Do NOT pull the lip outward to constantly check it (this restarts the bleeding).
Do NOT use topical numbing gels meant for external skin inside the mouth.
seek: See a doctor if the cut crosses the border of the lip (vermilion border), is gaping wide, or if bleeding won’t stop after 15 minutes.

title: Severe Friction Blister (Torn)
warn: ⚠️ INFECTION GATEWAY — A burst blister leaves a patch of raw, highly sensitive, weeping dermis exposed to bacteria.
steps: Wash your hands and the affected area gently with soap and water.
If the blister is already popped and the "roof" (dead skin) is dirty or torn, use sterilized scissors to carefully trim away the loose flaps of dead skin.
If the "roof" is clean and intact, LEAVE IT ALONE. It is the best biological bandage available.
Apply antibiotic ointment and cover with a hydrocolloid bandage (like a blister pad) or a non-stick dressing.
Protect the area with a donut-shaped pad to prevent further friction.
donot: Do NOT pop an intact blister unless it is in an area where it will inevitably burst and cause extreme pain (if you must, use a sterile needle to pierce the edge and drain fluid, keeping the roof intact).
Do NOT rip or peel the dead skin off forcefully.
Do NOT apply superglue to raw blister beds.
seek: Seek medical care if the fluid inside becomes cloudy/yellow (pus), or if expanding redness surrounds the blister.

title: Coral Cut / Marine Scrape
warn: ⚠️ AGGRESSIVE MARINE BACTERIA — Coral is covered in bacteria, animal proteins, and stinging cells. Wounds get infected incredibly fast.
steps: Scrub the wound vigorously with soap and fresh water immediately. You must physically remove all coral dust and slime.
Flush the wound with a mixture of half water and half hydrogen peroxide ONCE (to kill marine bacteria and bubble out debris), then rinse with pure fresh water.
If stinging cells (nematocysts) are suspected, rinse with vinegar first, then wash.
Apply antibiotic ointment and a sterile bandage.
Monitor the wound intensely over the next 48 hours.
donot: Do NOT close the wound tightly with butterfly strips or superglue (marine bacteria thrive in closed, oxygen-free environments).
Do NOT ignore increasing pain or swelling.
Do NOT go back in the ocean with an open wound.
seek: Seek emergency care IMMEDIATELY if red streaks develop, or if the wound rapidly swells and causes extreme pain (Vibrio bacteria can cause flesh-eating disease).

title: Ring Avulsion (Degloved Finger)
warn: ⛔ CATASTROPHIC TISSUE STRIPPING — A ring gets caught on a moving object (or while falling) and violently strips the skin, nerves, and blood vessels off the finger bone.
steps: Call 112 immediately. This is a severe microvascular trauma.
Apply direct, firm pressure to the stump or stripped finger to control bleeding.
Elevate the hand above the heart.
If the skin and tissue were completely torn off, recover the tissue, wrap it in moist sterile gauze, put it in a watertight bag, and place the bag on ice.
Keep the patient calm and treat for shock.
donot: Do NOT put the severed tissue directly in water or directly on ice.
Do NOT attempt to push the skin back onto the bone yourself.
Do NOT wear metal rings while operating heavy machinery, working with tools, or playing sports.
seek: Requires immediate transfer to a trauma center with specialized hand and microvascular surgeons.

title: Extremity Gunshot Wound (Flesh Wound)
warn: ⛔ HIDDEN CAVITATION — Bullets create massive shockwaves that destroy tissue, shatter bone, and sever arteries far beyond the visible hole.
steps: Ensure scene safety before approaching. Call 112 immediately.
Locate the wound. Cut away clothing to expose the area. Check the opposite side for an exit wound.
If there is massive, bright red, spurting blood, apply a tourniquet 2-3 inches ABOVE the wound immediately. Tighten until bleeding stops.
If bleeding is controllable, pack the wound tightly with gauze and apply heavy, continuous direct pressure.
Keep the patient warm to prevent shock.
donot: Do NOT assume the wound is minor just because the entrance hole is small.
Do NOT remove a tourniquet once it is applied.
Do NOT dig into the wound to try and find the bullet.
seek: Absolute trauma emergency requiring surgical exploration, fracture stabilization, and vascular repair.

title: Metal or Wood Shaving in Skin
warn: ⚠️ RUST AND TOXICITY RISK — Metal shavings rust quickly. Some woods (like cedar or treated lumber) are highly toxic and cause severe inflammation.
steps: Wash the area gently with soap and water.
If the shaving is metallic and close to the surface, you can sometimes use a strong magnet to draw it out painlessly.
If removing with tweezers, ensure you grab the entire shaving. Metal often splinters and leaves microscopic barbs behind.
If it is a treated wood splinter, it must be removed entirely, as the chemicals will cause the tissue to necrotize (die).
Apply antibiotic ointment and bandage.
donot: Do NOT rub the area (this pushes the sharp shaving deeper or breaks it).
Do NOT use chemical solvents to try and draw the shaving out.
Do NOT ignore it if the area becomes swollen, red, or starts oozing clear fluid.
seek: Seek medical care if you cannot get the entire shaving out, or if the wound shows signs of an allergic or toxic reaction (extreme redness and swelling).

title: Bleeding Varicose Vein
warn: ⚠️ MASSIVE VENOUS BLEEDING — Enlarged, weak veins in the lower legs can rupture from a tiny bump or scratch, causing blood to pour out alarmingly fast.
steps: Have the patient lie flat on their back IMMEDIATELY.
Elevate the bleeding leg high above the heart (this uses gravity to drain blood away from the vein and instantly slows the bleeding).
Apply firm, direct pressure exactly on the bleeding spot using a clean pad or towel.
Maintain pressure continuously for 15-20 minutes.
Once stopped, apply a tight, cohesive bandage wrap over the pad to keep pressure on the vein.
donot: Do NOT let the patient stand up or dangle their legs (gravity will force blood back into the vein, causing it to burst open again).
Do NOT apply a tourniquet (elevation and direct pressure are almost always sufficient for venous bleeds).
Do NOT remove the pad to check if it stopped bleeding within the first 15 minutes.
seek: If bleeding does not stop after 20 minutes of elevation and pressure, call 112. Follow up with a vascular doctor to treat the underlying weak veins.

title: Paracetamol (Acetaminophen) Overdose
warn: ⛔ Liver failure may not be apparent for 48-72 hours. Treat within 8-10 hours for best outcome.
steps: Call National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) immediately: 1800-116-117 (India NPIC, toll-free).
Note: time of ingestion, dose, and formulation.
If within 1-2 hours of large ingestion: activated charcoal may be given (medical guidance only).
Hospital: measure paracetamol level at 4 hours post-ingestion.
N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is the antidote — administer based on Rumack-Matthew nomogram.
donot: Do NOT wait for symptoms.
Do NOT induce vomiting unless instructed by National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117).
seek: All deliberate or accidental large overdose — even if symptom-free.

title: Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose
warn: ⛔ Rapidly fatal. Anticholinergic syndrome + cardiac arrhythmias.
steps: Call 112 and National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) immediately.
Recognize: hot, dry, flushed skin, dilated pupils, tachycardia, sedation, seizures.
Airway management priority.
Sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening and cardiac arrhythmias.
Avoid physostigmine.
Do NOT induce vomiting (aspiration risk, rapid deterioration).
donot: Do NOT induce vomiting.
seek: Immediate emergency — rapid deterioration.

title: Pericardial Tamponade
warn: ⛔ Beck Triad: hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds = EMERGENCY.
steps: Recognize: hypotension, jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds after chest trauma.
Call 112 immediately.
Position patient upright.
Pericardiocentesis at hospital (definitive).
IV fluids to maintain preload temporarily.
donot: Do NOT delay transport.
seek: Immediate surgical emergency.

title: COPD Exacerbation
warn: ⚠️ Controlled oxygen only — high flow may suppress respiratory drive in COPD.
steps: Position upright (tripod).
Administer short-acting bronchodilator (salbutamol MDI x 4 puffs or nebulized).
Controlled oxygen: target SpO2 88-92% in known COPD.
Systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 40mg).
Antibiotics if evidence of infection (increased sputum/purulence).
Call 112 if severe.
donot: Do NOT give high-flow O2 in known COPD without monitoring SpO2.
seek: Inability to speak in sentences, SpO2 <88%, cyanosis, altered consciousness.

title: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
warn: ⚠️ 10% risk of stroke within 48 hours of TIA. URGENT assessment required.
steps: Recognize: stroke symptoms that resolve within 24 hours (usually minutes).
Call 112 or transport urgently — treated as stroke until proven otherwise.
Aspirin 300mg immediately if not contraindicated.
ABCD2 risk score determines urgency of neurology review.
CT scan and echocardiogram required.
donot: Do NOT assume symptoms resolved = problem resolved.
seek: Same urgency as stroke — immediate evaluation.

title: Anaphylaxis from Insect Sting
warn: ⚠️ Envenomation anaphylaxis can be faster and more severe than food allergy.
steps: Remove stinger by scraping (not pinching).
Administer EpiPen if anaphylaxis develops.
Call 112.
Ice pack to sting site.
Antihistamine for local reaction.
Monitor for 4 hours minimum.
donot: Do NOT squeeze stinger (injects more venom).
seek: Any systemic symptoms after sting.

title: Animal Bite (Rabies Risk)
warn: ⚠️ Rabies is 100% fatal once symptomatic. PEP must begin within 24-72 hours.
steps: Irrigate wound vigorously with soap and water for 15 minutes.
Apply antiseptic (povidone iodine).
Contact local health authority regarding rabies risk assessment.
If high-risk (unprovoked bat, wild carnivore, or unvaccinated animal): start PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) within 24 hours.
Tetanus prophylaxis.
Do NOT close wound primarily.
donot: Do NOT delay PEP decision.
seek: All animal bites require medical evaluation for PEP assessment.

title: Jellyfish Sting
warn: ⚠️ Box jellyfish (Indo-Pacific) = life-threatening. All others: rinse with saltwater.
steps: Remove from water.
Do NOT rub sting area.
Rinse with seawater (NOT fresh water — worsens nematocyst discharge).
Remove visible tentacles with tweezers or card (NOT bare fingers).
Apply vinegar for 30 seconds for most jellyfish (NOT for box jellyfish in some regions — check local guidelines).
Hot water immersion (43°C/109°F) for pain relief.
Box jellyfish: antivenom if available, call 112.
donot: Do NOT urinate on sting (ineffective).
Do NOT use fresh water.
seek: Box jellyfish, systemic symptoms, anaphylaxis, or extensive stings.

title: Compartment Syndrome
warn: ⛔ 5 Ps: Pain out of proportion, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paraesthesia, Paralysis. SURGICAL EMERGENCY.
steps: Recognize: pain out of proportion to injury, pain with passive stretch of muscles.
Call 112 immediately.
Remove cast, bandages, tight clothing.
Position at heart level (NOT elevated — reduces perfusion pressure).
Hospital: emergency fasciotomy within 6 hours.
Do NOT elevate limb if compartment syndrome suspected.
donot: Do NOT elevate the limb.
seek: Immediate surgical emergency — irreversible damage after 6 hours.

title: Ectopic Pregnancy
warn: ⛔ Ruptured ectopic = catastrophic hemorrhage. Classic: amenorrhea + one-sided pain + vaginal bleeding.
steps: Call 112 immediately if hemodynamically unstable.
Lay patient flat.
IV fluids if available.
Transport urgently to hospital.
Do NOT give analgesics that mask pain (important diagnostic tool).
donot: Do NOT delay transport.
seek: Immediate surgical emergency upon rupture.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome Response
warn: ⛔ Begin infant CPR and call 112. Continue resuscitation until EMS arrives.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Place infant on firm flat surface.
Begin infant CPR: 30 compressions (2-finger technique on sternum) + 2 breaths.
Rate 100-120/min, depth 1.5 inches.
Open airway: slight head tilt (neutral position — NOT full extension like adult).
Cover mouth AND nose with your mouth for rescue breaths.
Continue until EMS arrives.
donot: Do NOT stop CPR until EMS takes over.
seek: All infant unresponsiveness = immediate 112.

title: Contact Dermatitis
warn: ⚠️ Poison ivy resin washes off — decontaminate before touching other body parts.
steps: Remove allergen: wash skin with soap and water within 10 minutes of exposure.
Apply cool compresses for itch.
Over-the-counter hydrocortisone 1% cream.
Oral antihistamine for systemic symptoms.
Calamine lotion for drying and itch.
Prescription: topical/oral steroids for severe reactions.
donot: Do NOT scratch — breaks skin, introduces infection.
seek: Eyelid/genital involvement, spreading beyond contact site, or systemic symptoms.

title: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State
warn: ⚠️ BG often >600mg/dL in Type 2. Massive fluid deficit — mortality 10-20%.
steps: Recognize: extreme thirst, lethargy, confusion, glucose usually >600 mg/dL.
Call 112.
IV fluids — massive deficit (often 8-10 liters).
Hospital: cautious insulin, electrolyte replacement.
Look for precipitating cause: infection, MI.
donot: Do NOT give rapid large insulin doses without careful glucose monitoring.
seek: Immediate hospital.

title: Salicylate (Aspirin) Overdose
warn: ⚠️ Mixed acid-base picture. Severe toxicity causes cerebral and pulmonary edema.
steps: Call National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117).
Recognize: tinnitus, hyperventilation, confusion, fever.
Hospital: sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize urine, hemodialysis for severe cases.
IV fluids.
Monitor glucose closely.
donot: Do NOT give activated charcoal beyond 1-2 hours.
seek: Immediate for intentional overdose or tinnitus with confusion.

title: Eclampsia
warn: ⛔ Seizures in pregnancy after 20 weeks. Give magnesium sulfate immediately.
steps: Recognize: seizure in 3rd trimester/postpartum woman.
Call 112.
Protect from injury; do NOT restrain.
IV/IM magnesium sulfate (4-6g loading dose) — antidote: calcium gluconate 1g IV.
Left lateral position to prevent aorto-caval compression.
O2 supplementation.
Expedite delivery at hospital.
donot: Do NOT give phenytoin as first line.
seek: All seizures in pregnancy = immediate emergency.

title: Crush Injury
warn: ⛔ Release after prolonged crush releases myoglobin — can cause renal failure and cardiac arrest.
steps: Call 112 before releasing crush.
Start IV fluids BEFORE release if possible (to prevent crush syndrome).
After release: aggressive fluid resuscitation (1-1.5L/hr).
Monitor urine output and color (dark = myoglobinuria).
Cardiac monitoring — hyperkalemia risk on release.
Do NOT elevate limb.
donot: Do NOT release trapped person without medical backup present if possible.
seek: All crush injuries >1 hour require hospital.

title: Altitude Sickness (AMS/HACE)
warn: ⚠️ High Altitude Cerebral Edema (HACE) = DESCEND immediately.
steps: Recognize AMS: headache + one of: nausea, fatigue, dizziness above 2500m.
Stop ascent. Acclimatize.
Oral ibuprofen/paracetamol for headache.
Descend 300-1000m if not improving.
Dexamethasone 8mg then 4mg q6h for HACE.
Portable hyperbaric chamber (Gamow bag) if available.
O2 supplementation.
donot: Do NOT ascend further with AMS symptoms.
seek: HACE: confusion, ataxia, altered consciousness = descend immediately regardless of time of day.

title: Tetanus Risk Assessment
warn: ⚠️ Tetanus is preventable. Unvaccinated + dirty wound = immediate TIG + vaccine.
steps: Assess wound: clean/minor vs all others (puncture, contaminated, deep).
Vaccination history: <3 doses or unknown = ALWAYS give Td/Tdap.
Tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) 250 units IM for high-risk wounds in unvaccinated.
Clean wound thoroughly.
Antibiotics (metronidazole) for contaminated wounds.
donot: Do NOT assume patient is immune.
seek: All wounds with unknown or incomplete vaccination history.

title: Status Epilepticus
warn: ⛔ Seizure >5 minutes = Status Epilepticus. Irreversible brain injury after 30 minutes.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
Benzodiazepine first line: lorazepam 0.1mg/kg IV OR diazepam 10mg PR OR midazolam 10mg buccal/IN.
If no IV access: buccal/intranasal midazolam or rectal diazepam.
Protect airway.
Check glucose — treat hypoglycemia.
If not controlled: phenytoin/levetiracetam IV.
Refractory: propofol/thiopental infusion in ICU.
donot: Do NOT delay benzodiazepines.
seek: Immediate — all seizures >5 minutes.

title: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma
warn: ⚠️ Permanent blindness within hours. Sudden severe eye pain + halos around lights.
steps: Recognize: sudden severe eye pain, headache, nausea, halos around lights, blurred vision.
Call ophthalmologist or emergency room immediately.
IV/oral acetazolamide to reduce IOP.
Topical pilocarpine and timolol.
Analgesics for pain.
Laser iridotomy at hospital (definitive treatment).
donot: Do NOT give atropine/anticholinergics.
seek: Immediate ophthalmology emergency.

title: Achilles Tendon Rupture
warn: ⚠️ Often painless pop with inability to plantarflex. Often misdiagnosed as sprain.
steps: Recognize: pop sound, inability to push off foot, Thompson test positive.
Immobilize ankle in equinus (plantarflexed) position.
Elevate limb.
Analgesics.
Non-weight bearing — crutches.
Orthopedic referral for surgical vs non-surgical management decision.
donot: Do NOT dorsiflex ankle (worsens gap).
seek: Orthopedic referral within 48-72 hours.

title: Acute Pancreatitis
warn: ⚠️ Severe pancreatitis mortality >30%. IV fluids are cornerstone of treatment.
steps: Recognize: severe epigastric pain radiating to back, nausea, elevated amylase/lipase.
Call 112 or urgent transport.
IV fluid resuscitation (aggressive: 250-500ml/hr initially).
NPO — bowel rest.
Pain management: IV/IM morphine or ketorolac.
Monitor for complications: SIRS, organ failure.
donot: Do NOT give oral fluids.
Do NOT delay IV fluids.
seek: All suspected pancreatitis requires hospital admission.

title: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome
warn: ⛔ Drug-induced. Mortality up to 30% for TEN. Stop offending drug IMMEDIATELY.
steps: Recognize: target lesions, blistering mucous membranes, skin detachment, fever after drug.
Stop offending drug immediately.
Call 112.
Treat like burns: IV fluids, sterile wound care.
Ophthalmology urgent — eye complications.
Burns unit or ICU.
donot: Do NOT continue suspected offending drug.
seek: Immediate hospital — burns center.

title: Tension Hemothorax
warn: ⛔ Absent breath sounds + shock + dull percussion = hemothorax.
steps: Recognize: absent breath sounds on affected side, dull percussion, hypotension, tachycardia.
Call 112.
Needle thoracocentesis if tension hemothorax suspected (trained provider).
Chest drain (tube thoracostomy) in hospital.
IV fluids — 2 large-bore IVs.
Blood transfusion.
Thoracic surgery for >1.5L initial drainage or continued high-volume loss.
donot: Do NOT delay treatment.
seek: Immediate surgical emergency.

title: Intussusception
warn: ⚠️ Classic: episodic severe abdominal pain, knees-to-chest, current jelly stool. Peak 6mo-2yr.
steps: Recognize: colicky abdominal pain (pulls knees to chest), vomiting, current jelly stool.
Call 112 or urgent transport.
NPO.
IV access and fluids.
Hospital: air/hydrostatic enema reduction (success 80-90%).
Surgery if enema fails or perforation.
donot: Do NOT give analgesics before diagnosis if possible.
seek: Urgent surgical evaluation.

title: Food Allergy Reaction
warn: ⚠️ Any throat tightness after food = epinephrine, not antihistamine.
steps: Remove food allergen.
Mild symptoms (hives only): oral antihistamine.
ANY systemic symptoms (throat tightness, wheeze, vomiting, BP drop): administer EpiPen.
Call 112.
Antihistamines and steroids after EpiPen as adjunct.
Hospital observation minimum 4-6 hours.
donot: Do NOT use antihistamines as primary treatment for systemic reactions.
seek: All systemic food allergic reactions.

title: Diabetes-Related Foot Infection
warn: ⚠️ Neuropathy masks pain — diabetics may present late with severe infection.
steps: Examine foot thoroughly: ulcer depth, probe to bone (osteomyelitis if positive).
Check vascular status: pulses, ABI.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Off-load pressure from wound.
Urgent surgery for gas in tissues (necrotizing fasciitis), abscess, or deep infection.
Control blood glucose aggressively.
donot: Do NOT ignore foot wound in diabetic — even painless ones.
seek: All diabetic foot ulcers with infection signs, probe-to-bone positive, or systemic symptoms.

title: Placental Abruption
warn: ⛔ Concealed hemorrhage — external bleeding underestimates blood loss.
steps: Recognize: sudden onset abdominal pain, rigid uterus, fetal distress, vaginal bleeding.
Call 112 immediately.
Left lateral position.
IV large-bore access x2.
Aggressive fluid resuscitation.
Fetal monitoring.
Emergency C-section usually required.
donot: Do NOT perform vaginal examination if bleeding in pregnancy (placenta praevia possible).
seek: Immediate obstetric emergency.

title: Impetigo
warn: ⚠️ Highly contagious — avoid sharing towels.
steps: Topical fusidic acid or mupirocin for localized.
Oral antibiotics (flucloxacillin) for widespread.
Keep lesions clean and dry.
Avoid school/childcare until lesions crusted or 24hr on antibiotics.
donot: Do NOT scratch lesions.
seek: Widespread, periorbital, or not responding to topical treatment.

title: Necrotizing Fasciitis
warn: ⛔ "Flesh-eating bacteria" — 30-70% mortality. Rapid spread.
steps: Recognize: pain out of proportion, skin discoloration, bullae, crepitus, LRINEC score >6.
Call 112 immediately.
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Emergency surgical debridement.
ICU admission.
donot: Do NOT delay surgery.
seek: Immediate surgical emergency.

title: Sunburn
warn: ⚠️ Severe sunburn with blistering = 2nd degree thermal burn protocol.
steps: Cool water soak or cool compresses.
Oral ibuprofen for inflammation and pain.
Aloe vera gel topically.
Hydration: extra fluid intake.
Moisturizer.
Avoid further sun exposure until healed.
donot: Do NOT use butter or petroleum jelly.
Do NOT pop blisters.
seek: Blistering, fever, dehydration, or extensive areas.

title: Gastroenteritis
warn: ⚠️ Dehydration is the primary risk, especially in elderly and children.
steps: Oral rehydration solution (ORS) in small frequent sips.
BRAT diet once vomiting controlled.
Antiemetics (ondansetron) if available.
Avoid dairy and fatty foods.
Hand hygiene (especially norovirus — bleach surface cleaning).
donot: Do NOT give antidiarrheal medications to children under 2 or if bloody diarrhea (may indicate bacterial cause).
seek: Signs of dehydration, blood in stool, fever >38.5°C, >7 days, or extremes of age.

title: Migraine with Aura
warn: ⚠️ First severe "thunderclap" headache = subarachnoid hemorrhage until proven otherwise.
steps: Dark, quiet room.
Oral triptan (sumatriptan) taken at aura onset.
Aspirin/ibuprofen + antiemetic (metoclopramide).
Caffeine may help with analgesic-resistant migraine.
Hydration.
Ice pack to head.
donot: Do NOT delay if worst headache of life — CT needed.
seek: Thunderclap onset, fever + headache, first or worst ever, or neurological deficits.

title: Pneumonia — Community Acquired
warn: ⚠️ Use CURB-65 to risk stratify: confusion, urea, respiratory rate, BP, age >65.
steps: CURB-65 score: 0-1 = home, 2 = consider hospital, 3+ = hospital.
Antibiotics: amoxicillin ± clarithromycin.
Hydration.
Analgesics for pleuritic pain.
Supplemental O2 if SpO2 <94%.
Physiotherapy and deep breathing exercises.
donot: Do NOT give antitussives.
seek: CURB-65 ≥2, SpO2 <94%, unable to maintain oral intake.

title: Urinary Tract Infection
warn: ⚠️ Pyelonephritis (upper UTI) requires IV antibiotics. Any UTI in children = kidney imaging.
steps: Oral antibiotics: trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin (uncomplicated).
Increase fluid intake.
Phenazopyridine for symptom relief (turns urine orange).
Review urine culture results and adjust antibiotics if needed.
donot: Do NOT treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in non-pregnant adults.
seek: Fever, loin pain, or rigors (pyelonephritis). UTI in men, children, or pregnant women.

title: Cellulitis vs DVT Differential
warn: ⚠️ DVT and cellulitis can coexist — suspect DVT with D-dimer and ultrasound.
steps: Assess: warmth, erythema, tenderness (cellulitis); swelling, calf pain (DVT).
Antibiotics for cellulitis.
Anticoagulation for DVT.
Wells score for DVT probability.
Duplex ultrasound if DVT suspected.
donot: Do NOT elevate infected cellulitis (may worsen)... actually elevation IS appropriate.
Do NOT miss concurrent DVT.
seek: Bilateral, suspected DVT, or systemic symptoms.

title: Tennis/Golfers Elbow
warn: ⚠️ Steroid injections provide short-term benefit but may worsen long-term.
steps: Rest from aggravating activity.
Ice 15-20 min x3/day.
Ibuprofen/naproxen.
Physiotherapy: eccentric strengthening exercises.
Tennis elbow brace/strap.
Steroid injection for refractory (short-term).
donot: Do NOT return to sport too quickly.
seek: Progressive weakness, numbness, or no improvement after 6 weeks.

title: Neonatal Jaundice
warn: ⚠️ Bilirubin >25 mg/dL = kernicterus risk (permanent brain damage).
steps: Assess jaundice: appears day 1 or extreme = pathological.
Transcutaneous bilirubin measurement.
Ensure adequate feeding (breast or formula) — 8-12 feeds/day.
Phototherapy if bilirubin at threshold on nomogram.
Exchange transfusion for extreme hyperbilirubinemia.
donot: Do NOT sunbathe newborn as treatment.
seek: Jaundice in first 24 hours, level rising rapidly, unwell infant.

title: Hyperemesis Gravidarum
warn: ⚠️ Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency if prolonged.
steps: IV fluid rehydration (Hartmanns or NS with antiemetics).
Thiamine 100mg IV before dextrose.
IV ondansetron, metoclopramide, or promethazine.
Small frequent meals, avoid triggers.
Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) supplement.
Ginger supplements may help mild cases.
donot: Do NOT give dextrose before thiamine.
seek: Weight loss >5%, unable to tolerate any oral intake, ketonuria.

title: Acute Psychosis
warn: ⚠️ Safety first — patient and others. De-escalation before medication.
steps: Ensure safety: remove sharp objects, maintain distance, do NOT corner patient.
Calm, non-threatening voice.
Do NOT argue with delusions.
Call emergency services if danger to self or others.
Hospital: antipsychotics (haloperidol, olanzapine) + benzodiazepine if agitated.
donot: Do NOT argue about delusions.
Do NOT leave agitated patient alone if possible.
seek: All first episode psychosis, violence risk, self-neglect, or substance withdrawal.

title: Cyanide Poisoning
warn: ⛔ Classic: smell of bitter almonds. Rapid unconsciousness.
steps: Remove from exposure with PPE.
Call 112 and National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117).
High-flow O2.
Antidote: hydroxocobalamin 5g IV (Cyanokit) immediately.
If not available: dicobalt edetate or sodium thiosulfate.
CPR if indicated.
donot: Do NOT administer nitrites in smoke inhalation victims (may worsen CO poisoning).
seek: Immediate emergency.

title: High Voltage Electrical Injury
warn: ⛔ Internal injuries far exceed visible burns. Cardiac monitoring mandatory.
steps: Ensure power is off.
CPR if indicated.
Spinal precautions — thrown by arc flash.
Cardiac monitoring (48 hours).
IV fluids — higher than Parkland Formula (significant deep tissue injury).
Check urine myoglobin.
Fasciotomy for compartment syndrome.
donot: Do NOT underestimate injury from small entry/exit wounds.
seek: All high-voltage injuries require hospital admission.

title: Temporomandibular Disorder
warn: ⚠️ Usually benign — but acute locked jaw may require specialist reduction.
steps: Soft diet.
NSAIDs (ibuprofen 400mg TDS).
Warm compress to jaw.
Night guard for bruxism.
Gentle jaw exercises.
Physiotherapy referral.
donot: Do NOT chew gum.
Do NOT open mouth wide until symptoms settle.
seek: Acute locked jaw, significant trauma, or if infection suspected.

title: Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever
warn: ⚠️ Dengue shock syndrome: plasma leakage, hemorrhage, shock. Critical phase day 4-6.
steps: Recognize: high fever, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, rash, thrombocytopenia.
Oral rehydration for mild.
IV fluids for warning signs (bleeding, vomiting, rapid breathing, lethargy).
Paracetamol for fever ONLY.
Monitor platelets closely.
donot: Do NOT give aspirin or ibuprofen (hemorrhage risk).
seek: Warning signs: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, rapid breathing, bleeding, lethargy.

title: Bell Palsy
warn: ⚠️ Upper AND lower face affected = LMN lesion (Bells). Only lower = UMN (Stroke). Rule out stroke.
steps: Oral prednisolone 50mg/day x 10 days (start within 72 hours of onset).
Aciclovir if Ramsey Hunt suspected.
Eye protection: lubricating drops, moisture chamber, tape eyelid shut at night.
Physiotherapy: facial exercises.
donot: Do NOT assume facial weakness = Bell palsy without excluding stroke.
seek: If also hearing loss, vesicles, forehead spared, or young with stroke risk factors.

title: Peptic Ulcer — Perforated
warn: ⛔ Rigid board-like abdomen = peritonitis. Surgical emergency.
steps: Recognize: sudden onset severe epigastric pain, board-like rigid abdomen.
Call 112.
NPO.
IV fluids.
IV antibiotics.
Emergency surgical repair (laparotomy).
donot: Do NOT give oral medication.
seek: Immediate surgical emergency.

title: Human Bite
warn: ⚠️ Fight bites over metacarpal joints penetrate into joint space — risk of septic arthritis.
steps: Irrigate with saline under high pressure.
Debride dead tissue.
Do NOT close wound primarily.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics (co-amoxiclav) covering Eikenella and streptococci.
Tetanus prophylaxis.
Surgical irrigation if joint penetration suspected.
donot: Do NOT close human bite wounds.
seek: All clenched fist injuries over knuckles. Any sign of joint involvement.

title: Epiglottitis — Adult
warn: ⛔ Rapidly fatal airway obstruction. "Thumb sign" on lateral X-ray.
steps: Recognize: sore throat out of proportion to exam, drooling, muffled voice, tripod position.
Do NOT examine throat without airway management available.
Call 112 and head to nearest emergency department.
IV antibiotics: ceftriaxone.
Airway management: anaesthetist for intubation in theatre.
donot: Do NOT examine throat.
seek: Immediate emergency department.

title: Cauda Equina Syndrome
warn: ⛔ Saddle anaesthesia + bowel/bladder dysfunction = SURGICAL EMERGENCY within 24h.
steps: Recognize: saddle anaesthesia (inner thighs/perineum), urinary retention or incontinence, bilateral leg weakness.
Call 112.
Urgent MRI spine.
Emergency surgical decompression within 24 hours.
donot: Do NOT delay imaging.
seek: Immediate emergency for any suspected cauda equina syndrome.

title: Toxic Shock Syndrome
warn: ⛔ Remove tampon/foreign body immediately. Mortality 5-15%.
steps: Remove tampon or foreign body immediately.
Call 112.
IV fluids aggressively.
IV antibiotics: clindamycin + flucloxacillin.
IV immunoglobulin for severe Strep TSS.
ICU admission.
donot: Do NOT leave tampon in.
seek: Immediate emergency.

title: Beta-Blocker Overdose
warn: ⚠️ High-dose insulin euglycemia therapy (HIET) is increasingly used.
steps: Call National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117) and 112.
IV fluids.
Glucagon 5-10mg IV bolus — antidote for bradycardia.
Atropine for bradycardia.
Calcium chloride.
High-dose insulin euglycemia (HIET).
Lipid emulsion therapy for refractory arrest.
donot: Do NOT use beta-agonists as first line.
seek: Immediate emergency.

title: Black Widow Spider Bite
warn: ⚠️ Systemic effects (latrodectism): severe muscle cramps, diaphoresis, hypertension.
steps: Clean bite site.
Ice pack.
Call National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117).
Analgesics: opioids for severe pain.
Calcium gluconate IV (10ml of 10%) for muscle cramps — controversial.
Antivenom for severe/systemic cases.
Benzodiazepines for muscle spasm.
donot: Do NOT incise bite site.
seek: Systemic symptoms, hypertensive crisis, or in children/elderly.

title: Ebola/Viral Hemorrhagic Fever
warn: ⛔ Highly contagious. Full PPE required. Report to public health authorities.
steps: Isolate patient immediately.
Full PPE: gown, gloves, face shield, N95/respirator.
Contact public health authorities.
Supportive care: IV fluids, antiemetics, analgesics.
Specific antiviral treatment (remdesivir, mAbs) per outbreak protocol.
donot: Do NOT expose unprotected staff.
seek: Immediate isolation and public health reporting.

title: Meconium Aspiration Syndrome
warn: ⛔ If meconium-stained amniotic fluid and infant not vigorous: intubate, suction, NICU.
steps: Assess at birth: is infant vigorous? (strong cry, good muscle tone, HR >100).
If vigorous: routine care only.
If not vigorous: move to radiant warmer, suction mouth/nose, intubate and suction trachea.
PPV if still bradycardic after stimulation.
NICU admission.
donot: Do NOT stimulate before suctioning if not vigorous.
seek: All meconium aspiration with respiratory distress.

title: Metformin Overdose/Lactic Acidosis
warn: ⚠️ Serum lactate >5mmol/L = severe. Hemodialysis is definitive treatment.
steps: Call National Poison Information Centre (1800-116-117).
IV fluids.
IV sodium bicarbonate for severe acidosis.
Hemodialysis for elevated metformin levels, renal failure, or severe lactic acidosis.
Vasopressors for shock.
donot: Do NOT delay dialysis in severe cases.
seek: Immediate emergency.

title: Cord Prolapse
warn: ⛔ Every minute cord is compressed reduces fetal survival. Call 112 IMMEDIATELY.
steps: Call 112 immediately.
If cord visible at vagina: place mother in knee-chest position OR Trendelenburg.
Elevate presenting part off cord with gloved hand inside vagina.
Do NOT attempt to replace cord.
Maintain hand position maintaining pressure until emergency C-section.
100% O2 to mother.
donot: Do NOT wrap cord.
Do NOT attempt to replace cord.
seek: Immediate surgical emergency — C-section within minutes.
